- [Transgrancanaria 128 km 2020 | Toughest one Yet?](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/transgrancanaria-128-km-2020): Blog Running Running Transgrancanaria 128 km 2020 | Toughest one Yet? Stephen Cousins 22 March 2020 13 min read I swear they looked at every kilometre of the Transgrancanaria 128km Classic and asked themselves how they could piss off the runners even more at each point in the race. My running buddy Richard and I have run some pretty tough mountain ultras in our time. Transvulcania three times, Tenerife Bluetrail and CCC in Chamonix stick out as particular highlights, along with my DNF at TDS last year. We know a little bit about this ultra running, skyracing malarkey. It’s safe to say the Transgrancanaria Classic is right up there as one of the killer mountain ultras in the world. It is part of the Ultra World Tour and is well attended by the elite running community. 2019 UTMB Champion, Pau Capell has won this race for the last two years and was there towing the line again. Also running was Harry Jones from the UK who finished 15th at UTMB last year and Dylan Bowman from the USA. Kaci Licteg and Kathryn Gerbin were in the women’s race along with Azara Garcia from Spain. In recognition of International Women’s Day, this year the race adopted a mini rebrand of its logo with a woman featured in the image and a new tag line, Trail is Female. They also made sure the elite women started at the front of the race, normally dominated by the elite men. An acknowledgment that we need to increase the ratio of men to women taking part in ultra races. Richard and I didn’t actually see any of this because we were a good few metres back in the Zone 2 starting pen. As usual, we had conned our wives into believing that this would be a great family holiday and so both families arrived in Gran Canaria for a week of sun, with the added bonus of a stupid hard ultra run thrown in for the dads. We had booked a hotel very near the finish line in the south of the island at Maspalomas. On the night of the race we caught an official bus to the start, which left at 8pm from outside the expo, where we had collected our numbers. The expo was not spectacular at all when we were there, although it may have been busier and more exciting the day after. The bus took us all the way from the south to the start line in the north at Las Palmas. It’s around an hour’s journey and they are always nervy affairs. People trying to catch some sleep. Not much talking, anxious faces. It’s a pensive time. We did get chatting with Toby from the UK who is relatively new to ultra running. I was surprised he had chosen this race so early in his ultra career. The three of us went to Starbucks on our arrival in Las Palmas to while away an hour. I have recently taken to drinking Oat milk lattes. Before long though, we joined the masses gathered on the beach. Some 800 runners were going to attempt this and only just over 50% would succeed. There are a number of races to enter during Transgrancanaria week. The longest is the TGC 360 which is 268km . There’s also the 65km Advanced race, a Marathon and the Starter 30km race and even a 17km run. But the 128km Classic is the stellar event. Many of these big races start with rock music blaring out of the speakers. Transvulcania in particular is very good at this ramping up the intensity at the start. In contrast, we had a Male voice choir at the start of TGC! It was good though and we still had the familiar voices of Eoin Flynn and Depa building up the excitement until the start at 11pm. Richard and I set off together but he was away from me before we even got off the beach. The first 500 metres or so is on the sand and then it’s up on to the promenade for the next 3k. The elite guys are pushing this out at 3:50 per kilometre. That’s my 5k pace! I set off at a rather more sedate speed. The first few kilometres is taken up with exiting the urban sprawl that is Las Palmas. Our new friend Toby came past me early on during one of the first climbs. I was sticking to my plan. Having looked at the cut offs and the elevation, I decided to start out at 24 hour pace. There’s an app called LiveRun which I used to set up the required splits to get me to a 24 hour finish. At each checkpoint I would look at it to make sure I was hitting the times. This worked really well for the first half of the race. During the night section there’s obviously not much of a view to look at, so it’s just a case of getting to the next aid station. For the first half of the race each checkpoint is around 12km apart and I had between two and two and a half hours to get to them, depending on the severity of the climbing and the technical nature of the terrain. Early on there’s a pretty grim dry river bed which is stony and difficult to run on. Other than that, underfoot the first 50km is relatively easy running. The weather was colder than I had expected and I kept my waterproof on for the whole night section. It didn’t rain but there was drizzle and a cold wind for much of the night. I was finding that I was just about hitting my splits without over exerting myself. That was about to change though. Daylight arrived as I was descending into and then climbing out of a spectacular valley. I was loving it. But Richard was over an hour ahead of me by now and Toby was over 30 minutes ahead. Still I stuck to my plan. Eventually it was time to take my head torch and jacket off and don my sunglasses. There wasn’t a cloud in the sky and it was going to be a scorcher off a day. As we climbed higher, the trail became more beautiful. We were running through forests with sunlight glinting through the trees and views out over the mountains and valleys to the sea. But it was getting hot and the climbs were getting steeper and more technical. There’s a big difference between climbing or descending a mountain where the ground underfoot is flat and smooth and ground which is strewn with loose stones, tree roots, sharp volcanic rock and uneven steps. It slows you down enormously. If you are elite or just very confident, you might be able to fly down the
- [Transgrancanaria Classic 2022 | Snow in the Canaries](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/transgrancanaria-classic-2022): Blog Race Reports Race Reports Transgrancanaria Classic 2022 | Snow in the Canaries Stephen Cousins 4 March 2022 12 min read In Brief 125km across Gran Canaria. I expected sunshine and stunning views. Instead, I got the worst weather conditions I've ever raced in - freezing rain, howling winds, and temperatures so cold that runners were dropping out in droves at the mountain checkpoints. Nearly 27 hours of suffering, but I made it. 125km Distance 6,439m Elevation 26:46 Finish Time 800+ Starters I would never have believed it could be that cold in Gran Canaria. The Canary Islands sit off the coast of Africa. They're supposed to be warm. That's literally why people go there - for the sunshine, the beaches, the reliable weather. When I signed up for the Transgrancanaria Classic, I imagined running through volcanic landscapes under clear skies, with stunning views down to the Atlantic. What I got instead was one of the most brutal weather experiences of my ultrarunning career. The Calm Before This was my second Transgrancanaria. The race covers 125 kilometres from Las Palmas in the north of the island to Maspalomas in the south, crossing the mountainous interior with over 6,000 metres of climbing. It starts at 11pm - you run through the night, through the following day, and hopefully finish before midnight on day two. Standing at the start line among 800 runners, I knew the forecast mentioned "a little bit gnarly" weather at altitude. What I didn't appreciate was quite how gnarly things would get. Into the Night The first few hours went smoothly enough. We climbed away from the coast under clear skies, the lights of Las Palmas fading behind us. By the time I reached Fontanales at 31 kilometres - nearly five hours in - the first signs of trouble were appearing. Rain. Not heavy, but persistent. And mud. So much mud. The trails that should have been dusty and fast had turned into a slippery mess. Every descent became an exercise in damage limitation, trying not to fall while simultaneously trying not to destroy my quads with constant braking. This Is Not What You Expect Dawn broke to reveal a very different Gran Canaria than the one I'd imagined. Grey clouds hung low over the mountains. Rain fell steadily. The wind had picked up and showed no signs of stopping. At 55 kilometres, I remember looking at my watch and thinking: this is going to be a very long day. But even in the gloom, I couldn't deny the beauty. I came down through a valley I remembered from my previous Transgrancanaria, when I'd descended it in near-darkness. This time I could see it properly - the steep green walls, the winding trail, the occasional glimpse of peaks above the clouds. Stunning, even if I was too cold to fully appreciate it. The one silver lining? The British runners seemed to be faring better than the Spanish. They weren't used to this. We were. Cold, wet, windy - that's just a normal training run back home. "The wind was howling. It was freezing. It was raining. And runners were dropping out everywhere." Artenara: The Breaking Point I reached Artenara at 67 kilometres, just over halfway, and found a scene I hadn't expected. The aid station was full of runners who'd decided they'd had enough. Not injured, not sick - just broken by the conditions. The wind at altitude was ferocious. The rain had turned to near-sleet. Hypothermia was a genuine risk. I was seriously cold. I'd come prepared for warm weather, not this. A kind stranger named John lent me his gloves - a small act of kindness that quite possibly kept me in the race. Standing there, warming my hands around a cup of soup, I had to make a decision. Press on into the storm, or join the growing list of DNFs? I've never been afraid to pull out of a race when it makes sense. There's no shame in a smart withdrawal. But I wasn't there yet. Not quite. Over the Top The climb out of Artenara was brutal - wind howling, visibility poor, every step a battle. But then something shifted. As we crested the high point and began the descent towards the south side of the island, the weather started to change. First just hints - occasional glimpses of blue sky, the faintest warmth of sun on my legs. Then, gradually, properly. The clouds began to break. The rain stopped. And suddenly, there it was: the view I'd been promised all along. Valleys dropping away below me. Mountains rolling towards the coast. And there, in the distance across the sea, Tenerife - with Mount Teide, the highest peak in Spain, rising 3,500 metres into the clear sky. That's what we should have had all day. That's what Transgrancanaria is supposed to look like. The Final Push With 42 kilometres still to go - a full marathon - my legs were wrecked. The mud and the descents had done their damage. Running downhill had become genuinely painful, and even the flats required effort I didn't feel I had left to give. But the worst was behind me. The weather held. The trail wound down through increasingly lush terrain - volcanic rock giving way to greenery, eventually feeling almost tropical. The final aid station came and went. Just 14 kilometres remained, most of it downhill to the coast. The descent felt endless. Technical in places, requiring concentration I could barely muster. By the time I reached the outskirts of Maspalomas, darkness had fallen for the second time. I'd been moving for nearly 27 hours. The Finish My family had waited. Despite the delay, despite my optimistic prediction of "midnight tomorrow" turning into something far later, they were there at the finish line. I crossed the line in 26 hours and 46 minutes. Not the time I'd hoped for - I'd been targeting 24 hours - but given the conditions, I was just grateful to have finished at all. "Thank you for staying," I said to Victoria. "I'm sorry I'm so late." That was the hardest Transgrancanaria has ever been. The organisers later confirmed it was some of the worst weather in the race's history. Runners with far more experience than me had called 
- [The Liberating Experience of Running Without a Watch](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/the-liberating-experience-of-running-without-a-watch): Blog Running Running The Liberating Experience of Running Without a Watch Stephen Cousins 26 March 2023 6 min read Have you ever considered running without a watch? No, not literally running naked, but leaving your trusty timepiece at home and just enjoying the experience of running without the burden of tracking your pace, heart rate, and other metrics. It may sound crazy, but hear me out. As runners, we are constantly bombarded with data and numbers. We obsess over our splits, our heart rate zones, and our pacing strategy. It's as if we're wearing a psychological straightjacket that limits our enjoyment of the run. But what if we could break free from this constraint and just run for the pure joy of it? Recently, I tried running a half marathon without looking at my watch, and it was a liberating experience. Instead of constantly checking my pace, I was able to focus on my surroundings and enjoy the feeling of running fast. Here's a breakdown of my experience and why I think every runner should try running without a watch at least once: The Straightjacket of a Watch We're so used to relying on our watches to dictate our pace and effort level that we forget to listen to our bodies. We train with goal paces in mind and lock into specific paces for different types of runs. We check our heart rate zones to make sure we're in the right zone. We glance down at our watch and adjust our pace accordingly, even if it means deviating from our natural rhythm. By running without a watch, I was able to break free from this constraint. I had no feedback on how fast or slow I was going, and it was surprisingly liberating. I could focus on my surroundings and enjoy the feeling of running fast without worrying about hitting a specific pace. The Mind-Body Connection There's a strong connection between our mind and body, and we often forget that they don't function independently. By running without a watch, I was able to reconnect with my body and listen to its cues. I could tell when I was running fast, and I knew when to settle into a comfortable pace. I also noticed that my effort level remained consistent throughout the race in terms of heart rate. It gradually rose during the race and spiked towards the end when I could smell the finish line. But overall, I was able to maintain a steady effort level without constantly adjusting my pace based on my watch. The Freedom to Run Fast When we're tied to our watches, we tend to be more conservative in our pacing strategy. We tell ourselves not to be a hero, not to go off too fast, and to stick to the plan. But by running without a watch, I was able to let go of these constraints and just run fast. I didn't have to worry about hitting a specific pace, so I could start fast and settle into a comfortable rhythm. I could let go of the fear of going too fast and just enjoy the feeling of running fast. [embedyt] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zalac7m4Wbk[/embedyt] The Results So, what were the results of running without looking at my watch? Well, I finished the Surrey Half Marathon in 1 hour 24 minutes and 10 seconds, which was faster than I thought I was going. In fact, the last 10k was faster than my official 10K PB of 39 minutes and 43 seconds. But more importantly, I enjoyed the experience of running without checking the watch every few seconds! I was able to focus on my surroundings and connect with my body. I was able to let go of the burden of tracking my pace and just enjoy the feeling of running fast. Conclusion Running without a watch may sound crazy, but it's an experience that every runner should try at least once. By breaking free from the constraints of tracking our pace, we can reconnect with our bodies and enjoy the pure joy of running. We can let go of the fear of going too fast and just run fast for the sheer pleasure of it. Of course, I'm not suggesting that you should throw away your watch altogether. Tracking your progress and seeing your improvement over time can be incredibly motivating. But by running without a watch every now and then, you can reconnect with the joy of running and remind yourself why you fell in love with the sport in the first place. So, the next time you lace up your running shoes, why not leave your watch at home and just enjoy the freedom of running without constraints? Who knows, you may surprise yourself with what you're capable of achieving. And if you're still not convinced, here are some FAQs that may help: FAQs What if I get lost without my watch? Well, as long as you know the route, you should be fine. And if you're worried about getting lost, you can always use a phone app to track your distance and time. How will I know if I'm improving without tracking my pace? You can still track your progress by timing yourself on certain routes or comparing your times from previous races. And remember, running isn't just about improving your pace. It's also about enjoying the experience and feeling good. What if I slow down too much and don't finish in time? Unless you're running a race with a strict time limit, there's no need to worry about finishing in a specific time. Just enjoy the experience and focus on finishing strong. Can I still use my watch for safety reasons? Of course! If you're running in an unfamiliar area, it's always a good idea to have a watch or phone app to track your distance and time. Safety should always be a top priority. What if I can't resist the urge to check my watch? That's okay! It's a habit that's hard to break. But try to resist the urge as much as possible and focus on the experience of running. And remember, it's okay to run without a watch every now and then.
- [Autumn 100 2023: Today is a Good Day](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/autumn-100-2023-today-is-a-good-day): Blog Running Running Autumn 100 2023: Today is a Good Day Stephen Cousins 14 October 2023 7 min read In Brief The final race of our Centurion Grand Slam—four 100-milers in one year. Victoria had been throwing up since mile 44, but nothing was going to stop her completing what she'd set out to achieve. 27 hours and 20 minutes of fighting, suffering, and ultimately, triumph. 27:20:04 Finish Time 100mi Distance 4 of 4 Grand Slam 64th Ultra Thames Path was mud. South Downs Way was absolutely boiling hot. North Downs Way was rain, rain, rain. But the Autumn 100? It looked like today might just be a good day for running. Sunshine most of the way, cold but perfect conditions. Everyone told us the Autumn 100 would be easy. It's your victory lap, they said. Little did we know what Victoria would have to go through. The Grand Slam Every runner completing their fourth race of the Centurion Grand Slam gets a red number with a black background, so marshals and other runners can identify and cheer on those attempting the full slam. Victoria and I had earned those red numbers. Four hundred-milers in one year: Thames Path, South Downs Way, North Downs Way, and now Autumn. Race day begins The Autumn 100 is unique among the Centurion races. It's four out-and-back spurs of roughly 25 miles each, all starting and finishing at Goring Village Hall. You get access to your drop bag every time you return—a luxury compared to the other races. "This is the beauty of ultra running. You can't be certain how it's going to turn out. So much can happen between miles one and 100." A Good Start We set off in good spirits. The first leg headed north along the Thames Path—a section we knew well from the Thames Path 100, though we'd only ever run it in darkness before. It was lovely to see it in daylight, watching the Oxford University boat crews training on the river. We were running at the back of the field, but exactly where we needed to be time-wise. At the turnaround, only three runners were behind us out of 200-odd starters. But we weren't here to race. We were here to finish. Back at Goring after leg one, we saw Ken Fancett—a 74-year-old about to complete his 100th 100-mile race. An inspiration to us all. When Things Went Wrong Leg two took us east onto the Ridgeway, Britain's oldest road—5,000 years of history under our feet. We were more fatigued than expected. The long summer of ultras, plus recovering from COVID six weeks earlier, was catching up with us. Taking in the views And then, around mile 40, Victoria started being sick. From that point onwards, she couldn't keep anything down. Water, food, gels—everything came back up. We tried different things, hoping something would settle. Nothing worked. "Victoria has had just the most torrid time. She's constantly throwing up. She can't keep anything down. It's hard work, but she is absolutely determined to get this finished." The Long Night At the Chain Hill turnaround—the western end of leg three—the aid station offered Ukrainian vodka with honey and chilli, or cherry liqueur. Not exactly what Victoria needed. 50 kilometres remained. 31 miles. Nine and a half hours to complete them. The maths said we'd make it, but Victoria was suffering badly. At 3:30 in the morning, we still had a marathon to run. By 5am, we'd started the final leg along the Thames Path towards Reading. Victoria was still throwing up. I finally joined her, losing my stomach at the Reading checkpoint. My first issues of the whole race, just as we entered the final stretch. The Final Push The sun rose on a spectacular morning. Ethereal mist lifted from the river. For a moment, it was serene and otherworldly—a reward for surviving the night. The journey continues At Pangbourne, our friend Jaco knew exactly what we needed. A pint of full-fat milk for me. A mug of Earl Grey tea for Victoria. Sometimes it's the simple things. With less than 10k to go, we were going to finish. There was no question now. We could walk it in and still make the cutoff. "If you have ever thought about running 100 miles, or an ultra, or even starting with your first 5k—do it today. Because today is a good day." Grand Slam Complete We crossed the line at Goring Village Hall. 27 hours and 20 minutes. The Grand Slam was complete. 2023 had been an incredible year for Victoria: three marathons in three weeks across three countries (including Boston and London), followed by four 100-milers. Having never run 100 miles before this year, she'd now completed four of them—and done so at age 50. "If I can do it, anyone can," she said at the finish. "We need more people, particularly women, running these races. Not for the medal or the T-shirt, but for the challenge. Because we can achieve things we never thought possible." There's no time to borrow. Your time is now. Today is a good day. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [London Marathon 2022: One Race, Two Medals](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/london-marathon-2022-one-race-two-medals): Blog Running Running London Marathon 2022: One Race, Two Medals Stephen Cousins 2 October 2022 6 min read In Brief London Marathon 2022, my fifth, coming off the back of Lakeland 100, TDS, Ben Nevis Ultra, and Berlin Marathon. I wanted Good for Age (sub-3:15) but had to learn from Berlin's mistakes. Finished in 3:23:12—a minute faster than Berlin, more controlled, and with two medals: London and the Abbott World Marathon Majors Age Group Championship. 3:23:12 Finish Time 42.2km Distance 4,467th Position 5th London Marathon How can you train for an ultra distance mountain race and a flat fast road marathon at the same time? Actually, scratch that—is it possible to train for multiple ultra distance mountain races back to back and then two flat road marathons in quick succession? The answer depends on your goals. If all you want is to finish, you've got every chance. But if you really want to perform? Good luck with that. The Summer That Wouldn't End I arrived at London 2022 off the back of a ridiculous summer: Lakeland 100 in July (100 miles, 5,000m of elevation), TDS in August (145km with 9,000m of ascent), Ben Nevis Ultra in September (53km, 4,000m climbing), and Berlin Marathon a week before London where I'd foolishly gone out at sub-3 pace and died a slow death. Race day begins So when I lined up in London, I was determined to be more disciplined. The problem was, I really wanted that Good for Age qualification—sub-3:15. A risk, but one worth taking. "I was supposed to put my predicted finish time on my application and I neglected to do so. Which means I've been put in wave 14. An official actually suggested I jump into an earlier wave. So that's exactly what I did." The Accidental Front Runner Due to my application error, I found myself in the no-man's land between blue waves five and six. The streets of London were deserted—I'd never seen anything like it on marathon day. For a brief, surreal moment, I felt like I was leading the London Marathon. Taking in the views 5km in just under 23 minutes, down the big opening downhill. 10km in 46 minutes as we passed the Cutty Sark. "Wave to the cameras live on TV," I joked. "We're not live on TV because they're following the leaders, aren't they." The Dodging Game Congestion became an issue as I caught up with the earlier waves. "This is ridiculous, Andrew," I lamented to my club mate as I squeezed past. "You just can't get a rhythm, can you?" The journey continues 15km in 1:09:30—still on pace for 3:15 but already doubting my legs would last. 20km in 1:33 over Tower Bridge, the most iconic moment of the London Marathon. Halfway in 1:37:30—only just on target. The Isle of Dogs Reality Check Heading into the Isle of Dogs, the support thinned out and the mental battle began. By Canary Wharf—where your GPS watch goes haywire among the skyscrapers—my legs told me they'd had enough. 25km in 1:56. The 3:15 dream was fading. 30km at 2:20. The Good for Age qualification was gone for another year. But we found the Run Dem Crew outside Limehouse Town Hall, and Zac the extreme DJ was in the house. If we couldn't have the time, at least we could have the party. "I did slow after 20 miles, but it wasn't so much of a slow as Berlin. The race was much more controlled. I felt stronger towards the end." The Finish 35km in 2:45—exactly the same as Berlin. But this time I pushed through the tunnel, past the London Eye and Westminster Palace with more purpose. 40km in 3:12. Along Birdcage Walk, towards Buckingham Palace, and finally onto The Mall. 3:23:12. A minute faster than Berlin. More controlled. And with an unexpected bonus: the Abbott Age Group Championship medal. Not for winning an age group—just for participating in the World Championships. One race, two medals. In St James's Park afterwards, space blankets fluttering, medals glinting in the sunshine, I reflected on the madness of my summer schedule. Five London Marathons now. The finish line is always special, no matter what time you achieve. 26.2 miles is an iconic distance, and London remains one of the great races. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [UTMB 100 2023: Seven Years in the Making](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/utmb-100-2023-seven-years-in-the-making): Blog Running Running UTMB 100 2023: Seven Years in the Making Stephen Cousins 1 September 2023 8 min read In Brief Seven years after deciding I wanted to run UTMB, I finally made it to the start line—and 44 hours, 47 minutes later, I crossed the most iconic finish line in ultrarunning. It wasn't pretty: stomach issues, throwing up repeatedly, and a moment at Arnouvaz where I genuinely wanted to quit. But I earned that gilet. 44:47:11 Finish Time 170km Distance 10,217m Elevation 16th Hundred Miler This journey started seven years ago when I decided I wanted to run UTMB. And finally, after years of watching from the sidelines, filming others crossing that finish line, dreaming about my own moment—this was the day. Now was the time. Race day begins Standing at the start in Chamonix, the atmosphere was electric. The thunderclap rang out across the square, and the announcer began his countdown. This is the most iconic race in the world. The place to be. The best race you will ever run. The Start The first 8km to Les Houches was a whirlwind—flat but incredibly congested. I chatted with runners, tried to stay calm, reminded myself that we were barely scratching the surface of what lay ahead. At Les Houches, I topped up my bottles. We hadn't done any climbing yet. The leaders were already disappearing into the distance. La Fouly. Champex Lac, where I threw up fizzy water but managed to keep down pasta bolognese. Three more climbs, all around 800 metres. A long night ahead. At Trient, as dawn broke on day three, I threw up again. But something had shifted. The new day brought new hope. My stomach was starting to settle. The worst was behind me. Taking in the views The Final Push By Valorcine—the last stop before the final climb—I was feeling great. Well, my feet were wrecked, but mentally I was flying. I'd even stopped at a café for coffee and Perrier. I couldn't wait to finish. The 900-metre climb to La Flegere was hard work. I bumped into Herbert from Zwift, who'd had to pull out of CCC with breathing issues. We walked together for a bit before I made the final push. Then the descent into Chamonix. A couple of kilometres of tarmac, people lining the streets, cheering us home. The best finish line in the world. "You don't get a medal or a buckle at UTMB. You get a gilet. And I tell you what—I'd well and truly earned that one. Friday, Saturday, Sunday." The journey continues What It Meant 44 hours and 47 minutes. Three days. Countless moments of doubt. Multiple episodes of throwing up. One full-body river immersion. And finally, finally, the gilet. Earlier that week, I'd watched Courtney Dauwalter complete her triple crown—UTMB, Hard Rock, and Western States all in the same year. I'd seen Jim Walmsley finally realise his dream, breaking Kilian's course record in 19:37. The greatest week in ultrarunning. And somewhere in among all that elite brilliance, I'd achieved my own seven-year goal. Not fast. Not pretty. But done. What a race. What a week. See you all in 2024. Pushing through Watch the Video Strava Activity

- [Berlin Marathon 2022: How NOT to Pace a Marathon](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/berlin-marathon-2022-how-not-to-pace-a-marathon): Blog Running Running Berlin Marathon 2022: How NOT to Pace a Marathon Stephen Cousins 25 September 2022 5 min read In Brief What you are about to read is the perfect example of how NOT to pace a marathon. Berlin 2022: started at sub-3 pace despite legs being wrecked from Lakeland 100, TDS, and Ben Nevis Ultra. By 5km I knew I'd made a terrible mistake. By 15km I was just trying to survive. Finished in 3:24:19, watching Kipchoge break the world record on the same day. 3:24:19 Finish Time 42.2km Distance 3,893rd Position 81st Marathon It was a surprise when I was selected in the ballot for the Berlin Marathon. The race had to be slotted in at the end of a calendar already full of very long, very mountainous races: Lakeland 100, TDS, Ben Nevis Ultra. My legs were shot to pieces. But this is Berlin! One of the fastest marathon courses in the world, with one of the most iconic finishes through the Brandenburg Gate. I'd be a fool not to go for another sub-3, right? The Delusional Optimism I arrived at the Expo at Templehof Airport—the old airport closed in 2008, now transformed into this fantastic space—tired and with battered legs, but with an inner confidence bordering on the delusional. Race morning: Coca-Cola and milk in my hotel room. The milk to drink now, the Coke decanted into small bottles for later in the race. I made my way to the start, found my club mates Phina and Charles, and tried to convince myself that everything would be fine. "Secretly I still think I can do sub-3 hours. My legs are shot to pieces after Lakeland 100, TDS, and Ben Nevis Ultra. It's just not going to happen. But secretly... I still think I can do it." The Inevitable Collapse I took off at sub-3 pace. By 5km, I had already accepted my fate. Like an idiot, I started out at 3-hour pace. My legs were in no fit state for it. By 10km, I'd slowed to 3:10-3:15 pace. By 15km, I was running 4:25-4:30 per kilometre, trying to stay relaxed but feeling my hamstrings and calves tighten with every step. Halfway in 1:34. "Very tired though," I told the camera. "It's not happening today at all. Just got to enjoy it." And that was the realisation I needed. If I couldn't get my goal time, the least I could do was embrace the experience. Learning to Enjoy It From around 25km onwards, I resolved to stop fighting and start enjoying. Berlin Marathon is about feeling part of something bigger—the wider community of running, the iconic city streets, the incredible atmosphere. 30km in 2:18. 35km in 2:45. I was still slowing, but I'd stopped caring about the splits. The sun came out in the final kilometres. I could sense the finish approaching. Phina appeared at the roadside: "Come on Stephen! You've got this! Rally, rally, rally!" I had no idea she was there—I was locked into the endgame, tunnel vision taking over. "The moral of the story is that confidence, experience, and even a delusional belief in your own ability are not enough. Race-specific training is vital." The Finish Into the final kilometre, I upped my speed for one of the most iconic marathon finishes in the world. Through the Brandenburg Gate, across the line. 3:24:19. Mixed feelings: joy, relief, disappointment. My splits were terrible, but I finished. My second Marathon Major was done. And on the same day, Kipchoge broke the marathon world record with 2:01:09. A reminder of what true marathon excellence looks like—and how far from it I was running. The Lesson After 140 marathons and ultras, I ought to know better. You need to be realistic about your goal time. Starting too fast doesn't just hurt your time—it ruins the entire experience. The whole thing was a struggle from kilometre 5, when I knew I'd gone out too hard. But it's still Berlin. Still one of the great World Marathon Majors. Still a beautiful city and an incredible race. And I'll know better next time. Probably. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Thames Path 100 2023: Victoria's First 100](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/thames-path-100-2023): Blog Running Running Thames Path 100 2023: Victoria's First 100 Stephen Cousins 6 May 2023 7 min read TL;DR Victoria's first ever 100-miler and our first Grand Slam race Run on King Charles's Coronation Day - bells ringing as we passed Windsor Castle 340 starters, only 207 finished - a 39% DNF rate due to relentless mud Oladance headphones lasted 16+ hours through rain and mud Finished 27:16:56 - just 44 minutes inside the 28-hour cutoff Not content with running three marathons in three weeks in three different countries the previous month, my wife Victoria had decided that now would be a great time to run her first 100-mile race. This was also to be the first race in our Centurion Grand Slam attempt - four 100-milers in one year. Having volunteered at the event the previous year, we rocked up at the start of the 2023 Centurion Thames Path 100 at Richmond Old Town Hall. The twelfth edition of the race would take 340 runners on a 100-mile journey along the Thames to Oxford. 27:16:56 Finish Time 186th Position 100 miles Distance 39% DNF Rate Coronation Day It was drizzling at the start - not absolutely pouring, but that light drizzle would rapidly become steady rain that persisted well into the evening. Our aim was around 24 hours, but we weren't bothered as long as we got in under the 28-hour cutoff. The Thames Path 100 is notorious for people going off too fast in the opening miles. We tried to remain disciplined with a walk-run strategy as we made our way through Kingston, past Hampton Court Palace, through Walton on Thames, past the lock gates at Sudbury and Bell Weir, and on towards Runnymede - site of the signing of the Magna Carta. "It's six and a half hours into the race and we're arriving in Windsor. It's the coronation of the King. There's Windsor Castle right there, and the bells are ringing out." Whatever your feelings about the monarchy, there's no denying the palpable sense of history that running along the Thames Path can elicit. I'd been listening to the coronation on the radio through my headphones, and it felt special to be passing Windsor Castle as the bells rang out for the new King. The Pain Cave Opens At Cookham aid station, 40 miles in, I was still managing to stuff my face with sandwiches, peanuts and crisps. However, Victoria was starting to go off her food and beginning to feel nauseous. At under halfway, this was concerning. Psychologically, this is a tough stage for many people. In a 100-miler, you've run quite a long way already, but you're not even halfway there. That can play on your mind. And when it's your first 100, you simply have no reference for how you're feeling - no experience of fighting through the negativity and coming out the other side. "Everything hurts. Absolutely hideous. Why did I think this was a good idea?" At Pangbourne - 66.6 miles, the number of the beast - Victoria had officially run further than ever before. The course had deteriorated considerably in the latter stages, with what the race director described as "epic" mud that severely tested finishers. A Race Against Time There was no let-up in the mud throughout the night and into the next morning. We'd kissed goodbye to the 24-hour goal some time before and were now beginning to worry about the cutoff. By quarter to six on Sunday morning, we had 36 miles to go and just over 7 hours to do it. The funny thing was that it was supposed to be me pacing Victoria, but more often than not during a walking break, it would be Victoria who started running first. She would leave aid stations before me, and I could see a steely determination in her face to get the job done no matter what. At Clifton Hampden - where I'd DNF'd on my first attempt years ago - we stayed only briefly. We had to keep moving. At the final aid station, Victoria was already on her way before I could catch up. She was running stronger than me. Inside the Cutoff With 3 miles to go, the path finally became a little easier and we gave it one last push. We passed a couple more runners as we crawled ever closer to Oxford. The first dropout in the race hadn't occurred until 5 hours 36 minutes in - remarkably resilient. But between miles 51 and 89, organisers lost a further 117 runners to the conditions. 27 hours, 16 minutes and 56 seconds. Just 44 minutes inside the cutoff. Only 207 runners finished of approximately 340 starters - a 39% DNF rate that was unheard of for this event. But Victoria and I made it. My Absolute Hero Crossing the finish line of a 100-mile race is a unique experience, and I felt an overwhelming sense of pride in Victoria's achievement. She is blessed with an unshakable drive and determination which had seen her complete the Paris, Boston and London marathons and now her first 100-mile race, all in less than six weeks. Meanwhile, at the front of the race, Geoff Cheshire had claimed victory in 14:18 - described as "a truly remarkable run" given conditions. Line Caliskaner from Norway dominated the women's race, winning in 17:02 despite a navigation error. Ninety-six runners achieved the coveted sub-24-hour buckle. One down, three to go. Victoria is my absolute hero.
- [Vanguard Way Marathon | First Race Back After Lockdown](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/vanguard-way-marathon-first-race-after-lockdown-2020): Blog Running Running Vanguard Way Marathon | First Race Back After Lockdown Stephen Cousins 2 August 2020 7 min read TL;DR My first official race since UK lockdown began. The Vanguard Way Marathon takes you 13 miles out through the fields and woodlands of South London, crossing under the M25, then turns you around for an identical return. Finished 7th in 4:15:33 - over an hour faster than my previous attempt four years earlier. 26.2 Miles 4:15:33 Finish Time 7th Place 1hr+ Improvement After months of lockdown, virtual races, and training on empty streets, the Vanguard Way Marathon represented something more than just 26.2 miles of trail. It was my first official race since the pandemic began - a return to something approaching normality in what had been an utterly abnormal year. I'd run this race four years earlier and it had been my slowest marathon ever. This was a chance at redemption. Lloyd Park, Croydon The race starts in Lloyd Park in Croydon, South London. From there, the route heads south through an unexpected corridor of green - fields, parks, and woodland that feel a world away from the city despite being firmly within the M25's embrace. The format is beautifully simple: 13 miles out, 13 miles back. You run until you hit the turnaround, then retrace your steps exactly. There's something psychologically satisfying about an out-and-back course - every landmark you pass in the first half becomes a countdown marker on the way home. COVID Protocols This was racing in the COVID era. Socially distanced starts, self-service at aid stations, filling up our own cups. It felt strange but also precious - the fact that we could race at all was something to be grateful for. The organisers had worked hard to make it safe, and there was an unspoken agreement among runners to respect the protocols. By 40 minutes I was through the first 4.5 miles, winding through the beautiful wooded sections that make this course special. Even with the M25 motorway visible below at points, there's a wildness to the Vanguard Way that surprises you. The Climb Every out-and-back trail race has a moment where you realise your earlier joy is about to become your later suffering. On the outward leg, there's a steep, slippery descent that feels almost reckless - you're trusting your footing on terrain that wants to send you sliding. Beautiful, but treacherous. "We came down earlier on, now it's payback time." On the way back, of course, that descent becomes the steepest, toughest climb on the course. By the time I hit it, I was already deep into the hurt locker. Payback, indeed. Chasing Seventh At 18 kilometres, the leaders came flying past on their return journey while I was still heading out. First and second place, moving with the kind of efficiency that makes you question your own efforts. But that's ultra running - you're rarely racing the leaders, you're racing yourself. By 37 kilometres, with 4 or 5 to go, I was flagging. The time showed 3:49, and while I knew I was in seventh position, the runner behind me wasn't far back. Navigation became crucial now - the Vanguard Way isn't the most clearly marked route, and four years earlier I'd added 4 kilometres through a wrong turn. Not this time. The Finish Crossing the line back at Lloyd Park in 4 hours 15 minutes, I was genuinely pleased. Seventh place in a trail marathon - top ten is always a good result. But more importantly, I'd run over an hour faster than my previous attempt. Same course (minus the navigation error), completely different athlete. Four years of consistent training, better nutrition, and race experience had transformed me from someone who survived marathons to someone who could race them. Watch the Film I captured my return to racing on film. Here's the full race video: The Route Back to Racing The Vanguard Way Marathon felt like a reset button. After months of uncertainty about whether racing would ever return, here was proof that it could. Adapted, socially distanced, but undeniably real. The effort was genuine, the finish line was there, and the satisfaction of completing something official felt disproportionately meaningful. The rest of 2020 would bring more races as organisers found ways to make events work within restrictions. But this one - my first since lockdown - will always hold a special place. It wasn't just a marathon. It was a reminder that we could still do this, that the community would find a way, that running would endure. Also, it was nice to finally put that four-year-old result to rest. Sometimes the best races aren't the fastest - they're the ones where you prove you've grown.
- [Paris Marathon 2021 | A Decade of Running the City of Light](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/paris-marathon-2021-decade-of-running): Blog Running Running Paris Marathon 2021 | A Decade of Running the City of Light Stephen Cousins 17 October 2021 8 min read TL;DR Our tenth consecutive Paris Marathon and Victoria's quest for sub-4 hours. After struggling through the middle miles and nearly losing hope at 25k, she produced a remarkable final 10k to cross the line in 3:57:30. One of the best marathons in the world, one of our best finishes. 26.2 Miles 3:57:30 Finish Time 10th Consecutive Year Sub-4 Goal Achieved Paris Marathon holds a special place in our hearts. We've been running it every year since 2012 - ten consecutive years of crossing the Champs-Élysées, passing the Eiffel Tower, and finishing on the Arc de Triomphe. When COVID pushed the 2021 edition from spring to autumn, we weren't going to let anything stop us from keeping the streak alive. This year was about Victoria. She had a clear goal: break four hours. We came in with a plan - goals A, B, and C - but really, there was only one goal that mattered. The City of Light There's a reason Paris is consistently rated one of the best marathons in the world. The course takes you on a grand tour of the city's greatest landmarks. We started near the Champs-Élysées, passed the Hotel de Ville, caught glimpses of Notre Dame Cathedral (still under reconstruction after the fire), ran through the Place de la Bastille, and eventually swept past the Eiffel Tower around the 30-kilometre mark. The atmosphere in Paris is electric. French crowds bring an energy that's hard to describe - they genuinely love running and they show up in force to support everyone from the elites to the back-of-packers. The Plan Unravels At halfway, we were on track. Just about on course for goal A, which was ambitious. The problem with marathons is that halfway really isn't halfway - the race doesn't truly begin until around 30 kilometres, when glycogen stores deplete and the real mental battle starts. By 25 kilometres, Victoria was suffering. I could see it in her stride, in her face. The pace was dropping and with it, our hopes for sub-4. I remember thinking at around 30k that we might not make it. The maths wasn't looking good - just under 7k to go and about 43 minutes to do it. The margins were razor thin. "I thought we'd lost it at 25k. Victoria was really suffering, slowing down. I didn't know if we were going to make four hours." The Comeback Then something remarkable happened. The last 10 kilometres saw a Victoria I hadn't seen all race. Where most runners fade, she found another gear. I don't know where she got it from - that deep reserve that experienced marathoners learn to tap into when everything seems lost. At 24 miles we did the maths again: 2.2 miles to go, 25 minutes on the clock. It was going to be close but suddenly it was back within reach. The Louis Vuitton Foundation building, a recent addition to the course, marked our entry into the final stretch through the Bois de Boulogne. With less than a kilometre to go, we had eight minutes. We were going to do it. The Finish on the Champs-Élysées Turning onto the finishing straight on the Champs-Élysées is one of the great moments in marathon running. The Arc de Triomphe ahead, the crowds lining both sides, the clock ticking down - it's everything a marathon finish should be. 3 hours 57 minutes and 30 seconds. Sub-4 with two and a half minutes to spare. Victoria had done it, and she'd done it the hard way - by refusing to give up when everything suggested the goal was slipping away. Watch the Film I captured our tenth Paris Marathon on film. Here's the full race video: The Route A Decade of Paris Ten years. Ten Paris Marathons. What started in 2012 as my first major city marathon has become an annual pilgrimage, a non-negotiable fixture in our calendar. The course has changed slightly over the years - the addition of the Louis Vuitton building, route modifications here and there - but the essence remains the same. There's something about running through a city you love. Every landmark becomes a mile marker in your memory. Notre Dame at 7k, Bastille shortly after, the long stretch through Vincennes, the sweep past the Eiffel Tower when you know you're in the home stretch. Victoria's sub-4 felt like a culmination of all those years. She'd learned the course, understood the marathon, and found that mental fortitude that separates good marathon runners from great ones. When it mattered most, she dug deep and delivered. We'll be back for number eleven. Paris has that hold on us now. It's not just a marathon - it's an annual reunion with a city, a course, and a version of ourselves that only emerges when we're 35 kilometres in with everything on the line.
- [Tenerife Bluetrail 2019 | Sea to Summit](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/tenerife-bluetrail-2019-sea-to-summit): Blog Running Running Tenerife Bluetrail 2019 | Sea to Summit Stephen Cousins 12 June 2019 10 min read TL;DR A night start from sea level, climbing 3,500 metres to the summit of Mount Teide - Spain's highest point. Volcanic moonscapes, altitude sickness, running out of water, and walking backwards down the final descent. 22 hours of the most unique ultra running experience you can find in Europe. Date: 7th June 2019 | Distance: 102km (63 miles) | Time: 22:02:42 | Elevation: 3,500m There's something otherworldly about the Tenerife Bluetrail. You start at sea level at 11:30pm on a Friday night, and by dawn you're climbing through volcanic landscapes toward the summit of Mount Teide - the highest point in Spain at 3,500 metres. It's unlike any other race in Europe. Into the Night The start was chaotic. Within 500 metres we were at a standstill, trying to get through a bottleneck. But that's part of the experience when you're running with hundreds of others through the dark streets of a Canarian town. Eleven and a half kilometres in, we were already climbing hard - 800 to 900 metres up. Looking back at the town, it was an amazing view of lights stretching all the way to the horizon. Absolutely incredible. By 21km and the third aid station, we'd climbed 1,500 metres. Three hours and 39 minutes in, with a cutoff of 4 hours 15 minutes. Comfortably ahead, but with a long way still to go. The terrain was a real mixture - runnable at times, but also really rocky, difficult volcanic ground. Through the Night to Dawn At 31km, nearly 20 miles, we'd climbed over 2,000 metres - about a third of our total climbing. Just under seven hours of running, and it was finally getting light. Made it through the night. Let's hope I don't have to put the head torch on again later. Three thousand metres climbed. The final aid station before the summit sat at a pretty little church backing onto Teide itself. 48 and a half kilometres done, and I was actually doing okay. Tired, obviously, because there had been so much climbing. But relative to CCC and Transvulcania, I was in decent shape. The Push to 3,500 Metres Then came the real work. 54 kilometres done, four more to the top. It was really hard. Very hot, although there was a cool breeze at altitude - one small saving grace. I was worried about water, trying to conserve what I had left, which meant I was parched. The landscape was barren - sandy volcanic stuff mixed with boulders to climb over. Four kilometres to the aid station at the top, eleven hours and nineteen minutes into the race. With about a kilometre to go, everyone was running out of water. We were all parched. Then, like a mirage, we found it - the race directors had left loads of water for us. An absolute godsend. Summit Fever This is the top of the climb. We did it. You can see for miles up here. But I was so dizzy and tired with the altitude - 3,500 metres above sea level will do that to you. I had literally ten minutes rest at the top aid station, drank some tea, threw up massively (which was awesome), and then we were off again. Thirteen kilometres to the next aid station. We were all very tired. Disaster struck: I hadn't brought my watch charger, and it had died. Now I was relying on other people to tell me how fast to go and what the time was. Not ideal when you're trying to make cutoffs. The Never-Ending Descent At 72.5km, another big descent to come, then that nasty final climb. The descent went on far too long. My legs were hurting, my quads absolutely destroyed. Then look - we're here, and we've got at least 500 metres of climbing still to do. Up through the forest, back touching the clouds again at that altitude. So hard. Never-ending. Then finally, hopefully, back onto the beach for the finish line. Do you remember my first Transvulcania video where I was walking down the street backwards? Well, it came to that again. We're going backwards, and I think it's actually quicker. Still nine kilometres to go. Then eight. Before Sunset There it is. I'm going to make it before the sun goes down. 22 hours and 2 minutes of climbing from sea level to Spain's highest point and back down to the northern coast. It's an experience unlike any other race I've done. The night running through the darkness, the volcanic landscapes, the altitude, the heat, the endless climbing - it all combines into something truly special. 3,500 metres above sea level, I was so dizzy and tired. But you can see for miles. That view made every step worth it. Yeray Duran won the men's race in an incredible 11:48:09, controlling the race from the early hours. Leire Martinez Herrera took the women's title in 14:36:42. Both performances were stunning on a course that takes no prisoners. Race Stats 102km Distance 3,500m Peak Altitude 22:02 Finish Time 11:30pm Night Start Watch the Film Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [1066 Ultramarathon 2019 | Harold's March](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/1066-ultramarathon-2019-harolds-march): Blog Running Running 1066 Ultramarathon 2019 | Harold's March Stephen Cousins 12 July 2019 10 min read TL;DR Following King Harold's 1066 battle-march from London to Battle Abbey - 100 miles of bizarre contrasts. The Thames Path past Tower Bridge, fly-tipping in Dartford, overgrown nettles, and finally the historic battlefield. 26 hours 46 minutes, 10th place, and one of the strangest hundred-milers I've ever run. Date: 7th July 2019 | Distance: 100+ miles | Time: 26:46:02 | Position: 10th In 1066, King Harold of England, fresh from defeating Vikings in York, marched his army back to London and then south towards Hastings upon hearing of William of Normandy's invasion. His army had three days for the march. I had thirty hours to replicate it. Along the Thames Within half a mile of the start, we were on the Thames Path, following it for the next 50 kilometres. I never thought I'd run a 100-mile ultra past the London Eye, but here we were. Parliament. The river. London Eye just ahead, about 4km into the race. St Paul's Cathedral. The Millennium Bridge. The Tate Gallery. We were running along the Thames Path through the heart of London, past landmarks I'd only ever seen as a tourist. Tower Bridge. The Tower of London. Through the Greenwich Foot Tunnel, going from the north bank to the south. This was surreal - a 100-mile race through one of the world's greatest cities. By Millwall, officially 15 miles in (though most of us had done about 17 because we went all over the place), we were looking at 20 miles to the next checkpoint. No doubt we'd be stopping at Costa, Waitrose, Sainsbury's on the way. Maybe Pizza Hut. This is urban ultra running. The Dartford Low By Dartford, about 40 miles in, I was absolutely wrecked. It wasn't even that hot - about 22 degrees, 70 Fahrenheit - but it was just hot enough to make me wilt. My stomach was feeling horrible. I couldn't eat any food. At the checkpoint in a little church, I just looked at the food and couldn't stomach any of it. Had a couple of grapes - even that made me feel sick. Bought myself a coffee. Managed to have a couple of pints of milk from various shops since the previous checkpoint. I was walking an awful lot. Caught up with Richard and Jay at one point, then stopped at a shop and they went on. Hadn't seen them since. Seven hours 50 minutes for 40 miles. This was going to be a long day. There's a really horrible bit through Dartford - areas with fly-tipping and rubbish everywhere. Just a horrible place to run through. Lots of tarmac, tough on your feet. Then overgrown pathways that seemed to go on forever. The Bizarre Middle It's been the most bizarre hundred-mile race. Given the elevation - only about 1,600-1,700 metres - I'd expect to do this in 24 hours. It was going to take 27. Really, really hard. Loads of walking. Lucky if I was covering a kilometre in ten minutes. But around 6 o'clock in the evening, it finally started cooling down. I was feeling a bit better. Starting to run a bit - not fast, but at least running. Twenty hours and about 25 minutes in, still 23 miles to go. The whole run was at least 104 miles with all the extra mileage thrown in. This is what we do it for. All good fun, right? The Overgrown Nightmare With six kilometres to go, four miles, we were pushing through grass up to our waists. Stinging nettles. Thorn bushes at eye level and waist level. Sometimes you couldn't even tell if you were on the right path, even when the GPS said you were. I went right through the middle of a bunch of stinging nettles, straight through one of the vineyards because I couldn't work out which way around it was. Just went right through the bloody middle of it. Battle Abbey And then, finally, there it was. Battle Abbey. The site of the Battle of Hastings. I always think it's really weird how they managed to fight in a place called Battle, but there we are. I finished the 1066 100-mile ultra in 26 hours and 46 minutes. That was really, really hard work. But I came in 10th place, which shows that it was hard for everyone. I'd expect to do this in 24 hours given the elevation. It took 27. The most bizarre hundred-mile race - from Tower Bridge to fly-tipping to stinging nettles to Battle Abbey. English Heritage had permitted the finish under Battle Abbey Gatehouse - the same spot where Harold's army would have faced William's Normans all those centuries ago. To finish a 100-mile race there, having followed the same route, was something special despite all the suffering along the way. Race Stats 100+mi Distance 1,700m Elevation 26:46 Finish Time 10th Position Watch the Film Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Sunrise Ultra 2021 | 83 Miles Through the Norfolk Night](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/sunrise-ultra-2021-norfolk-coast): Blog Running Running Sunrise Ultra 2021 | 83 Miles Through the Norfolk Night Stephen Cousins 11 December 2021 12 min read TL;DR 83 miles along the Norfolk Coast Path, starting at sunset in Snettisham and finishing at Great Yarmouth. The Sunrise Ultra answered that question comprehensively over the next twenty-three hours. Standing at the start line in Snettisham as the December sun began its early descent, I spotted Dan Lawson warming up nearby – the man who holds the JOGLE record – and realised I was probably about to learn something about myself. The Premise The concept behind the Sunrise Ultra is beautifully simple: start at sunset, run 83 miles along the Norfolk Coast Path, and if you're fast enough, finish before sunrise. It's poetic, really. The name isn't ironic – the quick runners genuinely do see the sunrise from the finish line. The rest of us see it somewhere around mile 55, wondering why we're still in the dark while our legs have long since stopped cooperating. About 50-60 runners gathered in Snettisham that afternoon, with trackers strapped to our wrists so loved ones at home could watch our little dots crawl across Norfolk. The atmosphere was subdued, focused. This wasn't anyone's first rodeo – at least, it shouldn't have been. Race director Giles makes no apologies for the difficulty. In some years, only 15% of starters reach Great Yarmouth. The bus ride from the finish to the start gave me an hour and a half to contemplate the return journey on foot. I ate my customary pre-race rice pudding and checked my kit: two head torches, spare batteries, survival bag, enough food to last between the widely-spaced aid stations. Twenty miles apart, some of them. Self-sufficiency isn't optional here. Into the Darkness By three kilometres in, the light was already failing. By five miles, running through Hunstanton, I was in full darkness. The promenade that would be charming in summer felt bleak and exposed in December. I imagined families eating ice cream, children on the beach. None of that now. Just the beam of my head torch and the sound of other runners' footfalls gradually fading as we spread out along the coast. Twelve miles in, the rain started. Proper rain. The kind that finds every gap in your waterproof and sets up residence there. Boardwalks appeared – long, endless stretches of wooden slats that were actually quite pleasant underfoot, a welcome change from what was to come. At Wells-next-the-Sea, 27 miles in, I grabbed crisps and a BabyBel at the checkpoint. The volunteers were cheery despite the conditions. "Ready salted?" they asked. I nodded, not yet reduced to the single-syllable communication that comes later in long races. That would come. The Mud and the Shingle Cley. 38 miles. This is where the race truly began. The section before Cley – roughly between miles 25 and 38 – was something else entirely. The rain had turned the coastal path into a treacherous mud bath, the kind where each step requires a decision: do I try to run through this, or accept that walking is the only sensible option? I walked loads of it. My back started aching from the constant adjustment, the endless micro-corrections as my feet slipped and slid. At the Cley checkpoint, 8 hours 44 minutes into the race, I learnt that Dan Lawson was already approaching the next aid station. He'd finish in around 13 hours. I was looking at 19-20. The mathematics of ultra running can be cruel. "I'm going out in the cold and wet now," I announced to the checkpoint volunteers. "Does anybody want to come with me?" No takers. And then: the shingle. Four miles of shingle beach. If the mud had sapped my will, the shingle attacked my legs directly. Every step absorbed by loose stones, calves burning, forward progress measured in inches. I stopped trying to film while running – holding a camera and maintaining balance on shingle is a fool's errand. "I'm not going to DNF. That's for sure." The Long Night At 3am, running along cliffs near Cromer, my back was aching but my spirits had recovered. That's the strange rhythm of ultra running – you pass through low points, sometimes lasting miles, and then suddenly find yourself okay again. The mud had been my low. Having survived it, the cliffs felt almost pleasant. Overstrand aid station: 53 miles. "I thought it was 52," I said. "Bonus mile." At this point, you take victories where you find them. Dawn was threatening at the edges of the sky, and some runners were calling it quits. Without a GPX file, the navigation in darkness had become too much for several of them. I'd got lost more times than I could count, but the coast path signs, when you could find them, kept pointing the way to Great Yarmouth. By 7:20am, with about 37 kilometres still to go, I was walking along a beach, unable to find a way off it, waiting for an opportunity to scramble up the small cliff to my left. Absolutely done in. Legs empty. Back protesting. Still over 20 miles to go. "I'm not going to DNF," I told the camera. "That's for sure. It'll just be very, very slow." Sun, Seals, and the Final Push When the sun finally came out properly, something shifted. My legs found a rhythm again – nothing impressive, but forward motion that felt almost like running. At Sea Palling, with 14 miles to go, the number suddenly seemed manageable. We'd done so much. What was 14 more? Somewhere in those final miles, I spotted seals. Actual seals, lounging on the beach, utterly unbothered by the shell-shocked runner shuffling past. It was a moment of unexpected beauty in what had been a grinding exercise in endurance. - [Serpent Trail 100k | Forests, Football, and Fading Legs](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/serpent-trail-100k-2021): Blog Running Running Serpent Trail 100k | Forests, Football, and Fading Legs Stephen Cousins 3 July 2021 10 min read TL;DR 103 kilometres through the Sussex and Hampshire countryside, following the ancient Serpent Trail from Haslemere to Petersfield. Started at 5am, finished 13 hours 42 minutes later – just in time to catch England thrashing Ukraine 4-0 at the finish. Beautiful forests, sudden rain, and legs that hadn't quite recovered from the South Downs Way 100. 103km Distance 13:41:59 Finish Time 1,600m Elevation 4-0 England Result "I did it about four years ago," I told the camera at 5am in Haslemere, spooning rice pudding into my mouth. "There were a lot fewer people then. Chances of a top 10 finish are gone." I wasn't wrong. The Serpent Trail 100k had grown significantly since my last attempt, and my legs – still carrying the memory of the South Downs Way 100 from a few weeks earlier – were about to remind me that recovery isn't optional. The Serpent Trail The route follows the ancient Serpent Trail, a 64-mile path that winds through the western Weald of Sussex and Hampshire. It's named not for any slithering wildlife but for the serpentine route it takes through the landscape – a constant weaving through forests, across fields, and over rolling hills that feels more like a journey through Middle-earth than southern England. We gathered in Haslemere in the dark, coffee in hand, watching the field assemble. The race had grown popular, and the nervous energy was palpable. At 5am, we set off into the early morning light. A Strong Start Seven and a half miles in, an hour and a quarter of running, 400 metres of climbing done. The conditions were perfect – cool, overcast, not too hot. The kind of weather that makes you think optimistic thoughts about finish times. By 13 miles, I'd climbed 700 metres and was moving well through beautiful forest trails. The navigation required attention – we were following little purple triangle signs that occasionally seemed to hide behind trees – but the route on my watch kept me honest. At 20 miles, three and a half hours in, I made a dangerous calculation. If I kept this pace, I'd finish in ten and a half hours. That felt too fast. I told myself to slow down. Looking back, I should have listened to my own advice earlier. Rain and Reality A marathon's worth of trail running in 4 hours 50 minutes – not bad for hilly terrain. The rain that arrived shortly after was actually welcome, taking the edge off what threatened to become a warm afternoon. Of course, it also turned the trails into a mud bath, but you can't have everything. Petworth marked the midway point: 51 kilometres in 5 hours 50 minutes. My watch was already showing more than 100k would require – the race distance was actually closer to 103 kilometres. A bonus three kilometres. Just what you need at halfway. "That's me done. I am absolutely shattered now." The Collapse At 60 kilometres, seven hours in, reality arrived. People started passing me. My legs, which had been cooperative all morning, simply stopped cooperating. The experiment of running the hills had failed. I was walking them now. "I think it's to do with the South Downs Way 100 recently," I told the camera at 80 kilometres. "My legs just aren't recovered enough." It wasn't my stomach – that was fine. The temperature wasn't brutal. But somewhere deep in my quadriceps, a message was being sent: you asked too much, too soon, and now we're done. The section from 70 to 90 kilometres was pure survival. My back ached. My legs had nothing. The knowledge that most of the elevation was done meant little when even flat ground felt like climbing. Coke, Marmite, and Beautiful Countryside At each aid station, I'd grab Coca-Cola and marmite sandwiches – my fuelling strategy for the day. Not scientific, but it worked. The volunteers were brilliant, as they always are, and despite being completely knackered I made sure to thank each one. At 90 kilometres, the sun came out. The countryside revealed itself in all its summer glory, and suddenly the world didn't seem quite so harsh. "When it's like this," I said to the camera, "you know you can't complain. It's so beautiful here." That moment – wrecked beyond measure but surrounded by stunning English countryside – is what ultra running is really about. The suffering creates the appreciation. You can't have one without the other. Petersfield and a 4-0 Win The watch hit 100 kilometres with 13 hours 19 minutes elapsed. Two and a half kilometres still to go. I jogged them at nine-minute kilometres, each step hurting but knowing the end was coming. Coming through Petersfield, people were beeping their car horns – whether for the runners or the football, I couldn't tell. Probably both. The finish line appeared at the rugby club, and I crossed it in 13 hours 42 minutes, 103 kilometres done. After a shower, I emerged to find a party atmosphere. The England vs Ukraine Euro 2020 quarter-final was showing – 4-0 to England – and runners were finishing all around, bells clanging, people cheering, food cooking. It was, quite simply, lovely. "The run was really hard," I told anyone who'd listen. "Really hard. I'm so tired." But isn't that the point? Final Thoughts The Serpent Trail 100k is a beautiful race through some of the finest countryside southern England has to offer. The navigation requires attention – those purple triangles can be elusive – and the 1,600 metres of elevation will test your legs, but the reward is a day spent weaving through ancient forests and rolling hills. Would I do it again? Absolutely. Though maybe I'll let my legs recover properly first next time. Watch the Race The Route Strava Activity
- [CROC 100 | One Community, 100 Miles During Lockdown](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/centurion-croc-100-2020): Blog Running Running CROC 100 | One Community, 100 Miles During Lockdown Stephen Cousins 30 May 2020 10 min read TL;DR During the 2020 lockdown, Centurion Running created the One Community (CROC) virtual event. I ran 100 miles by linking four local races: Beachy Head Marathon, South Downs Way 50 (in reverse), Three Forts Marathon, and Steyning Stinger. 163 kilometres, 28 hours, one community of 4,000 runners worldwide. 163km Distance 27:42:30 Finish Time 4 Races Linked 4,000 Runners Worldwide In 2020, across the world, friends and families were torn apart. Communities were fractured by an invisible enemy. But this is a story about coming together – about an adventure designed to beat the separation and loneliness. Centurion Running's One Community event attracted 4,000 runners and walkers from all over the world. Distances from 5K to 100 miles could be completed over a week, either at home on a treadmill or outdoors on road or trail. It was, in its own way, a collective act of defiance against isolation. The Plan My plan was ambitious but logical – at least to me. I would link together four local races that I knew well: the Beachy Head Marathon, the South Downs Way 50 (run in reverse), the Three Forts Marathon, and the Steyning Stinger Marathon. The routes would overlap and connect, creating a 100-mile journey through some of the most beautiful countryside in southern England. Victoria would join me for the first section – the Beachy Head Marathon – starting from Bo Peep car park on a beautiful late May morning. After that, I'd continue alone. Given that this was a Centurion-organised event, it seemed appropriate to be running on such a well-known and well-loved Centurion course. The South Downs had seen me at my best and my worst over the years. It felt right to be here now. The Beachy Head Marathon We started at Bo Peep car park, working our way through the village of Litlington, through Friston Forest, past the Cuckmere Valley, and onto the Seven Sisters. The lighthouse at Beachy Head came and went – a landmark you don't actually see on the official marathon route, but we were taking a slightly different line. At the trig point near Beachy Head – the spot where South Downs Way 100 runners turn left to descend to Eastbourne – we continued straight, following the Bridle Way. Victoria completed her marathon, and I pressed on towards Worthing. The South Downs Way 50 (In Reverse) I feel really sick around 35 miles. I always do. It often lasts until about 60 miles, when I usually throw up. This race was no different. The famous White Bridge at Southease passed by. The evening light was stunning – 6pm, absolutely beautiful. As I ran, I could sense four thousand other runners across the world overcoming their own challenges right beside me. That's what this event was about. We were alone on our routes but connected in purpose. "Everything hurt by now. But it's supposed to. That's why we do it. That's why we love it." At 78 kilometres – almost halfway – I'd had food, some drink, and thrown up everywhere. Standard procedure. With a big push from my wife at Hill Barn, I headed into the night to start the Three Forts Challenge. Into the Night The Three Forts Marathon is named for the three ancient hill forts it links: Devil's Dyke, Chanctonbury Ring, and Cissbury Ring. At 10 past midnight, with 104 kilometres done, I reached the halfway point of this section and immediately broke off to add the Steyning Stinger into the mix. At 2:30am, I'd done 116 kilometres. The Steyning Stinger loop stretched ahead – that peculiar route that looks like an old man stooped over with a very large pointy nose when you see it on a map. The point of that nose was where I'd turn around. At quarter past four, 125 kilometres in, I reached the top of one of the major climbs. The early morning sunrise was emerging – that magical light that makes everything seem possible again. Sunrise and the Finish Making it through the night always feels good. I had been struggling, but sunrise gave me new strength in my legs and the knowledge that the finish was within reach. Steyning Stinger, Three Forts, and Beachy Head are all significant challenges in their own right. Linking them together had seemed like a perfect plan, but the reality of these things is often far less glamorous. Everything hurt by now. But it's supposed to. That's why we do it. That's why we love it. By 7:18am, I'd done 143 kilometres. All that remained was the final section back to Devil's Dyke. 163 kilometres. 28 hours and 3 minutes. One hundred miles done. Community Standing on Devil's Dyke as the world began to wake up, I thought about the other runners out there – thousands of them, in their own countries, on their own routes, facing their own challenges. We'd done it together. A collective journey. One community. The lockdown had separated us physically, but running had connected us in spirit. And that, perhaps, was the whole point.
