- [Run Jurassic Ultra 2019 | Finally, a Finish](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/run-jurassic-ultra-2019): Blog Running Running Run Jurassic Ultra 2019 | Finally, a Finish Stephen Cousins 28 September 2019 7 min read TL;DR 50 kilometres along the Jurassic Coast – one of the most spectacular stretches of coastline in Britain. A beautiful September day, sausage rolls at the aid stations, and finally a finish after four DNFs that year. 5 hours 47 minutes, 15th place. 50km Distance 5:47:00 Finish Time 15th Position 4 DNFs That Year After four DNFs in 2019, I needed a finish. The Run Jurassic Ultra – somewhere around 50 kilometres along the Dorset coast – seemed like the perfect opportunity to end the streak of disappointment. "Who knows what it might be," I muttered at the start line, regarding the somewhat imprecise distance. Anything up to 55 kilometres was possible. At this point, I just wanted to cross a finish line. The Jurassic Coast The Jurassic Coast is Britain's first natural World Heritage Site – 95 miles of coastline stretching from East Devon to Dorset. The cliffs tell a 185-million-year story, layers of rock revealing the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods. It's a landscape that makes you feel very small and very temporary. For runners, it offers something else entirely: relentless undulation, spectacular views, and trails that wind along cliff tops before plunging down to beaches and climbing back up again. The kind of terrain that looks beautiful in photographs and feels brutal underfoot. The weather, at least, was on our side. A beautiful September day – the kind where the sea sparkles and the sky stretches endlessly blue. Through Weymouth Ten miles in, we reached the second aid station in the middle of Weymouth. The coastal town was going about its Saturday business, tourists and locals mixing on the seafront while a stream of runners passed through. By the halfway point – two hours 33 minutes – I was feeling reasonably good. The pace felt sustainable, the weather was perfect, and for once my body seemed to be cooperating. At 20 miles, 3 hours 23 minutes in, I walked it out while eating sausage rolls and drinking coke. The classic ultra combination. I wanted to finish somewhere between five and a half and six hours, and that seemed achievable. "After four DNFs this year, I finally got one finished." Abbotsbury and Beyond The aid station at Abbotsbury came exactly four hours in – 37.5 kilometres done, one more station to go. The final section stretched ahead: four, five, six, seven kilometres depending on who you asked. The imprecision of the distance had become something of a running joke. But distances stop mattering when you can see the finish. The last miles passed in that strange state of tired determination that ultra runners know well – not running fast, but running nonetheless. Finally, a Finish 5 hours 47 minutes. 15th place. Top 20. As I crossed the line, the last runners of the marathon were coming in behind me. Not a world-beating performance, but after a year of setbacks and DNFs, it felt like victory. 2019 had been a difficult year. The Arc of Attrition in February had pushed me to my limits. Other races had ended early for various reasons. But here, on the Jurassic Coast on a beautiful September day, I'd finally completed what I set out to do. Sometimes that's all ultra running is: showing up, not giving up, and crossing the line. Watch the Race The Route Strava Activity
- [Guernsey GU36 | Victoria's First Ultra](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/guernsey-gu36-victorias-first-ultra-2019): Blog Running Running Guernsey GU36 | Victoria's First Ultra Stephen Cousins 19 May 2019 8 min read TL;DR Victoria's first ultra distance event - a 36-mile circumnavigation of Guernsey along the spectacular cliff paths and coastal roads. We finished together in 7:57:31, conquering the brutal 1000m of elevation in the first half before cruising the flat northern section to the finish at Liberation Monument. 36 Miles 7:57:31 Finish Time 1,000m+ Elevation 1st Victoria's Ultra There's something magical about running around an island. The finite nature of it - knowing you'll end up where you started - gives the challenge a completeness that point-to-point races can't quite match. When we signed up for the Guernsey GU36, it wasn't just about the race. It was about Victoria running her first ultra distance. A Family Affair We made the trip a proper family adventure. The Maunoir grandparents came along to look after the children while we ran, and we'd arrived a few days early to explore the island. Guernsey had been on our list for a while - small enough to feel manageable, beautiful enough to make any race memorable. The race starts and finishes at the Liberation Monument in St Peter Port, commemorating the island's liberation from German occupation in 1945. It's a fitting starting point for what would be Victoria's liberation into ultra running. The Gnarly First Half The race organisers are upfront about it: the first 16 miles contain pretty much all the climbing. We're talking 1000 metres of elevation gain packed into the southern cliff sections, with relentless ups and downs that test both legs and resolve. Steps cut into cliffs, scrambles over rocks, narrow paths with views that would be stunning if you dared take your eyes off your feet. The checkpoints came at 8 miles and 16 miles, with another at Cobo Bay around mile 23. Each one was a welcome sight, though the prospect of more climbing between them made every departure bittersweet. "Once you've done 16 miles in an ultra, you know you can finish. The hard part isn't physical - it's believing you can do it." Victoria was running beautifully. First ultras can go one of two ways - you either pace it perfectly or blow up spectacularly. She was nailing it, staying conservative on the climbs and making the most of the descents where her natural running ability could shine. Views for Days One of the joys of running around Guernsey is the ever-changing panorama. On clear sections we could see Herm off to the east, Sark to the southeast, and on the clearest stretches, Jersey far to the south. The Channel Islands laid out before us like a maritime map come to life. The German fortifications from World War II punctuate the coastline - concrete bunkers and observation towers that have become part of the landscape. There's something poignant about running past these relics of occupation, heading towards a finish at the Liberation Monument. The Flat Run Home After the brutality of the first half, the northern section of the island comes as blessed relief. The path levels out, following the coast road and promenade around towards St Peter Port. We'd done the hard work - now it was about steady progress. Victoria was still moving well, her pacing paying dividends as others around us began to struggle. This is where ultra running differs from shorter distances. It's not about who starts fastest; it's about who falls apart least. The last few miles along the harbour front into St Peter Port felt almost celebratory. We'd circumnavigated an island. We'd run 36 miles together. And Victoria had become an ultra runner. Sub-8 Hours We crossed the line in 7 hours 57 minutes and 31 seconds. The sub-8 hour finish was a nice bonus, but the real victory was sharing this experience. There's something special about running an ultra with your partner - the shared suffering, the mutual encouragement, the knowledge that you're both going through the same thing. The children were there at the finish with the grandparents, which made it all the more meaningful. Ultra running doesn't have to be a solo pursuit - it can be a family adventure, a shared challenge, a memory made together. Watch the Film I captured our day circumnavigating Guernsey on film. Here's the full race video: The Route Lessons Learned The GU36 reinforced something I've always believed about ultra running: it's accessible. You don't need to be an elite athlete to complete an ultra distance. You need patience, good pacing, and the belief that you can keep moving forward even when it gets hard. Victoria proved that day that first ultras don't have to be disasters. With sensible pacing and a positive attitude, you can finish strong, enjoy the experience, and actually want to do another one. Which, of course, she did. Guernsey is a perfect venue for an ultra. Small enough to be logistically simple, beautiful enough to distract from the pain, and challenging enough to feel like a real achievement. The GU36 might not have the prestige of bigger events, but it delivered everything we wanted: a complete island, a complete adventure, and a complete runner reborn as an ultra runner.
- [Atlantic Coast Challenge 2017 | Three Marathons to Land's End](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/atlantic-coast-challenge-2017): Blog Running Running Atlantic Coast Challenge 2017 | Three Marathons to Land's End Stephen Cousins 8 October 2017 10 min read TL;DR Three marathons in three days along the Southwest Coast Path in Cornwall, finishing at Land's End. Day one: glorious sunshine. Day two: rain and wind. Day three: gnarly, bouldering terrain. A family adventure with Victoria and the kids joining at various points. 78.6mi Total Distance 16:10:10 Total Time 3 Days Land's End Finish Back in March 2017, I'd run the Jurassic Coast Challenge in Dorset – three days of coastal running organised by Votwo Events. In October, I was back for the Atlantic Coast Challenge: three marathons in three days along the Southwest Coast Path, finishing at the most westerly point of mainland England. The premise was simple. Each day, we'd run a marathon (ish – the distances were approximate). Each day, the weather and terrain would bring new challenges. And at the end, we'd be standing at Land's End, having covered nearly 80 miles of some of the most beautiful coastline in Britain. Day One: Sunshine and Stunning Scenery Distance: 26.2 miles | Time: 4:49:00 The first checkpoint came at around 12-13 kilometres, and already the scenery was stunning. The Cornish coast in October sunshine is something special – dramatic cliffs, turquoise water, ancient paths winding along the clifftops. "Believe me," I told the camera, "it's not going to be like this tomorrow. It's going to be rainy and wet." Checkpoint two offered the classic ultra runner spread: bananas, Jaffa cakes, Mars bars, Coke, and – somewhat incongruously – ice creams. But why not? It was a beautiful day. We finished on the beach at Perranporth as the sun set over the Atlantic. 42 kilometres done, another 52 to go. Day Two: Rain, Wind, and Marmite Sandwiches Distance: 26.2 miles | Time: 4:51:22 "It's not as nice as yesterday," I observed as we gathered at the start in Perranporth. The beach where I'd finished in glorious sunshine was now grey and windswept. The forecast promised worse to come. The race organisers gave out hugs before we started. It was that kind of day. Eight miles in, we reached the Blue Bar in Portreath. This was significant – back in February, I'd run the Arc of Attrition 100, which starts in Coverack and finishes right there in Portreath. Standing in that same spot, 100-mile-weary legs still a memory, I was reminded of what this coastline can demand. "I don't know why I've chosen to have another Marmite sandwich. Two to go. Walking it out. Coffee." By checkpoint three – 30 kilometres in – I could see our campsite across the bay. But the route, of course, didn't go directly there. Another 12 kilometres of winding coastal path remained. Victoria and the kids joined me for the final section, running the last kilometres together before finishing at the caravan site. A family affair in the Cornish rain. Day Three: The Gnarly Section to Land's End Distance: 26.2 miles | Time: 6:29:48 Half past seven on Sunday morning. Runners, walkers, and joggers gathered for the final push to Land's End. "It's a tough section," warned the briefing. "Really gnarly. But hopefully the weather will hold." Fourteen kilometres in, we hit the most challenging terrain of the three days. This wasn't running; this was bouldering. The coast path here requires hands as well as feet, clambering over rocks and navigating sections that feel more like scrambling than trail running. Checkpoint one at Zennor (10 miles) was half a mile off the main path. Checkpoint two was perched in a location so dramatic that I filmed it for the video: "If that's not enough to convince you to come and do this next year, I don't know what is." Cape Cornwall came at five hours. Sennen Cove appeared behind me. And then, finally, Land's End rose over the next ridge. My watch died before the finish – typical – so I have no idea exactly what time I crossed the line. But it didn't matter. Three days, three marathons, nearly 80 miles of Southwest Coast Path. Done. Three Days, Three Weathers The Atlantic Coast Challenge delivered exactly what it promised: variety. Sun on day one, rain and wind on day two, and mild but technically demanding terrain on day three. The Southwest Coast Path is one of Britain's great long-distance trails. Running it in three-day chunks, with the support of Votwo Events and the company of fellow runners, is a wonderful way to experience it. Even when it rains – and it will rain – the beauty of the Cornish coast makes every step worthwhile. Come and run on the Southwest Coast Path. You will not regret it. - [Transvulcania Ultra or Poles? We don’t Need Poles](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/transvulcania-ultra-2016): Blog Running Running Transvulcania Ultra or Poles? We don’t Need Poles Stephen Cousins 18 May 2016 21 min read If you're going to put yourself through hell, you might as well do it in heaven, eh? When I took part in my first race back in 2010, at the age of 40, I thought running might become a nice hobby to keep me fit. But if completing the Transvulcania Ultra has proved one thing, it’s that running is no longer a hobby. It’s not even a habit or even a fixation. It’s a full blown obsession. An addiction so thoroughly embedded in my soul that I am willing to risk my life to get a fix. I suspect it’s the same for my running wife, Richard . Convincing Our Wives A few months ago we watched a TV documentary on the Transvulcania Ultra in La Palma. A race that is beginning to attract a lot of attention in the ultra running community. Seasoned runners like Kilan Journet, Emily Forsberg, Anna Frost, Blake Hose, Sage Canaday and Luis Alberto Hernando had all come to race 74km and nearly 4500 metres of elevation over and around the forests and volcanic mountains of this tiny Canary Island. It really caught our imagination and before we had time to question the wisdom of our actions, we had signed up for the 2016 instalment of the Transvulcania Ultra. Our wives are growing accustomed to our constant need for running adventure and the promise of a week in the sun at a nice hotel was easily enough to see them both flicking through holiday brochures and messaging each other about whether to hire a car or how to get the children out of school without being fined. We settled on the La Palma and Teneguia Hotel and Spa with 11 pools on the west coast of the island and only 10 minutes drive from the Transvulcania start line. Hill Training Richard and I duly began our regimented training program of simply running lots of marathons and ultras prior to the race. In all seriousness, we were well aware that the Transvulcania Ultra involved some serious elevation and that we really might need to do some hill work in preparation. We had planned to find a big hill and do a regular, once a week, hard session of climbing. As it was, from the turn of the year we were running so many races that we couldn’t fit any other training in. Almost every Saturday or Sunday from January to May, Richard and I raced an event. Thankfully, many of these were hilly trail races, including the South Downs Way 50 and the CTS Endurance Life Ultra in Sussex. Come the start of May 2016 we both felt pretty fit and ready to tackle the biggest physical and mental challenge of our running careers. We’ve had tough races before. Busting a gut to try and break your parkrun or your 10k PB can feel pretty darn tough. The World Half Marathon Championships and the London Marathon were huge personal challenges for me this year. But we run these kind of events all the time. We are experienced and the challenge is not completion, but by how much can we improve. For us, the Transvulcania Ultra was a step into the unknown. A challenge we were not sure we fully understood. A challenge we had no idea we COULD complete. Early Start Richard and I collected our race bibs from the expo in Los Llanos the day before the race. The expo was situated right next to the finish line so we were able to have a look at what would await us the next evening. In the afternoon our children took part in the Transvulcania Kids Race, held up in the forest at the finish line of the half marathon, at El Pilar. It is beautiful spot but the start of the kids races gave us a tiny glimpse of what the morning might bring. It was so tightly packed that when the gun went off there were children falling over here, there and everywhere. There were cracked heads, bloodied noses and tears a plenty! Luckily, none of our children were injured and they proudly came away with medals and t-shirts, having run the 500m course. https://youtu.be/cHSAsTa17d0 In stark contrast to my race prep the night before the London Marathon, which was calm, relaxed, quiet, controlled and perfect in every way, getting to sleep the night before the Transvulcania Ultra was a bit of a nightmare. In hindsight, perhaps I should have spent some time during the day preparing my clothing and other gear, rather than trying to do it at 10pm with two ratty children and a stressed wife in tow. But, I did get a little sleep before the alarm went off at 10 to 3 in the morning. Yes, you read that correctly, 2:50am for breakfast at 3am. There were coaches laid on from the hotel to take runners to the start line, leaving at 4am. Transvulcania Ultra Transvulcania is an increasingly prestigious race around the world, but it’s absolutely massive on La Palma itself and everyone knows about it. The hotels are therefore well versed in catering for the needs of the runners. Breakfast was no spartan affair. It was fully laid out at 3am as it would be on any other day at 8am. The restaurant was packed with runners and three full coach loads left for the race start at 4am leaving a good number still standing outside the hotel entrance. I’m sure one of the coaches must have gone back for them. Our hotel was literally only 10 minutes drive from the start line at Faro de Fuencaliente. We arrived well in time for the 6am start so there was rather a lot of standing around in the dark. Faro de Fuencaliente is on the south coast of the island. There is a big, red and white striped lighthouse similar to the one at Beachy Head in Eastbourne and next to it stands the smaller, rather grey looking, old lighthouse. A road leads from the car park down to an open area which could be an overflow car park about the size of a football pitch. On one side is the Atlantic Ocean crashing up against a sea wall of black volcanic rock. On the other, the rock rises from the floor like a huge prison wall. This is where the organisers have chosen to place the start line. Fantastic Atmosphere We were all held at the top until an hour before the start when we slowly fil
- [Paris Marathon 2022 | The Zwift Crew Takes On Paris](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/paris-marathon-2022-zwift-crew-takes-on-paris): Blog Running Running Paris Marathon 2022 | The Zwift Crew Takes On Paris Stephen Cousins 3 April 2022 8 min read TL;DR Our eleventh consecutive Paris Marathon, this time with a group of nine friends from the Zwift community. Perfectly paced from start to finish, Victoria smashed a 10-minute PB to run 3:47:30 - earning a London Good for Age qualifying time. A cold morning, brilliant execution, and an evening celebration with friends who'd all achieved their goals. 26.2 Miles 3:47:29 Finish Time 11th Consecutive Year 10 min Victoria's PB Every year Paris Marathon feels different. Sometimes it's just Victoria and me against the course. Sometimes it's about survival. But 2022 was something special - a gathering of friends, all with different goals, all running together through the streets of the world's most beautiful city. The Zwift Crew Nine of us stood shivering at the Arc de Triomphe on a freezing cold Sunday morning. The Zwift community had become a real-life running club, and Paris was our annual reunion. Victoria, Jamie, Cecilia, Grace, Theo, Sebastian, Clive, Kevin, Lee, Jackie - each with their own target, their own story, their own reasons for being there. The plan was simple: pace smart, stick together as long as possible, and get everyone across the line with smiles on their faces. For Victoria, the target was anything under 3:50. For Jamie, it was his first ever marathon. For Cecilia, a new PB. Everyone had something to prove. Precision Pacing We hit 10k in 54 minutes 30 seconds - bang on schedule for a 3:50 finish. Clive was still with us. Sebastian was still with us. Victoria was going strong. The group was holding together perfectly. Halfway came in 1 hour 55 minutes. Perfect. Textbook pacing. At this point in a marathon, everything feels possible. The danger is getting carried away by that feeling. "Tired but in control." - Victoria at 30 kilometres. That's exactly where you want to be. The Iconic Landmarks There's a reason we keep coming back to Paris. Running past the Louvre. Through Château de Vincennes at 12k. The Eiffel Tower at 29k, right when you need the boost. The course is a greatest hits tour of one of the world's most beautiful cities. By the time we reached the Eiffel Tower, the sun was out, not too hot - conditions had turned perfect. Sebastian was feeling very good. Victoria was "tired but in control" - exactly where you want to be with 12 kilometres remaining. The Final Push At 30k the maths becomes simple: 12 kilometres to go, stay on pace, don't blow up. The group began to stretch as faster runners pushed on, but the pacing had been so good that everyone was still in the hunt for their targets. With 7k to go, anything under 3:50 was looking achievable. We'd built a small buffer through smart pacing, and now it was time to cash it in. A Clean Sweep Victoria crossed the line in 3:47:30 - a 10-minute personal best and, crucially, a London Marathon Good for Age qualifying time. After years of running Paris, she'd finally cracked that barrier. But the celebrations didn't stop there. Cecilia came in at 3:44:30, a new PB, beautifully paced. Sebastian finished in 3:47, a massive PB for him. Clive matched that time. Jamie - running his first ever marathon - broke sub-4 with 3:54. You can't argue with a sub-4 debut at the Paris Marathon. Kevin had already finished with his target of 3:15. Grace came in around 4:30. Even Lee and Jackie, aiming for the back-of-pack experience, crossed the line with smiles. Watch the Film I captured our group adventure through Paris on film. Here's the full race video: The Route What Running Should Be That evening, with sore legs and full hearts, we gathered for a meal. Everyone had achieved something. PBs had been smashed. First marathons completed. Goals that had seemed ambitious in January had become reality in April. This is what running should be. Not just the solo pursuit, not just the numbers on a watch, but the shared experience. Friends pushing each other, supporting each other, celebrating each other. Eleven consecutive Paris Marathons now. What started as my first major city marathon in 2012 has become an annual pilgrimage, a non-negotiable fixture in the calendar. But 2022 was different. 2022 was about the community we'd built, the friendships forged through virtual miles on Zwift that had become real friendships on the streets of Paris. Victoria's Good for Age time means London 2023 awaits. But we'll be back in Paris too. The streak continues.
- [Arc of Attrition 2019: 100 Miles of Cornish Coast](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/arc-of-attrition-2019): Blog Running Running Arc of Attrition 2019: 100 Miles of Cornish Coast Stephen Cousins 1 February 2019 10 min read In Brief 100 miles along the Cornwall coast in February. Snow chaos nearly stopped us reaching the start line. Then came the gnarly cliffs, the night running, and the marble-sized hailstones hitting sideways at 4am. This was my third Arc of Attrition, and it delivered everything the name promises - 28 hours of beautiful, brutal coastline. A PB and a gold buckle. 100mi Distance 28:31:46 Finish Time PB Result Gold Buckle Has there ever been a race where so many people had so much trouble just getting to the start line? The Arc of Attrition is already one of the toughest 100-mile races in the UK. The clue's in the name. But before we could even worry about the gnarly Cornish coastline, we had to navigate something equally treacherous: British weather in February. Snow had hit the southwest hard, and the A30 over Bodmin Moor became an overnight car park. My friend Richard was stuck there all night and never made it to the start. Out of 192 entries, over 30 people couldn't even reach Coverack because of the snow. We got lucky. A snow drift on the A38 near Exeter slowed us down, but we made it to our hotel in Camborne that evening, got some sleep, and drove to registration the next morning. A New Start The Arc had a new race HQ this year - the Ecological Park in Portreath. More room, better parking, a proper coffee area. The old Blue Bar on the beach had been getting swamped by 200 runners every year, so this was a welcome change. From there, we bussed to Coverack - a tiny village on Cornwall's south coast where the race begins. The start itself was more theatrical this year: a booming drum, the race director introducing the elite runners, and when the gun went off, we ran down the hill flanked by marshals holding blue flares. Quite an event. At midday, we were off. 100 miles of coastline awaited. The Southern Cliffs The Arc doesn't ease you in. Once you leave Coverack, you're immediately onto gnarly, difficult terrain. It's relentless from the very beginning - the kind of running where you're grateful for every flat section because you know it won't last. Lizard Point came at just over ten miles, two and a half hours in. I was running conservatively, preserving energy for later. Victoria and the kids were there with the camera - I'd given it to them again this year rather than carrying it myself. The section from Lizard to Mullion Cove was classic coastal stuff. Muddy, windy, the sun occasionally breaking through. Mullion Cove itself is a pretty little fishing village, and then it's on to Porthleven - the first official checkpoint at 25 miles. "It is gnarly from the very beginning. There is no messing about with this race." Into Penzance The run into Penzance is where the Arc changes character. After miles of brutal cliffs, you suddenly get four or five miles of flat, lit tarmac road. I actually like this section - it breaks up the 100 miles, gives you a mental reset before the real suffering begins again. Penzance is around 38 miles, depending on how many wrong turns you've taken. I pushed through the flat section, running it all, which left me tired but happy to have reached this milestone. Get to Penzance, get to Land's End, and you're doing well. The sun was going down as I left the checkpoint. The idea was to reach Porthleven before dark. The night section was about to begin. The Dark Hours Lamorna Cove. Minack Theatre. Land's End. These checkpoints blur together when you're running through the darkness, focused on nothing more than the next step, the next marker. I reached Land's End around 2am, slightly ahead of schedule. Victoria wasn't there - or at least, I couldn't find her. She claims she was in the car park. I don't believe her. I grabbed a quick bowl of chicken soup from the Archangels (the incredible volunteers who man every checkpoint) and pushed on. From Land's End to Cape Cornwall, the terrain becomes genuinely spectacular - if you can see it. At night, you're climbing over boulders, wondering if there's a massive cliff drop to your left (there probably is), trusting your headtorch and your GPS. This is some of the best running on the whole course, but my headtorch chose this moment to die. Changing batteries in pitch darkness, tired and cold, is not ideal. I reached Cape Cornwall at around 4am. Victoria cleaned my feet and changed my socks - small acts that feel enormous at 62 miles. I was feeling worse for wear. At one point I said "St Ives" when I meant "Land's End." Mental focus was fading. Pendeen to St Ives: The Hardest Section If you want to find the toughest terrain in UK running, look no further than the section between Pendeen Watch lighthouse and St Ives. Thirteen miles with no support, mostly in the dark, over rocky, muddy, slippery ground that barely qualifies as a path. And then the weather arrived. The wind had been blowing a gale most of the night. Then came the rain. Then came the hailstones - not tiny ones, but marble-sized projectiles, hitting sideways for fifteen minutes at a time. You're not running at this point. You're surviving, picking your way over rocks with hailstones smashing into your face. "Marble-sized hailstones, sideways, at 4am. This is not easy running, guys." Somewhere in this section, I made a navigation error. My mental focus was gone. I climbed a hill, looked at my watch, and realised I was off track. Rather than backtrack, I convinced myself there'd be a path back to the coast. There wasn't. I ended up in the village of Zennor, asking someone in a car park how to rejoin the coast path. I'd added two miles and half an hour to my journey. Lesson learned: don't blindly follow the person in front, but also don't blindly trust your tired brain. The coast path has acorn signs on posts. When you're exhausted, even those become invisible. The Final Push St Ives felt like salvation. I arrived at 10:30am - 22 and a half hours in. A
- [Paris Marathon 2018: PBs in the Heat](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/paris-marathon-2018): Blog Running Running Paris Marathon 2018: PBs in the Heat Stephen Cousins 8 April 2018 5 min read In Brief Paris Marathon 2018—another April morning on the Champs-Élysées, this time in the heat. Victoria battling cramps and the sun, but coming away with a PB. First-time marathoners discovering what 26.2 miles really means. This is why I keep coming back to Paris. 26.2mi Distance 4:23:08 Finish Time Hot Conditions PB Victoria Ten past eight on a Sunday morning in April, standing on the Champs-Élysées in Paris. This is becoming an annual tradition—the early morning start, the packed streets, the 50,000 runners ready to take on 42 kilometres through one of the world's most beautiful cities. The Beautiful Chaos The thing about Paris is it's so packed. More people than London, all funnelling through the same historic streets. You really have to make sure you find your space early. After the start, you can see all the detritus on the ground—bottles, jumpers, gels—the evidence of thousands of runners shedding layers as they warm up. The route takes you past some of Paris's finest landmarks, but so many people are focused on their race that they completely miss the sights. The Eiffel Tower stands right there, massive signs, a big water station opposite it, and people run past without looking up. I get it—when you're suffering, the last thing you're thinking about is tourism. "So many people are so focused on their race that they completely miss the Eiffel Tower." Into the Heat The early splits were solid—5K in around 46 minutes, 10K in 57 minutes as we passed the beautiful Château de Vincennes. By 13.5 kilometres we were at 1:17, still running through the Bois de Vincennes. But the heat was building, and Victoria was starting to feel it. Halfway came in 2:01, but we were falling behind now. Victoria was getting cramps, suffering in the heat, so we made the decision to chill out and see how we do. Around 14-15 miles we dropped down to run alongside the Seine, one of the loveliest sections of the course. The Battle Continues By 16 miles, Victoria was absolutely shattered. The heat was really taking its toll, so we took walking breaks, passing water stations where I'd throw as much water over myself as possible. What you'll notice about Paris is the organisation—they've got bins all along the route, water stations are well-stocked, and the support is excellent. 30 kilometres came in exactly three hours, about 12 minutes behind schedule. 20 miles in 3:15, with Victoria really struggling but doing the best she could. There's something admirable about pushing through when conditions turn against you. It would be easy to stop, but that's not why we're here. "A big leap from a 1:46 half marathon to a PB marathon is not to be sniffed at." Why Paris Should Be a Major One thing that's really good about Paris compared to London is that you get a proper aid station at the end of the race—all this food waiting for you at the finish. You wouldn't get that in London. I don't know about Berlin or New York, but it's another reason I always think Paris deserves to be a major. It's so much better than so many of the marathons I've done. Victoria got her PB, fighting through the heat and the cramps to get it done. We also had a first-time marathoner with us who earned their PB by default—though they did declare "never again" at the finish line. We'll see about that. Final Thoughts 4:23:08 in challenging conditions, helping others get to the finish line. That's what Paris means to me now—not chasing my own time, but sharing this incredible course with people experiencing it for the first time. Watching someone go from a 1:46 half marathon to completing their first marathon, that's what it's about. See you next year, Paris. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Mouth to Mouth Marathon 2018: December on the Downs](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/mouth-to-mouth-marathon-2018): Blog Running Running Mouth to Mouth Marathon 2018: December on the Downs Stephen Cousins 2 December 2018 5 min read In Brief My first Mouth to Mouth Marathon, a 27-mile trail run along the South Downs Way from the River Arun to the coast. Rainy December conditions, beautiful views of Arundel Castle, and a finish line paramedic check after a pre-race health scare that turned out to be nothing serious. A proper December adventure. 27mi Distance 4:10:42 Finish Time December Month South Downs Terrain The Mouth to Mouth Marathon was a new one for me—a 27-mile trail run along the South Downs Way, starting at the River Arun and making its way to the coast. December running in England means one thing: expect rain. The forecast delivered exactly that, but there's something oddly satisfying about running through proper winter weather on trails that have seen centuries of feet. A Pre-Race Health Scare In the days before the race, I'd been dealing with a painful chest. I was fairly sure it was because I'd rolled over onto my headphones in the middle of the night—a mundane explanation for an alarming symptom. But when various people told me to get it checked out, I listened. A trip to the hospital, an ECG, and blood tests later, everything came back fine. It's the kind of thing that makes you realise how quickly we can catastrophise, and also how important it is to not ignore warning signs. Better to feel slightly foolish at A&E than to ignore something that could be serious. "Sometimes the sensible thing is getting checked out. Sometimes it's just headphones." River to Downs The race started near the river, crossing the bridge and then climbing up onto the South Downs Way. This is classic Sussex downland running—rolling chalk hills, muddy gates, and those long views that make you feel small in the best way. By ten miles in, I was settled into a rhythm, the earlier health concerns fading with each step. Passing through Amberley at around the 28km mark provided a welcome checkpoint. This stretch of the South Downs is particularly beautiful, with Arundel Castle visible in the distance as a constant landmark. There's the castle up there—a reminder that people have been moving through this landscape for centuries. The Final Miles With one and a half loops left, the December light was fading and the rain continued its steady accompaniment. This is the point in any marathon where you either find a groove or you start questioning everything. Today was a groove day—not fast, not pretty, but consistent. Coming into the finish, I apparently looked a bit pale. Pale enough that the paramedic on duty wanted to double-check everything was in order. Given my pre-race hospital visit, it seemed wise to let him do his thing. Heart check complete—one, two, three, go—and all was well. "Not always an easy run, but always worth finishing." Final Thoughts 4:10:42 for 27 miles of December trails along the South Downs Way. Thanks to the paramedic who looked after me at the finish, to Thomas for manning the aid stations, and to CJ for organising another fabulous run. Special mention to Terry and Dr. Phil who were out there putting in the work. Sometimes races are about personal bests and pushing limits. Sometimes they're about getting through, staying healthy, and appreciating that you're out there at all. This was the latter—a December reminder that the running community looks after its own, and that trails don't care about your times. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [RAT Plague 2018: 100km Around the Roseland Peninsula](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/rat-plague-2018): Blog Running Running RAT Plague 2018: 100km Around the Roseland Peninsula Stephen Cousins 11 August 2018 6 min read In Brief The RAT Plague—100 kilometres around the Roseland Peninsula in Cornwall, organised by Mud Crew. Starting in darkness, chasing the sunrise, a traditional sea dip, 2,500m of climbing, and finishing in the rain. I loved it so much the first year, I came back for round two. 100km Distance 15:13:20 Finish Time 2,500m Elevation 17th Position The Roseland August Trail weekend—RAT for short—is one of those events that sounds completely unreasonable on paper and even more unreasonable in practice. A 100km out-and-back along the Cornish coast, starting in the dark, with 2,500 metres of climbing thrown in for good measure. I loved it so much last year that I came back for a second helping. The Mud Crew Setup Base camp was the Portpion Outdoor Education Centre—tents scattered across the campsite, registration over there, food somewhere else, and the sea visible in the distance. The British summer was doing its thing, which is to say it wasn't terribly warm, but that's never stopped anyone here before. The Plague is the headline event—100km from Portpion to St Anthony's Head and back—but it's part of a full weekend that includes the Black Rat (50k), the White Rat (11 miles), and various other distances designed to cater to different levels of masochism. Richard was running with me this year, which always helps when you're about to spend fifteen-plus hours on your feet. "We go out in the dark, we come back in the rain. It's gonna be awesome." Into the Night Starting an ultra in the dark is a particular kind of experience. The headtorch creates a bubble of light around you, and the world shrinks to whatever's immediately ahead. By 1:30am we'd covered 11 kilometres through the Cornish night. Gorran Haven came at around 10 miles, just over two hours in. The early morning hours passed in that strange time-distorted way they do in ultras. By five o'clock, with 34 kilometres done and another 10 miles to the turnaround point, the first hints of daylight were appearing on the horizon. There's something magical about running through a sunrise—the world slowly revealing itself around you. The Turnaround and Sea Dip It wouldn't be a Film My Run video without a traditional sea dip. The water was cold enough to wake up every nerve ending, the perfect antidote to legs that had been working for six hours straight. A quick dip under, cool the legs off, and then back to business. Marathon distance came at 6 hours 21 minutes—slow by road standards, but this wasn't a road race. Paul was up front absolutely flying, with a lead of about a minute. The out-and-back format meant passing other runners coming the other way, trading encouragement and suffering in equal measure. "Nobody ever said anything about hills. I was promised a flat hundred K." The Long Way Home Portscatho brought bacon butties (which I admired but didn't eat), and then St Anthony's Head for the turnaround. That's when the real work begins—you've done the exploring, now you have to retrace every step, knowing exactly what's coming. By 60 kilometres I'd been running for over eight hours, but there was still that spring in your step that comes from turning around and heading home. See how long it lasts. The checkpoints became a blur of faces and coffee requests. At one point the generator had failed, meaning no coffee—I jokingly blamed this for not winning the race. The Cornish coast revealed itself in stages: rock formations, harbours, endless steps climbing out of fishing villages. We'd climbed 2,500 metres by the time we hit 75 kilometres. Rain and Resolution The rain arrived on cue for the final stretch. Gorran Haven at 86.5 kilometres, then the final aid station with 8K to go. My legs were shot by this point—really shot—but that's what ultras do to you. The White Rat runners were starting to come through, fresh legs making our shuffling look even more pitiful. 15 hours 13 minutes and 20 seconds. If you're going to come and do the Plague, know that it's really tough. But also know that it's great fun, with a fantastic crowd, and that it's absolutely worth it. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Three Forts Challenge 2015: A Week After London? Why Not.](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/three-forts-challenge-2015): Blog Running Running Three Forts Challenge 2015: A Week After London? Why Not. Stephen Cousins 3 May 2015 6 min read In Brief A 27-mile trail marathon across the South Downs, connecting three ancient Iron Age hillforts—Cissbury Ring, Chanctonbury Ring, and Devil's Dyke. Running this just one week after the London Marathon wasn't sensible, but sensible isn't really the point of trail running. 27.2mi Distance 4:27:23 Finish Time 1,016m Elevation 86th Position Running a trail marathon one week after the London Marathon is not what sensible people do. But then again, sensible people probably don't spend their weekends voluntarily climbing 3,450 feet over the South Downs either. The Three Forts Challenge had been on my radar for a while. Known locally as "The Tough One," it's been a Sussex institution since 1977—a proper old-school trail race that takes you over three Iron Age hillforts: Cissbury Ring, Chanctonbury Ring, and Devil's Dyke. Twenty-seven miles of rolling chalk downland, endless climbs, and the kind of views that almost make you forget your legs are screaming at you. Almost. The Questionable Decision A week earlier, I'd crossed the finish line on The Mall. My legs were still having conversations with me about that, none of them polite. But the Three Forts was a local race, starting just down the road from where I trained with Worthing Harriers, and the entry was already paid. So there I was on a foggy May morning, hydration vest strapped on, wondering what I'd got myself into. At the start line, the Worthing Harriers contingent was out in force. Maureen, my coach, was there—an absolute star who'd helped shape my running over the years. I spotted another runner kitted out almost identically to me—same vest, same waterproof, nearly the same shoes. It was her birthday, of all days to be running 27 miles over the Downs. And then there was Mike, who just wanted to say hello to his mum via the camera. The running community is a small world. Into the Fog The weather had other ideas about showing off those famous South Downs views. As we rounded Cissbury Ring—the first of our three forts—the fog was so thick you could barely make out the ancient ramparts. Not that there was much time for sightseeing. The wind had picked up too, making filming nearly impossible and conversation even harder. My legs, surprisingly, felt okay at first. Perhaps the muscle memory from London was still there, or perhaps my body simply hadn't woken up to what was happening yet. I settled into a steady rhythm, chatting with fellow runners when I could. One of those was Mark Cameron, a running buddy who'd transformed himself from a bodybuilder into a distance runner. He'd written a book about it— The Diary of an Average Runner —which was doing well on Amazon. We ran together for a stretch, swapping stories about training and racing. The Relentless Middle By 26 kilometres—around 16 miles—the honeymoon period was over. I'd pushed a bit on a downhill section and suddenly felt it. The legs that had been "feeling okay" were now making their complaints known. Walking up the hills became less of a choice and more of a necessity. "The route was relentless in that way only trail marathons can be. You'd crest one climb, catch your breath, start a descent, and there it was—another hill rising up ahead." Cissbury Ring done. Devil's Dyke done. Now the long slog towards Chanctonbury and back. At around 23 miles, I caught up with a runner called Louise. It was only her second marathon—her first had been Beachy Head, which is no joke—and she was declaring it would be her last. "I've just never done hills like this before," she said. Fair enough. The South Downs have a way of humbling you. Another runner, Mark (a different Mark), was on his sixth marathon but his first trail. His previous marathons had all been on road, including Berlin. "Couldn't get flatter than that, mate," he observed, looking at yet another climb ahead of us. He wasn't wrong. The Final Push For the last few miles, I found myself leapfrogging with a couple called Helen and Thomas. We'd been trading places for most of the race, but they pulled ahead in the final stretch. That's the thing about trail marathons—your position can change constantly depending on who's better at climbing, who's better at descending, and who remembered to eat enough at the checkpoints. The finish felt earned in a way that road marathons sometimes don't. There's something about dragging yourself over three Iron Age hillforts, through fog and wind, on legs that were already tired from the week before, that makes the medal feel heavier. I celebrated with a hot chocolate and watched some of my Worthing Harriers clubmates come in. The camaraderie at these local races is something special—everyone cheering each other on, sharing war stories about which climb nearly broke them. Looking Back The Three Forts Challenge was my fourteenth marathon and my ninth on trails. It taught me something I'd learn again and again in the years to come: running on tired legs isn't about being fast, it's about being stubborn. And sometimes the best races aren't the ones where everything goes perfectly—they're the ones where you show up anyway, knowing it might be stupid, and do it regardless. Since 1977, this race has been challenging runners across the Sussex Downs. The forts have been there even longer—thousands of years of history beneath your feet as you grind up those chalk paths. There's a certain perspective that comes from running through landscapes that ancient Britons once defended. Your tired legs suddenly seem like a smaller problem. Would I recommend running a trail marathon a week after a road marathon? Probably not. Would I do it again? Almost certainly. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Larmer Tree Marathon 2021 | Summer Llama](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/larmer-tree-marathon-2021-summer-llama): Blog Running Running Larmer Tree Marathon 2021 | Summer Llama Stephen Cousins 31 July 2021 8 min read TL;DR The Summer Llama at Larmer Tree Gardens - a White Star Running marathon through the beautiful Rushmore Estate. Running with Victoria through forests, country lanes, and open fields, meeting fellow runners from Bad Boy Running and Lonely Goat clubs. Finished together in 5:25:05 after 27 miles of summer trail running. 27 Miles 5:25:05 Finish Time Summer Llama Edition Together With Victoria White Star Running marathons are never quite what they say on the tin. A "marathon" is usually 27 miles. There are no llamas at the Llama races (it's Larmer Tree Gardens, spelled differently). But that's part of the charm - these are events for people who love trail running and don't take themselves too seriously. I'd done the Spring Llama years ago, so when the chance came to return for the Summer Llama with Victoria, we jumped at it. The Rushmore Estate Larmer Tree Gardens sits within the Rushmore Estate on the Wiltshire-Dorset border - a stunning setting for a trail marathon. The course winds through a mixture of forest, country lanes, and open fields, with the gardens themselves providing a spectacular start and finish venue. This was part of the Larmer Tree Festival weekend, with multiple events taking place: the marathon, a 10-miler, and shorter distances. The atmosphere was festive in the best sense - people out to challenge themselves but also to enjoy the day. Running Glitterati At the start, I bumped into representatives from two of the biggest running clubs in the UK - Bad Boy Running and Lonely Goat. Ann Davis was on either her 50th or 51st marathon (she couldn't quite remember), while Simon Lynch was on his third. When I asked what they were hoping for, the answer was perfect: "What are you hoping for today?" "To not die." That's the White Star Running spirit right there. We also met Kate, doing the 10-miler ahead of her wedding the following Saturday, and Harry from Frome, Somerset, on his first Larmer Tree but a White Star veteran. The Course The first 5k took just over half an hour - a gentle start through the varied terrain. By 13 kilometres, we'd reached the entrance to Rushmore Park Estate, 1 hour 22 minutes in. The aid stations were cheerful and well-stocked, as you'd expect from White Star. At 24.5 kilometres, with about 11 miles still to go, I could feel the distance. This wasn't a fast course - the terrain saw to that - but it was beautiful. Around 30k, three and a half hours in, came a long drag: not massively steep, but long and relentlessly upward. The Final Push At 33 kilometres, approaching four hours, I reckoned we had about 11k to go. White Star's generous marathon distances mean you can never quite trust the numbers. We hit 40k in 4 hours 57 minutes, with probably another 3 or 4 kilometres remaining. My target had been done by 5:20 something. We came in at 5:25:05 - close enough. Watch the Film I captured our Summer Llama adventure on film. Here's the full race video: The Route Why White Star? Seven and a half hours after the race started, the final runners were still coming across the line. That's what I love about White Star Running events - they're for everyone, from the speedsters at the front to the determined finishers at the back. Everyone gets the same medals, the same cheers, the same experience. The Larmer Tree Marathon isn't about PBs. It's about beautiful trails, good company, and the simple pleasure of running through the English countryside on a summer's day. Victoria and I finished together, which made it all the more special. Will we be back for another Llama? Almost certainly. Maybe Spring, maybe Summer. The gardens are waiting, and so is another 27-mile adventure through the Rushmore Estate.
- [Virtual London Marathon 2020 | Running My Own Race](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/virtual-london-marathon-2020-running-my-own-race): Blog Running Running Virtual London Marathon 2020 | Running My Own Race Stephen Cousins 4 October 2020 9 min read TL;DR The first ever Virtual London Marathon - running 26.2 miles from Worthing to Brighton in 3:24:49. Started with a brutal headwind that forced me to abandon the out-and-back plan and run point-to-point with the wind at my back. Audio broke on the camera, dropped all my Skittles, but smashed my target by running a fast finish along the Sussex coast. 26.2 Miles 3:24:49 Finish Time Virtual Format First Ever Virtual London 2020 was the year everything changed. The London Marathon, like so many other races, couldn't happen in its traditional format. Instead, the organisers created something new: a virtual marathon where you could run your own course, anywhere in the world, tracked by an app on your phone. I chose the Sussex coastline. The plan was simple: 5 kilometres out, 5 kilometres back, repeat four times with a little extra at the end. What could possibly go wrong? The Wind Has Other Ideas The moment I turned to head out along Worthing seafront, I knew this was going to be tough. The wind was absolutely brutal - a proper coastal headwind that felt like running through treacle. By 5 kilometres, I was already worried. If I had to run into this wind every other leg, it was going to wreck me. After the first out-and-back, I made a decision. One more leg into the wind, then I would change the plan. Instead of laps, I would run point-to-point - all the way from Worthing to Brighton with the wind at my back. Sometimes you have to adapt. The London Marathon App One of the clever touches of the virtual race was the London Marathon app. Every mile, Steve Cram or Paula Radcliffe would pop up in my headphones with commentary and encouragement. It wasn't the same as running through the streets of London with crowds cheering, but it was something. I also wasn't alone out there. Loads of people were running with their Virgin Money London Marathon bibs on. I'd decided not to wear mine, but seeing everyone else made me wish I had. There was a real sense of community, even in this strange new format. The Long Road to Brighton At 15 kilometres, I turned for the final time and headed east towards Brighton with the wind finally at my back. The relief was immediate. Suddenly the pace that had felt brutal going into the wind felt easy. Halfway came in 1 hour 44 minutes - bang on for a 3:30 finish. My wife met me at 20k for a quick pit stop: lukewarm tea, a bottle of Purdey's, and a load of Skittles to stuff in my pocket. Perfect. "I dropped all my Skittles. Managed to try and pull them out of my pocket and almost all of them fell on the floor. I had about four to eat." Through Shoreham, past the power station, along the grim but necessary stretch before Hove. At 30k I was at 2:26 - still well on course. The London Marathon app miles were ticking over faster than my watch, GPS drift on a phone app doing its thing, but I trusted my watch. The Brighton Seafront Push By 35 kilometres, running along the Hove seafront towards Brighton Pier with the wind strong behind me, I started to think bigger. Could I get under 3:25? Madeira Drive - the finish line of the Brighton Marathon - came at 37k and 3 hours flat. The maths was simple: 5 minutes per kilometre from here to get under 3:25. I pushed on towards Brighton Marina, then along the undercliff path. At 40k, 3 hours 14 minutes in, I knew I'd smash my 3:30 target. Now it was about that stretch goal. The Finish I crossed my finish line - climbing the steps from the undercliff path past Brighton Marina - in 3 hours 24 minutes and 49 seconds. The app claimed 3:21, but I trusted my watch. Either way, I'd absolutely smashed my target of sub-3:30. My wife was there at the top of the steps. The first ever Virtual London Marathon was done. Watch the Film I captured the run on camera - although the audio broke after the first few clips and had to be overdubbed. Here's the full race video: The Route A Different Kind of Marathon Was it the same as running the real London Marathon? Of course not. No crowds, no landmarks, no finishing on The Mall. But it was something. A marathon is a marathon, wherever you run it. 26.2 miles doesn't get easier just because you're running along a seafront instead of through city streets. The virtual format forced me to be creative - adapting my route when the wind made the original plan impossible, finding my own landmarks and milestones, creating my own race experience. In some ways, it was more challenging than a traditional marathon because every decision was mine to make. Looking back, the 2020 Virtual London Marathon was a strange but memorable experience. It proved that the running community could adapt, that we could find ways to keep going even when the world stopped. And it gave me a PB-level time on a course I designed myself, with the wind at my back and the Sussex coast stretching out ahead. Not bad for a pandemic.
- [Bewl Water Marathon 2020 | A September Gem](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/bewl-water-marathon-2020-september-gem): Blog Running Running Bewl Water Marathon 2020 | A September Gem Stephen Cousins 19 September 2020 8 min read TL;DR A stunning marathon around Bewl Water reservoir in East Sussex. Two laps of beautiful trails, woodland, and some surprisingly steep country lanes. Gorgeous September weather, great company, and a finish time of 4:02:35. The kind of race that reminds you why you run. 26.2 Miles 4:02:35 Finish Time 2 Laps Perfect Weather Some races are about times and PBs. Others are about the experience. The Bewl Water Marathon falls firmly in the second category - a gorgeous loop around one of the largest reservoirs in southern England, organised by people who genuinely love running. The Setup Hermes Running puts on this event, led by Dave Ross who also organises the Vanguard Way Marathon. When you see the same friendly faces at start lines around the South East, you know you're in good hands. The format is straightforward: two laps of Bewl Water reservoir, starting and finishing at the same spot. The weather gods were smiling on us - one of those perfect September days where the sun is warm but not oppressive, and the light catches the water just right. More Hills Than Expected Don't let the "reservoir lap" description fool you. By eight miles in, I'd already encountered quite a few steep climbs on country lanes that really took it out of the legs. East Sussex is rolling countryside, and the course doesn't shy away from that terrain. I met a runner called Dream along the way - this was his 58th marathon, well on his way to the hundred mark. He'd done Bewl Water seven times, with a fastest of 3:59. When I optimistically suggested we might be headed for 3:15, reality quickly set in. At 19 kilometres, we were already off four-hour pace. The Second Lap Two-lap courses have their own psychology. You know exactly what's coming, which is both reassuring and slightly daunting when you remember those steep hills waiting for you again. At 23 kilometres, the course was still delightful - lots of wooded areas like the section we were passing through, lots of open grassland with views of the reservoir. But everyone was starting to flag a little. The warm weather was taking its toll. "East Sussex is very famous for these oast houses - you'll find them dotted all around the county." The iconic oast houses of Kent and Sussex appeared at intervals along the route, those distinctive conical roofs that once dried hops for brewing. Running past them felt quintessentially English. The Long Road Home At 30 kilometres, nearly three hours in, we hit the long tarmac section. Hard surfaces after so much trail running feel jarring, and my legs were protesting. I met Sarah, who was doing the ultra distance - no surprise she was feeling tired too. The hills just kept coming. At 33k, three hours fifteen minutes in, I was really struggling on the climbs. The warmth that had felt pleasant earlier was now sapping energy. A first-timer I chatted with summed it up perfectly: "A little bit tired, but nothing that's going to make me not finish." That's the spirit of trail marathons right there. The Finish Coming up to 40k, the wind picked up but the end was in sight. I crossed the line in 4 hours 2 minutes and 35 seconds. Dave, the organiser, had beaten me at the last race we'd both done - a rivalry to continue. Because of COVID, we had to put our own medals on - one of those small adaptations that 2020 demanded. But the achievement was the same, and the medal was earned. Watch the Film I captured the beauty of Bewl Water on film. Here's the full race video: The Route Worth the Trip Bewl Water Marathon is the kind of race that doesn't make the big lists or attract thousands of runners. But that's part of its charm. A couple hundred people, a beautiful location, friendly organisers, and a properly challenging course. I flagged in the last 5k, as usual with marathons. The tarmac hills in the final stretch were brutal. But really, I enjoyed it. The gorgeous weather, the scenery, the company of fellow runners all pushing towards their own goals. I'll be back. Some races earn a place in your calendar, and Bewl Water has definitely earned its spot.
- [Dark Star River Marathon 2022 | January Benchmark](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/dark-star-river-marathon-2022-january-benchmark): Blog Running Running Dark Star River Marathon 2022 | January Benchmark Stephen Cousins 6 January 2022 7 min read TL;DR The Dark Star River Marathon - 28 miles along the River Adur in January. My third time running this race, and my best time and placing yet. Battled the wind on an out-and-back course to finish 7th in 3:58:05, just sneaking under my four-hour target. 28 Miles 3:58:05 Finish Time 7th Place 3rd Attempt January racing in England is always a gamble. The Dark Star River Marathon has become my annual early-season test - a 28-mile out-and-back along the River Adur that tells you exactly where your winter training has got you. This was my third attempt, and I was determined to make it my best. The Start Line Paul Sergeant was there, as always. Let's be honest - when Paul shows up, the win is out of the question for everyone else. He claimed he wasn't fit. He always says that. But the smile on his face at the start line told a different story. The format is simple: 22.5 kilometres out along the river, turn around at a tunnel, 22.5 kilometres back. No complicated navigation, no technical terrain - just you against the path and the wind. Wind and River Seven miles in, the conditions were clear: definitely wet, not too muddy, but the wind was a killer. A headwind on a river path is relentless - no trees to shelter behind, no hills to block it. You just put your head down and keep moving. At 20 kilometres, I clocked through in 1 hour 43 minutes. On target for four hours, but I knew the way back would be harder. It always is. The second half of an out-and-back is where the race really happens. "It's always the same on these races. Paul Sergeant is always in the lead." At the turnaround, Paul was already heading back, locked in a fight for first with the runner behind him. Nick Barter was solid in third. I grabbed a quick Coca-Cola and turned for home. The Way Back Halfway done. 22.5 kilometres completed in 1 hour 57 minutes - only just on target for four hours. The margin for error was slim. At 20 miles, with 13 kilometres still to go, I had an hour and 15 minutes to stay under four hours. The maths was simple but the legs were starting to tire. Every checkpoint became a mini-goal: hit 25k, hit Bramber, hit 3k to go. At Bramber, with 7.5 kilometres remaining, I was still in the hunt. At 3k to go, I had 20 minutes. It was going to be close. Sub-4 Secured I crossed the line in 3 hours 58 minutes and 5 seconds. Seventh place overall, and just barely under my four-hour target. Best time I'd ever run this race, best placing too. Paul Sergeant had won, of course. By the time I finished, he'd already had a shower, got changed, had a meal, phoned his wife, and probably walked home. That's the kind of gap we're talking about with Paul. My friends Joe and Nick had both finished around 3:48 - faster than me, but I couldn't begrudge them that. They'd run excellent races. Watch the Film I captured the wind and the river on film. Here's the full race video: The Route January Benchmarks There's value in returning to the same races year after year. The Dark Star River Marathon has become my January benchmark - a consistent course where the only variables are the weather and my fitness. Three attempts now, each one faster and higher placed than the last. It's not a glamorous race. No stunning mountain views, no exotic location. Just 28 miles of river path in the English January. But that simplicity is its strength. You can't blame the course when things go wrong. It's all on you. Third time, best time, best placing. The trend is pointing in the right direction. Maybe next year I'll catch Joe and Nick. Maybe next year I'll break 3:50. But I'll never catch Paul Sergeant. Nobody catches Paul Sergeant.
- [Beachy Head Marathon 2018 | The Seven Sisters and a Cup of Tea](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/beachy-head-marathon-2018-seven-sisters-cup-of-tea): Blog Running Running Beachy Head Marathon 2018 | The Seven Sisters and a Cup of Tea Stephen Cousins 27 October 2018 7 min read TL;DR The iconic Beachy Head Marathon - 25-something miles across the South Downs on a glorious October day. Stunning views of the Seven Sisters, a cup of tea at mile 17, and a finish time of 4:05:40. One of Britain's most beautiful trail marathons with free food and a swimming pool at the end. 25+ Miles 4:05:40 Finish Time Oct 2018 Iconic South Downs The Beachy Head Marathon isn't quite a marathon. It's "25 something miles" - that's just the way it is. Nobody seems to mind. You don't come to Beachy Head for accurate distances; you come for the views, the challenge, and the unique character of one of Britain's most beloved trail races. A Perfect Day on the Downs October 2018 gave us a gift: a beautiful sunny day on the South Downs. The kind of day that makes you grateful to be a runner, grateful to be outside, grateful to be tackling this iconic course from Eastbourne across the chalk cliffs and rolling hills of East Sussex. At the start, I caught up with Stuart Mills, who has won this marathon eight times. His last win was in 2015 - "He's getting old and past it now," someone joked. That's the Beachy Head spirit: irreverent, friendly, and fiercely competitive all at once. Through the Villages By four and a half miles, we were dropping down into Jevington - a beautiful village famous as the birthplace of the Banoffi pie. I was held up for traffic for the first time ever at Beachy Head, which felt like a minor milestone in itself. I met Mark, running his 13th Beachy Head ("Let's hope it's not unlucky for him"), and Ana, on her third. Everyone had the same assessment: beautiful day, just enjoy it. "How are you feeling on your first marathon?" "I can't say because it won't be publishable. I had a period where I just felt like crying." By seven miles we were dropping into Alfriston. At 12 kilometres, I'd done 1 hour 53 minutes - not quite halfway, but still on track for around four hours if we kept it up. The Cup of Tea Checkpoint At 17 miles, I stopped for a cup of tea. This is Beachy Head - civilised trail running at its finest. No gels, no energy drinks, just a proper brew to see you through the final third. I chatted with a first-time marathoner who admitted to having "a period where I just felt like crying." Anyone who's run a marathon knows that feeling. You'll have a few more of those moments before the finish, I told them. It's all part of it. The Seven Sisters And then came the view that makes Beachy Head special. With six miles to go, you enter the final stretch and there they are: the Seven Sisters, that iconic series of chalk cliffs rolling away towards the horizon. Absolutely beautiful. This is what you're paying for when you enter Beachy Head. Birling Gap at four miles to go marked the final aid station. From there, it's the home stretch along the cliff tops, the lighthouse visible in the distance, the finish getting closer with every step. The Finish I crossed the line in 4 hours 5 minutes and 40 seconds. Tom scraped in just under four hours at 3:59 - awesome work. James finished in 4:07. A good day out for all of us. One of the lovely things about Beachy Head is what happens after you finish: free food, and if you fancy it, a free swimming pool. They'd changed the medal design this year too - nice, decent medal to add to the collection. Watch the Film I captured our sunny October day on the South Downs on film. Here's the full race video: The Route Why Beachy Head? Beachy Head Marathon has been running since 1982. It's one of those races that has earned its place in the calendar through decades of consistent excellence. The course is challenging - proper South Downs terrain with all the ups and downs that implies - but the organisation is slick, the atmosphere is friendly, and the scenery is world-class. Come and run Beachy Head next year. You'll love it, I promise.
- [Purbeck Marathon 2018 | Beautiful Suffering on the Jurassic Coast](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/purbeck-marathon-2018-beautiful-suffering-jurassic-coast): Blog Running Running Purbeck Marathon 2018 | Beautiful Suffering on the Jurassic Coast Stephen Cousins 16 September 2018 7 min read TL;DR The Purbeck Marathon - one of the most beautiful trail marathons in the UK, running from Swanage along the Jurassic Coast and through the ghost village of Tyneham. I went out too fast, hit the wall hard, and death-marched to a 5:17:54 finish. Brutal, but absolutely gorgeous. 26.2 Miles 5:17:54 Finish Time Dorset Jurassic Coast Brutal But Beautiful It was a calm, serene, quiet, beautiful morning on the coast at Swanage. The kind of morning that makes you believe you can do anything. That belief would be tested. The Purbeck Marathon is one of the nicest trail marathons in the UK. The route runs from Swanage onto the coast path, then inland to Tyneham, up around the ridge to Corfe Castle, and back down. It's stunning. It's also brutal. The Perfect Start I'd done this race before, and I should have known better. But the glorious September sunshine and the beautiful coastal scenery tricked me into thinking I could push the pace. I went out aiming to do the first half in around two hours. Five miles in came the first major climb, heading inland off the coast. By the end of the second major climb, we'd gained about 360 metres and were coming into the village of Kingston. Still feeling strong. Still passing people. Still believing. Tyneham - The Ghost Village At 15 miles, I reached Tyneham, where my wife met me with a cup of coffee. Tyneham has a haunting history - the entire village was evacuated in the 1940s to make way for a military training range, and it's been frozen in time ever since. The church still stands, a monument to the community that once lived there. I walked up the hill drinking my coffee, enjoying the moment. And then everything changed. "You know those races where you start off really strong, passing loads of people, and then you get to halfway and everything drops away? Your motivation goes. Your momentum goes. Your legs go. I had one of those today." The Death March By 17 miles, 27 kilometres in, I'd lost all momentum since Tyneham. The coffee break, the hill, something - my legs were feeling very heavy. The pace that had felt sustainable was now impossible to maintain. At 21 miles, I was death-marching it in. That horrible phase of a marathon where you know you're slowing down, you can feel people catching up behind you, and one by one they're coming past. It's not a good feeling. I met Steve from Brighton and his daughters Mia and Thea along the way - a welcome distraction from the suffering. The Steam Railway One of the beautiful things about the Purbeck Marathon is crossing the Swanage Railway steam line. The engine we saw was built in Brighton in 1955, one of the last steam trains ever made. A little bit of transport history to appreciate while your legs scream at you. The Finish I crossed the line in 5 hours 17 minutes and 54 seconds. Jake finished in a much more respectable 3 hours 20 minutes. You win some, you lose some. Today, the Purbeck Marathon won. Each time I've done this race, I've got slower. But it's still beautiful. That's the thing about Purbeck - even when you're suffering, you can't deny the scenery. Watch the Film I captured the beauty and brutality of the Purbeck Marathon on film. Here's the full race video: The Route Come to Dorset Despite the suffering - or perhaps because of it - I've got a thing for the Purbeck Marathon now. I need to come back. I need to try and do this better. Come to Dorset. Come and run on the Jurassic Coast. Come and run anything on the Southwest Coast Path. The Purbeck Marathon is definitely one of the marathons to do in the UK. When the weather is like this, you cannot beat it. Absolutely gorgeous. Just maybe don't go out quite as fast as I did.
- [Val d'Aran 100 by UTMB | The Hardest Race I've Ever Done](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/val-daran-100-utmb-2021): Blog Running Running Val d'Aran 100 by UTMB | The Hardest Race I've Ever Done Stephen Cousins 9 July 2021 8 min read In Brief The hardest race I have ever done. 100 miles through the Spanish Pyrenees with 10,000 metres of climbing, two sleepless nights, and temperatures that had us throwing ourselves under mountain streams. Over 300 runners DNF'd. I finished in 46 hours and 51 minutes—and meant every word when I said I was just glad to be home. 100 Miles 46:50:32 Finish Time 10,000m Elevation 300+ DNFs That was the hardest race I have ever done. Not hardest by a small margin—hardest by a country mile, if you'll pardon the expression. The Val d'Aran 100 by UTMB was the inaugural edition of this race through the Spanish Pyrenees, and it lived up to every terrifying promise the elevation profile had made. The Start in Vielha In true UTMB style, the start and finish line sat right next to a quaint village church in Vielha. Everything was compacted into a few metres—registration, bag drop, information point, presentation area. It's the kind of intimate race village that UTMB does so well, making a 100-mile death march feel almost cosy. I was nervous. Really nervous. 100 miles with 10,000 metres of ascent and a 48-hour cutoff. The numbers alone were intimidating, but standing in that Spanish heat an hour before the start, handing in my drop bag, I felt the full weight of what I was about to attempt. UTMB Traffic Jams If you've ever run a UTMB race, you know what happens at the start. Four and a half kilometres in, we came to a complete standstill. Hundreds of runners bottlenecked on a narrow trail, shuffling forward a few steps at a time. This happens at every UTMB race anywhere in the world, and somehow I'm always surprised by it. By the first checkpoint—two hours and six minutes in, with 800 metres already climbed and 11 kilometres covered—I'd found my rhythm. And the views. My God, the views. Standing at the top of the first climb at 14 kilometres, looking out across the Pyrenees before the sun went down, I could see Aneto, the highest peak in mainland Spain. "It's more of a long slow hike than a run, this event." Into the First Night By the third aid station, six hours and 37 minutes in, reality started setting in. The cutoff was closing in about 35 minutes—we weren't far inside it. A big climb loomed ahead, and it was half past midnight. I grabbed soup and bread and got moving. At 38 kilometres, after a huge climb and descent, I could see the headlamp lights of other runners snaking up the next mountain behind me. Then up again. At five to three in the morning, with morning just starting to break, we'd covered 50 kilometres in 11 hours 55 minutes. Almost a third of the way. I didn't feel too bad, though the climbs were starting to take their toll. The Monster Climb At 64 kilometres, arriving at Canejan, the race briefing notes came back to haunt me: "And then we have the monster climb of the whole run." A 1,500-metre ascent up the side of a mountain, with a beautiful blue lake visible far below. At 75 kilometres, we were still slogging up that climb. Every time we came across a stream, we threw ourselves under it—the heat was relentless. At 20 hours and 24 minutes, we hit 80 kilometres. Halfway. That's when I realised this race would break me. Quads Destroyed The downhills were where the damage happened. By 95 kilometres, at 25 hours in, my quads were absolutely shot. I could run on the flat, make my way slowly uphill, but downhill running was agony. And we still had 65 kilometres to go. At 103 kilometres, I reached the aid station with my drop bag. I was very, very tired, rapidly losing patience with the race. So hard. I changed clothes, ate what I could stomach, and prepared for the second night on the mountain. The aid station volunteers told me over 300 people had already withdrawn. DNF'd. It was a beast of a race, and looking around at the empty chairs, I understood why. Tonight, I'd be alone on the hills. The Second Night By sunrise on day three, I felt sick. Two nights without sleep, stomach rebelling, feet screaming, legs completely trashed. And still 20 miles to go on the gnarliest course I'd ever seen. You can't deny it's beautiful though. That's the cruel trick of mountain ultras—they destroy you in the most spectacular settings imaginable. The Final Cutoff Like an idiot—as I always do—I'd failed to read the information correctly. I thought one aid station had the critical cutoff; it was actually the next one. But we had three hours to get there, with a climb and a 968-metre descent. Dai, my fellow sufferer, thought we could do it. I thought we could do it. We made it to the final aid station with a cutoff time with an hour to spare. Food, cooling down, one more big climb and one more little climb, then downhill to Vielha. Coming Home The final section followed the same pattern as the previous two days: trudging slowly through forest, emerging into open land, seeing the higher mountains in the distance. We'd done this four times now. But this was the last one. With three and a half kilometres to go, I could see Vielha below. My legs were rock solid—I could hardly move. But I was going to finish. "From the United Kingdom, well done Stephen. Ring that bell!" 46 hours, 51 minutes. The announcer called my name, I rang the bell, and the wave of relief that washed over me was unlike anything I'd experienced before. Stephen's coming home. Football's coming home. (It was July 2021—the Euros were on.) The Hardest Race I've run a lot of ultras. I've done 100-milers before. But nothing prepared me for the Val d'Aran. The combination of heat, elevation, technical terrain, and two sleepless nights broke something in me—and then put it back together again at the finish line. This was the inaugural running of this race. UTMB had created a monster, and over 300 runners couldn't tame it. But somehow, I did. That was the hardest race I have ever done. And I'm just so glad to be back home. Watch 
- [TDS 2021 | When the Mountains Took One of Us](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/tds-2021-race-abandoned): Blog Running Running TDS 2021 | When the Mountains Took One of Us Stephen Cousins 24 August 2021 7 min read In Brief TDS 2021—my second attempt at this UTMB race—was abandoned at 60 kilometres after a fatal accident on the course. A Czech runner, who had started with the same excitement and nervous anticipation as the rest of us, died doing what he loved. This isn't a race report.
