It's a reflection on risk, mortality, and why we keep running. 60 Kilometres Abandoned Result 145km Full Distance 9,000m Elevation I love trail running. I love the sense of adventure and the adrenaline of climbing in the mountains. There's an addiction to the sense of danger you get, holding on to a chain rope next to a steep drop or traversing an exposed ridge. None of us knew at the start of TDS 2021 that we were about to see those very real dangers exposed to us in such a tragic way. The Start in Courmayeur Of course, the race began like any other. Courmayeur, on the other side of Mont Blanc, was warm that afternoon. Race start was at 4pm, with the faster runners heading off first. I was in the third wave. In the second wave, just ahead, was an experienced runner from the Czech Republic. He was 15 years younger than me, but we'd both started our ultra running journeys in 2014. By coincidence, we'd both finished Transgrancanaria Ultra in 2020. I imagine he was just as nervous and excited as me as we stood on those start lines—145 kilometres of mountains and valleys between us and the finish in Chamonix. This was my second attempt at TDS. The year before had ended in a DNF. I was determined to make it work this time. Family and Fear The race start was as energised as always, with Eoin Flynn's recognisable voice filling the air as we passed under the start gantry. This time my wife and children were there to see me off. But often they're back at home or in a hotel, thinking of me. My wife says she's always in a heightened state of anxiety every time I take to the trails in a big race like this. I imagine the family of the Czech runner ahead of me had similar feelings. Knowing your runner is experienced and confident, but at the same time nervous that everything should go as smoothly as it had done so many times before. He was a much faster runner than me, with impressive podium positions in numerous ultras. I imagine him striding confidently up the mountain, relishing the beauty of his surroundings. Into the Mountains On fresh legs, the first climb out of Courmayeur was comfortable in the evening sun. First aid station at Checrouit—one hour eight minutes in, 700 metres climbed. The trails around the Mont Blanc massif are generally runnable; there are very few sections of truly technical terrain. What makes UTMB events so difficult is the sheer amount of elevation, the length and steepness of the climbs. At 2,417 metres above sea level, having climbed 1,300 metres in 10 kilometres, the sun started going in. At Lac Combal, runners were preparing for the night—hats on, gloves on, coats on. We heard thunder. They'd warned us at the start about a possible storm. Looking out for that, we descended towards Col du Petit Saint-Bernard, 16 kilometres and five hours to make the cutoff. "None of us knew at the start that we were about to see those very real dangers exposed to us in such a tragic way." Fort de la Platte By the time I reached Bourg-Saint-Maurice at 50 kilometres, nine hours and 14 minutes in, the Czech runner was already some 10 kilometres ahead. As I was descending from Col du Petit Saint-Bernard, he was at the top of the climb out of Bourg-Saint-Maurice near Fort de la Platte. That climb—1,500 metres straight up—was always going to be tough. But at 3am, I made it to Fort de la Platte. Well ahead of cutoff. There was a beautiful fire, and this year I had money, which meant I could buy an Orangina. I was happy. That happiness was short-lived. Race Abandoned Just a few kilometres further on, I arrived at the most technical section of the race. Standing at 60 kilometres, my phone buzzed with a text message: the race has been abandoned. All runners must turn back. Looking up the mountain, I could see headlamp lights stretching into the darkness—runners who now had to descend back down. Ten kilometres back to Bourg-Saint-Maurice. Buses back to Chamonix. The end of the race. My initial disappointment is understandable, but looking back it feels incredibly selfish. What I didn't know at the time was that the accident up ahead had been a fatal one. A Runner Lost The Czech runner—who had started with the same confidence, excitement, and nervous anticipation as I had just a few hours earlier—had fallen on the most technical and dangerous part of the course. A trail runner doing what he loved, doing the same thing as me, was dead. Walking back down in the darkness, all we knew was that there had been an accident. I wasn't aware of the countless runners stranded further up, unable to make it back down until ropes had been put in place. I didn't know runners had been turned around because the rescue helicopter couldn't see to retrieve the body—blinded by the headtorches below. Finally arriving back at Bourg-Saint-Maurice, waiting for a bus to Chamonix, news started to filter back. The mood turned to somber reflection. Reflection Much of that reflection is still selfish, of course. It could have been me. I'm so relieved it wasn't me. I hope my wife knows I'm okay. But it must have been absolutely heartbreaking for the family of the Czech runner. A man who went to the mountains to do what he loved, and didn't come home. "Don't stop running, my friend. Life is all about taking risks—it's the risk-takers who turn their own lives around or change the world." Why We Run I've thought about this a lot since that night on the mountain. Why do we take these risks? Why do we put our families through the anxiety of watching us head into the mountains for days at a time? The answer, I think, is that life isn't meant to be lived froz
- [Dorchester Marathon 2017: Victoria's First, Steve Edwards' 782nd](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/dorchester-marathon-2017-victorias-first): Blog Running Running Dorchester Marathon 2017: Victoria's First, Steve Edwards' 782nd Stephen Cousins 28 May 2017 5 min read In Brief The inaugural Dorchester Marathon—White Star Running's first road race. Pacing Victoria through her first-ever marathon, passing the house where Thomas Hardy lived, and sharing the course with Steve Edwards on his 782nd marathon. Yes, you read that correctly. 26.2mi Distance 4:41:41 Finish Time 376m Elevation 45th Marathon White Star Running doing a road marathon. I know. I had to double-check too. But when the local Rotary Club wanted to put on a big charity event, they came to "Britain's best race company"—Andy's words, not mine—and the Dorchester Marathon was born. This was the inaugural edition, about 800 runners lining up in the centre of Dorchester before heading out into the Dorset countryside. The route wound through country lanes past Woodford Castle, through villages with names like Tolpuddle (yes, of the Martyrs), and past Max Gate—the house where Thomas Hardy lived. If you're going to run a marathon in Wessex, you might as well lean into the literary heritage. First-Timer and 782-Timer I was running with Victoria, and this was her first marathon. The plan was to aim for around 3:30, but plans and marathons don't always cooperate. More on that later. At the start, I spotted a familiar figure: Steve Edwards. When I asked him how many marathons he'd done, the answer was 782. Seven hundred and eighty-two marathons. "All goes well," he added, because apparently at that number you stop counting chickens. Steve Edwards is a legend of the marathon community, and sharing a start line with him is one of those moments that reminds you how deep this sport goes. "On the right, first marathon. On the left, 170th." — The range of experience on the Dorchester course. That's the beauty of events like this. First-timers and centurions running the same roads, everyone in it together. As Traily as a Road Marathon Gets White Star promised this would be "as traily a road marathon as you can possibly get," and they weren't wrong. The route was hilly—376 metres of elevation, which doesn't sound like much until you're on lap... well, there were no laps. Just 26.2 miles of undulating Dorset lanes. The support was unexpectedly brilliant. I really didn't expect the level of cheering we got through the villages. The patrons of the Blue Vinnie pub had come outside to watch rather than staying at the bar—a sacrifice I don't take lightly. At one point I caught up with David Gold, who was running in zero-drop sandals—proper minimalist running sandals with an X strap. "You find them all right?" I asked. "I do, yeah," he said. Different strokes for different folks. Characters on the Course Megan was running because her friend had started training and she'd become his training buddy. "So then I thought I might as well do it," she said. That's how it happens—you start as moral support and end up crossing finish lines. I met a runner from Bournemouth who normally only does trail but had made an exception for Dorchester. "This is a lovely one," she said. Coming from a trail runner, that's high praise for a road race. And then there was the superhero theme. Capes, masks, spandex—because apparently running 26.2 miles isn't enough, some people need to do it dressed as Captain America. Fair play to them. The Finish Victoria and I crossed the line in 4 hours and 41 minutes. Not the 3:30 we'd hoped for, but her first marathon was done. That's the main thing. First marathons aren't about time—they're about getting around and discovering what you're capable of. At the finish, the rain started. Because this is Britain, and you can't have a marathon without at least a bit of weather. We collected our medals—White Star medals, so properly hefty—and headed for cover. "If you want a road marathon that's as near to a trail marathon as you can get, come and do Dorchester." White Star should be proud of what they created here. It had all the hallmarks of their trail events—the atmosphere, the support, the community feel—just on tarmac and country lanes instead of muddy paths. The inaugural Dorchester Marathon was a success, and I'd be surprised if it wasn't on the calendar for years to come. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Centurion CROC 100 | Running Through Lockdown](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/centurion-croc-100-lockdown-2020): Blog Running Running Centurion CROC 100 | Running Through Lockdown Stephen Cousins 30 May 2020 7 min read In Brief During the 2020 lockdown, when races were cancelled and communities were isolated, 4,000 runners across the world came together for the Centurion Running One Community event. I designed my own 100-mile route linking the Beachy Head Marathon, South Downs Way 50, Three Forts Marathon, and Steyning Stinger. 28 hours of running through the night, throwing up at 35 miles as always, and finishing at Devil's Dyke with the sunrise. 100 Miles 27:42:30 Finish Time 4,000 Runners Worldwide 4 Races Linked In 2020, across the world, friends and families were torn apart. Communities were fractured by an invisible enemy. But this is a story about coming together—about an adventure designed to beat the separation and loneliness. One community, no longer bound by convention but by a shared passion, set out on a journey. And together, during the global lockdown, they were set free. The CROC Event Centurion Running's One Community event—CROC—attracted some 4,000 runners and walkers from all over the world. Distances from 5k to 100 miles could be completed over a week, either at home on a treadmill or outdoors on road or trail. Given that this was a Centurion-organised event, it seemed appropriate to be running on their well-known and well-loved courses. I designed a route that would link four classic South Downs races into one continuous 100-mile adventure. The Beachy Head Marathon Victoria started running with me that morning. We began the Beachy Head Marathon from Bo Peep car park—kind of halfway around the loop. The plan was simple: she'd do the marathon, I'd keep going. We headed down into the village of Litlington, through the wooded area of Friston Forest, and down through the Cuckmere Valley. Stunning doesn't begin to describe it. Then up and over the Seven Sisters, towards Belle Tout lighthouse, before reaching Beachy Head itself. One thing you don't actually see during the Beachy Head Marathon is the Beachy Head lighthouse—the route takes you slightly inland. But the views are spectacular regardless. "As I ran, I could sense four thousand other runners across the world overcoming their own challenges right beside me." South Downs Way 50 in Reverse With Victoria's marathon complete, I carried on alone. From Beachy Head, I followed the Bridle Way and then the South Downs Way, heading all the way to Worthing—essentially running the South Downs Way 50 in reverse. I passed the famous white bridge at Southease, a landmark known to every South Downs runner. And then the familiar feeling hit: around 35 miles, I started feeling really sick. It often lasts until 60 miles, when I usually throw up. This time was no different. The plan was elaborate: run to Devil's Dyke, then start the Three Forts Marathon, do the entire Steyning Stinger Marathon, then run back to Devil's Dyke to finish the Three Forts. If that makes any sense. I hope it does, because it didn't make much sense to me either. Into the Night By 78 kilometres, I'd thrown up everywhere. Halfway done. Part of me wanted to call it a day, but with a big push from my wife, I headed into the night to start the Three Forts Challenge—so named because it links the three ancient hill forts of Devil's Dyke, Chanctonbury Ring, and Cissbury Ring. At 104 kilometres, just past midnight, I reached Hill Barn. I'd officially finished the South Downs Way 50 in reverse and the first half of the Three Forts Marathon. Time to start the Steyning Stinger. At half past two in the morning, standing in the middle of the road outside Steyning Leisure Centre, I began yet another marathon. By quarter past four, I'd covered 125 kilometres and was near the top of one of the Stinger's major climbs, watching the early morning sunrise paint the hills gold. The Final Push Making it through the night always feels good. I'd been struggling, but sunrise gave me new strength in my legs and the knowledge that the finish was within reach. Steyning Stinger, Three Forts, and Beachy Head are all significant challenges in their own right. Linking them together had seemed like a perfect plan, but the reality of these things is often far less glamorous. Everything hurt by now. But it's supposed to. That's why we do it. That's why we love it. At 143 kilometres, I finished the Steyning Stinger and headed back towards Devil's Dyke for the final section of Three Forts. At 151 kilometres, I began the last climb. "It doesn't matter who you are. And you made it through. A collective journey—we did it together. Community." Devil's Dyke 163 kilometres. 28 hours and 3 minutes. Standing on the gorgeous Devil's Dyke as the world began to wake up around me. That's it. The Centurion Running One Community event was over for me. 100 miles done. Four races linked. One night without sleep. One sunrise that made it all worthwhile. And somewhere across the world, 4,000 other runners were finishing their own adventures, overcoming their own challenges. We weren't together physically, but we were together in spirit. During the darkest days of the lockdown, running set us free. Watch the Film The Route
- [Goodwood Marathon 2020: Breaking Three Hours](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/goodwood-marathon-2020-sub-3): Blog Running Running Goodwood Marathon 2020: Breaking Three Hours Stephen Cousins 6 December 2020 8 min read In Brief Eight years after my first marathon, I finally broke three hours. 2:58:57 at Goodwood Motor Circuit on a freezing December morning, running eleven laps into a bitter wind. This wasn't luck - it was the culmination of years of consistent training, high mileage weeks, and learning to trust the process. Here's how I did it. 2:58:57 Finish Time Sub 3 Achievement 120+ Marathons Run 8 years Journey I ran my first marathon in April 2012. I was 42 years old. Until then, I'd been a casual runner - school sports, the occasional jog along the seafront near home, nothing serious. My first 10k was in 2010. A half marathon followed. Before I knew it, I was on the slippery slope: trail marathons, running clubs, ultra races. My marathon times improved gradually from around 3:30 to 3:15, and eventually in 2016 I ran London in 3:09. But sub-3 remained elusive. The barrier. The goal that separated casual marathoners from serious ones. After 120 marathons, I was finally ready to attempt it properly. The Training Training to achieve a sub-three marathon takes years. Some people are gifted, genetically primed to run under three hours with minimal preparation. For the rest of us, it starts when you first step out the door to run your first mile. That's when you begin training for a sub-3 marathon, whether you know it or not. Initially it's about building a strong aerobic base and conditioning your body. New runners suffer niggle after niggle as their bodies adapt. It can take many years of consistent running to reach a stage where you rarely get injured, where you can run 10 miles without breaking a sweat and complete a half marathon without needing water. Once you've got that base, the next step is volume. For quite a few years I was running about 40 miles a week. Then I upped my game to a consistent 100 kilometres weekly. In the six months before this race, I ran at least 100km every week, with some weeks at 130km, some at 140km, and one week at 150km. "No one is going to hand you a sub-3 marathon on a plate. You need to work for it." The 80/20 Approach I adopted an 80/20 strategy: 80% of sessions at a very slow pace, 20% hard efforts. This enabled me to achieve high volume without getting over-fatigued or injured. The hard sessions were either high-intensity intervals on the treadmill or short, sharp 5k time trials where I'd push my heart rate into zones 4 and 5. I tried to stay clear of the comfortable zone 3 void. It's unavoidable that you spend some time there, but I'd never plan a session to be a zone 3 session. That grey area where you're working too hard to recover easily but not hard enough to improve significantly. The benchmarks told me I was ready: an 18:33 5k, a 38-minute 10k, a 1:25 half marathon. Race predictors said I was right on the cusp - some predicting just over three hours, some just under, all with margins of error. Race Day Goodwood Motor Circuit in December. Freezing cold, exposed, windy. The course was roughly a 4km loop, meaning eleven laps with two and a half kilometres into the wind every single time. You'd dread that bend every lap. Race day breakfast was my standard: a tin of rice pudding and a couple of cups of coffee. Rice pudding sits easily on my stomach and provides slow-release carbohydrates. I wore a light Montane fleece over my race singlet for the first three laps, then threw it to the side of the road. Nike Vaporfly Next% on my feet - carbon-plated shoes that are legal and help you go faster, so why not? For pacing, I'm a huge fan of even splits and negative splits. I ran most kilometres at exactly the same pace, watching my average pace in km/h and lap pace in min/km. For sub-3, you need 14.1 km/h or 4:16 per kilometre or 6:50 per mile - ideally a little faster to account for not running the perfect racing line. "This was not a case of fingers crossed and hope for a good day. This was executing a plan I was perfectly capable of doing." Nutrition During the Race I didn't eat or drink anything for the first 20 miles. This wasn't recklessness - it was the result of training fat-adapted, running many sessions on empty to teach my body to burn fat more efficiently. At 20 miles I had half a banana and a small bottle of fizzy fruit drink. That was it. Many gastric problems in long-distance running come from too much sugar intake - overloading on gels and Coke. If you can train your body to need less fuel, you avoid those problems. On a cold day like this, I didn't even need to drink water because I wasn't losing fluid through sweat. The Finish I crossed the line in 2 hours 58 minutes 57 seconds. My watch showed 42.4 kilometres - an extra 200 metres from not running the perfect line. I had to sprint the last bit just to make sure I got under three hours. My friend Richard finished in 3:03, his PB. We stood in the freezing cold afterwards, not realising how bitter it was until we stopped running, talking about the wind on that bend, the eleven laps, the achievement. "I can now retire," I said. "I never have to run another marathon ever again." I was joking, of course. Final Thoughts After eight years of running marathons, I was finally there. A sub-3 marathoner. Not gifted, not genetically primed - just consistent, patient, willing to put in the miles week after week, year after year. Now I think I'd be disappointed if I didn't get close to sub-3 every time I run a road marathon. The standard has changed. The barrier has been broken. And it only took eight years of stepping out the door, one run at a time. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Crafty Fox Marathon 2018: Two Loops of Dorset Hills](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/crafty-fox-marathon-2018): Blog Running Running Crafty Fox Marathon 2018: Two Loops of Dorset Hills Stephen Cousins 8 September 2018 5 min read In Brief The inaugural Crafty Fox Marathon by White Star Running delivered everything you'd expect from this race organiser: brutal hills, friendly faces, questionable navigation, and a guestbook in the middle of nowhere. Two loops, 44km, 1200m of climbing, and a finish time that reflected every single contour line on the map. 44km Distance 5:14:51 Finish Time 1,200m Elevation 2 Loops White Star Running has a reputation for putting on races that hurt in the best possible way, and their inaugural Crafty Fox Marathon was no exception. Set in the hills of Dorset, this was trail running at its most character-building—the kind of event where you're walking within the first two kilometres and wondering what life choices brought you here. Welcome to White Star Country I'd done a few White Star events before and knew what to expect: grassroots organisation, friendly vibes, and courses designed by someone who clearly enjoys watching runners suffer. The Crafty Fox was billed as a marathon, but White Star marathons come with an asterisk—this one clocked in at 44 kilometres with 1200 metres of elevation gain spread across two loops. The start field was the usual mix of ultra veterans, trail enthusiasts, and a few road runners about to have their world view adjusted. Standing at the start line, I spotted Richard Palmer, who I'd see again at various points throughout the day, and reconnected with Chris from the South Downs Way 100 earlier in the year. "Two kilometres in and we're down to a walk already. That set the tone for the entire day." The Two-Loop Challenge The course format meant running the same loop twice, which has its pros and cons. On the positive side, you know what's coming the second time around. On the negative side, you know exactly how much suffering awaits. That first loop was a voyage of discovery—each hill revealing another, each descent a temporary reprieve before the next climb. One of the unique features was the guestbook at Dorset Gap, placed there by the race organisers for runners to sign as they passed through. It's these little touches that make White Star events special. In the middle of a gruelling climb, you stop to scribble your name in a book while catching your breath. It's absurd and wonderful. Aid Station Highlights White Star aid stations are always an experience. The volunteers were brilliant, keeping spirits high even as runners shuffled in looking progressively more dishevelled with each lap. The ginger cake became a particular highlight—proper fuel for the hills ahead, and a reminder that sometimes the simple things matter most during a long race. Carolyn was out sweeping the course, ensuring no one got lost or left behind. These unsung heroes of trail running deserve more recognition—standing out in the elements for hours, walking the entire course at the back of the field, making sure everyone gets home safe. The Final Push The second loop brought fresh challenges. Knowing what was coming didn't make it easier—if anything, the anticipation made certain climbs feel longer. But there's also something satisfying about ticking off landmarks you remember from the first lap, knowing exactly how far you have to go. The final stretch included a delightful ploughed field section that had clearly been designed to test whatever leg strength remained. By this point, running had become more of a philosophical concept than a physical activity. But that's the joy of these events—you dig deep, find something you didn't know was there, and eventually cross a finish line that feels genuinely earned. "White Star marathons come with an asterisk. That's part of the charm." Final Thoughts 5:14:51 for a "marathon" that was actually 44km with 1200m of climbing. Not my fastest, but times don't tell the whole story. The Crafty Fox was a proper day out in the Dorset hills, surrounded by like-minded people who'd chosen to spend their Saturday getting muddy and exhausted for the sheer joy of it. White Star Running continues to deliver events that feel different from the mainstream. No chip timing, no huge expo, just well-marked trails, friendly faces, and courses that will test everything you've got. I'll be back. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [South Downs Way 100 2018 | Third Time Lucky](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/south-downs-way-100-2018): Blog Running Running South Downs Way 100 2018 | Third Time Lucky Stephen Cousins 15 June 2018 10 min read TL;DR Third attempt at the South Downs Way 100. Managed it once before, failed last year. Hot conditions made for a brutal day, but the stunning chalk downs and incredible volunteers got me through to a 24:44 finish and that coveted buckle. Date: 9th June 2018 | Distance: 100 miles | Time: 24:44:57 | Elevation: 4,000m Third attempt at the South Downs Way 100. Managed it once before, failed last year. Let's do it again. The SDW100 holds a special place in my heart. It's run on home turf - 100 miles along the chalk spine of England from Winchester to Eastbourne. I know these trails. I've trained on these hills. And yet, somehow, they never get any easier. A Record Field This was the seventh edition of Centurion Running's flagship event, and a record 305 runners lined up at the start. It also marked the organisation's 10,000th starter across all events and their 27th 100-mile race. There was a real sense of history in the air. The weather forecast was good - perhaps too good. The day dawned warm and dry, and it would stay that way throughout. For some, that's ideal conditions. For me, someone who wilts in the heat, it was going to be a long day. The Beautiful Struggle By the first aid station I was already feeling the warmth. Old Winchester Hill at the half marathon mark was a gorgeous climb, but the sun was relentless. At Queen Elizabeth Country Park - 33.5km in, just over four hours - I could feel the day ahead weighing on me. The section through Harting Down at around 28 miles is honestly one of the most beautiful parts of the South Downs Way. Five hours and 40 minutes in, absolutely beautiful scenery, but I was suffering. I don't like the hot weather. Never have. "I'm dying today," I admitted to a fellow runner at the Cocking aid station, 35 miles in. "The heat is just unbearable." "I say it's worse than the Thames Path," he replied. "Why are you here then?" "Because my favourite's always been the Arc. I'll be back again next year." That's ultra runners for you. We complain about the suffering while planning the next one. Halfway and Beyond At Washington, well over halfway, I got changed and felt fresher. My wife was there, as she always is, a beacon of support in the chaos of an aid station. 92km in 13 hours and 18 minutes. We're so lucky to run on these gorgeous downs. Much as I was suffering - tired, hot, mentally beaten up at only 43 miles - the beauty of the landscape kept pulling me forward. The climb up to Devil's Dyke at 66.6 miles was a proper grind. Some runners were wearing Devil's horns - 666, you see. Very clever. I didn't even think of that at the time. I was too focused on putting one foot in front of the other. The Dark Hours At Housedean Farm - 76 to 78 miles depending on who you ask - I was just throwing up. Delightful, isn't it? You all wanted to know that. But sometimes after you've been sick, you feel much better. Twenty hours and 24 minutes in, just 22-23 miles to go. Coming into Southease at half past four in the morning, 15 miles from home, the world was quiet and beautiful. The sunrise over the Downs is something special. Alfriston at dawn, that pretty little village with its ancient church - I was so tired but so grateful to be there. Did you know banoffee pie was supposedly invented in Alfriston? At the Hungry Monk restaurant, which is now cottages. The things you think about at mile 92. The Final Push Jevington, the final aid station. I didn't go in. Let's just get on and finish this race. 23 hours and 48 minutes. The top of the final climb at the trig point, looking back down at how far I'd come, looking forward to those last three miles of descent to Eastbourne. Yes, buddy. Eastbourne Sports Park. The end of the South Downs Way. One lap around the track and that's it - the finish line. 24:44:57 Given yesterday's conditions, I'll take that. I will take that. Any finish is a good thing. I'd earned that buckle today. 24 hours and 46 minutes of forward motion through some of the most beautiful countryside in England. We're so lucky to run on these gorgeous downs. Much as I was suffering, the beauty of the landscape kept pulling me forward. Charlie Harpur won the men's race in 15:01 - the second fastest time in the event's history. Sarah Cameron took the women's title in 18:14. A record 223 buckles were awarded, with a 73% finish rate. John Fanshawe, in the MV70 category, set a new record of 25:11, improving the previous mark by three hours. Incredible performances across the board. For me, it was simply about getting the job done. Third time lucky. Well, third time successful at least. There's nothing lucky about running 100 miles. Race Stats 100mi Distance 4,000m Elevation 24:44 Finish Time 73% Finish Rate Watch the Film Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Gun 31 Guernsey 2019 | Redemption on the Cliffs](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/gun-31-guernsey-2019): Blog Running Running Gun 31 Guernsey 2019 | Redemption on the Cliffs Stephen Cousins 17 November 2019 5 min read In Brief 29 miles along the Guernsey cliff paths, starting at midnight, racing the sunrise. Last year I was the only person who didn't finish. This year? 7:08:07—with 22 minutes to spare before the cutoff. Redemption on the steps of Guernsey. 29 Miles 7:08:07 Finish Time 7:30am Cutoff Time 0 Sleep Welcome to Film My Run on this beautiful evening. It's a lot calmer than it was when I was here this time last year on a hill fort, overlooking the town of St Peter Port in Guernsey. We're here for the Gun 31—not actually quite 31 miles, more like 29 miles-ish—all the way along the coastal cliffs of Guernsey, out to the end and back again. Starting at midnight. The idea is to get back here by 7:30 in the morning. Sunrise. Cutoff. A Score to Settle Last year, I was the only person who didn't finish this course. Seven hours and 36 minutes, just missing the cutoff. That failure had been eating at me for twelve months. At the start line, I caught up with Tom Chamberlain, who won this race last year. "Are you looking at a time?" I asked. "About five and a half hours," he said casually. The cutoff is seven and a half hours. I had a score to settle; Tom was just here to win again. The Cliff Steps The entire cliff coastline of Guernsey is littered with steps. Up and down, up and down, endless stone staircases carved into the cliffs. Red markers tell you you're going the wrong way; white markers keep you on course. At the first checkpoint—about 5 miles in, one hour thirty minutes—the lead runners were already pulling away. Second place came through, then Graham in fourth. "Living the dream, dude," someone shouted. We all were, in our own sleep-deprived way. At halfway—24 kilometres, around 3:30am—the cutoff was tight. I got through with about 8 minutes to spare. Still climbing steps. Four hours ten minutes. Twenty-nine kilometres done, just over ten miles left to go. "Last year, I was the only person who didn't finish. This year, I had a score to settle." The Difficult Section The back half is where it gets really tough. Lots of elevation still to climb—500 metres of ascent in the final section. Eleven kilometres to go, six and a half miles, seven miles depending on your watch. I was trying to get in under seven hours, but I didn't think I was going to manage it. And there was a guy about 200 metres behind me, chasing me down. Four kilometres to go. The race wasn't just against the clock anymore. Sunrise Finish I didn't make it in seven hours. But I held off the guy behind me. 7:08:07—just coming up to the finish as the sun started peeping over the horizon. Better than last year. Twenty-two minutes inside the cutoff. Redemption. The final runner came in right at the end, crossing the line just before 7:30. "Don't come home if you don't finish," his children had told him. He finished. That's what ultras are all about. Why Gun 31? I spoke with Peter, one of the organisers, after the race. Who should come and do this race? "Anyone who wants a challenge," he said. "There's a dual cutoff—if you get in under seven and a half hours, you get a medal and a t-shirt. If you finish in under nine hours, you get a t-shirt but no medal. It's good for people training for other races, or looking to step up to longer distances that extend into the darkness." The beauty of Gun 31 is the paradox: you feel completely isolated on those cliff paths in the dark, but you're never actually far from civilization. It's safe. There's a motorised sweeper. You can practice night running on technical terrain without the anxiety of being truly alone. "You get the feeling of isolation, but you're never actually far from civilization." I flew in at 4 o'clock yesterday, sat in a café, raced at midnight, and I'm flying back today. No hotel needed. It's an adventure you can fit into a weekend. If you've never been to Guernsey, come and do the GU36 in May. If you love it—which you will—come back for Gun 31 and have a real challenge. Now I'm going to go sit in a café for a few hours. Until next time. Watch the Film The Route
- [Atlantic Coast Challenge 2017: Three Marathons to Land's End](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/atlantic-coast-challenge-october-2017): Blog Running Running Atlantic Coast Challenge 2017: Three Marathons to Land's End Stephen Cousins 6 October 2017 7 min read In Brief Three marathons in three days along the Southwest Coast Path, finishing at Land's End. Day one: glorious sunshine. Day two: driving rain and wind. Day three: gnarly bouldering terrain. Family camping trip, Arc of Attrition flashbacks, and a watch that died right before the finish. 78+ mi Total Distance 3 Days Duration Land's End Finish Cornwall Location Back in March, I'd run the Jurassic Coast Challenge—three days of coastal marathons in Dorset. Now it was October, and Votwo Events had brought us to Cornwall for the Atlantic Coast Challenge. Same format: three consecutive marathons, each around 26 miles, camping in between. Except this time we'd finish at Land's End, the most southwesterly point of mainland Britain. We'd turned it into a family holiday. Caravan, Victoria, the kids—a proper Cornish adventure with a bit of running thrown in. Or rather, a lot of running with some family time squeezed around the edges. Day One: Sunshine and Stunning Scenery The first day was blessed with the kind of weather that makes you want to live in Cornwall. Blue skies, sunshine, the coastal path unfurling ahead of us like a postcard. "Absolutely lovely," I kept saying to the camera, knowing full well that this wasn't going to last. The checkpoints had everything you'd want: bananas, Jaffa cakes, Mars bars, and—crucially—ice creams. Votwo Events know how to look after their runners. We wound through the Cornish countryside, 26 miles of coastal path, finishing on the beach at Perranporth as the sun dropped towards the Atlantic. "Believe me, it's not going to be like this tomorrow. It's going to be rainy and wet." I was right. Day Two: The Rain Arrives The second morning started with a very different sky. "It's not as nice as yesterday," I observed—a masterpiece of understatement. The rain had arrived, and the wind had brought friends. The format for these multi-day events is simple: you get a hug at the start, then you run. We set off from Perranporth with waterproofs on and heads down. Eight miles in, we passed the Blue Bar in Porthleven, and I had a moment of recognition. This is where the Arc of Attrition finishes—that brutal 100-miler I'd run back in February, starting in Coverack and ending right here. Running past a finish line you've crawled to in the dead of night, now in daylight with relatively fresh legs, gives you a strange perspective. The coast path is beautiful, but it doesn't get easier just because you've done it before. At checkpoint three, I made the questionable decision to have another Marmite sandwich. At 30 kilometres, you take whatever motivation you can get. Victoria and the kids joined me for the last stretch, and we finished back at the caravan site together. A family finish to a thoroughly damp day. Day Three: The Gnarly One Half past seven, Sunday morning. "Welcome to day three of the Atlantic Coast Challenge," I announced to the camera. "Today it's a tough section. It's really gnarly. But hopefully the weather will hold." The weather held. The terrain, however, was brutal. This final stretch to Land's End is the most technical section of the Southwest Coast Path. By 14 kilometres, we were in what I could only describe as a bouldering section—not running, barely hiking, more like scrambling over rocks with increasingly tired legs. "How about this for an extreme checkpoint? If that's not enough to convince you to come and do this next year, I don't know what is." The checkpoints were spectacular—perched on clifftops, views stretching out to sea. Zennor. Cape Cornwall. Each one a reminder of why people fall in love with this coastline. And then, with Land's End finally in sight, my watch died. Typical. "I have no idea what time I've done," I admitted as I stumbled towards the finish. But the time didn't matter. We'd made it—three days, three marathons, 78-plus miles of Cornish coast. Three Days of Cornwall Looking back, the Atlantic Coast Challenge gave us three completely different days: Day 1: Sun, stunning scenery, ice creams at checkpoints. 26 miles in 4:49. Day 2: Rain, wind, Marmite sandwiches, family finish. 26 miles in 4:51. Day 3: Gnarly terrain, extreme checkpoints, a dead watch. 26 miles in 6:29. The Southwest Coast Path is one of the most beautiful long-distance trails in Britain, and running it in October means you get the full range of Cornish weather. Sun one day, horizontal rain the next, then calm but challenging terrain to finish. That's the deal, and it's worth every step. If you're thinking about doing the Atlantic Coast Challenge—or the Jurassic Coast version in Dorset—just do it. Even if it rains, you will not regret it.
