- [Serpent Trail 100k 2021: A Lesson in Pacing](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/serpent-trail-100k-july-2021): Blog Running Running Serpent Trail 100k 2021: A Lesson in Pacing Stephen Cousins 3 July 2021 7 min read In Brief 100 kilometres through the forests and heathland of Surrey, Sussex and Hampshire. I went out too fast, collapsed around halfway, and ground out the final 20 miles on willpower and marmite sandwiches. Finished under 14 hours while England beat Ukraine 4-0 in the Euros. Sometimes ultras are about surviving, not thriving. 103km Distance 13:41:59 Finish Time ~1,800m Elevation Haslemere Start Ten to five in the morning. Rice pudding for breakfast. Coffee in hand. This is how ultras begin. The Serpent Trail 100k follows the waymarked trail of the same name through Surrey, Sussex and Hampshire - from Haslemere down to Petersfield. I'd run it about four years earlier when the field was much smaller. This time there were loads of us, which meant any hopes of a top-10 finish were gone before we started. Never mind. We'd see what we could do. The Good Start The first section was beautiful - cool, overcast, perfect running conditions. By seven and a half miles we'd climbed 400 metres and I was feeling strong. By 13 miles and two hours in, we'd covered over 700 metres of ascent through stunning forest trails, following the little purple triangle signs that mark the Serpent Trail. The navigation wasn't always obvious. I missed the signs a couple of times and went wrong, though my watch kept me from straying too far. Self-navigation adds an extra layer to these races - you can't switch off mentally even when you're physically comfortable. Twenty miles came in three and a half hours. I did some quick maths: at this pace I'd finish in ten and a half hours. That was too fast. I knew I should slow down. Did I slow down? Of course not. "I knew I should slow down. Did I slow down? Of course not." The Rain and the Reckoning Marathon distance came at 4 hours 50 minutes - respectable for a trail marathon with this much climbing. The rain had started by then, which was actually welcome. It kept the temperature manageable even as we approached halfway, and the mud it created was a small price to pay for not overheating. Petworth arrived at 51 kilometres, five hours fifty in. The midway aid station. And somewhere around there, things started to unravel. At 60 kilometres - seven hours in - I was very tired. People were starting to pass me, which is never a great sign. I was still running, but not running up the hills anymore. That little experiment had failed. The Long Grind Seventy kilometres. Eight hours forty-five. I was absolutely shattered. My legs had nothing. My back was aching. Most of the climbing was done and the terrain was flattening out, but I still had 20 miles to go. Twenty miles. I think my legs hadn't recovered from the South Downs Way 100 recently. My stomach was fine, the weather wasn't too hot - it was purely a case of tired legs that hadn't been given enough time to recover. Lesson learned, again. The aid stations kept me going. Coke and marmite sandwiches became my fuel of choice. Despite being completely knackered, I made sure to thank every volunteer. They're standing out there for hours making this possible. "I'm still so wrecked, but when it's like this you know you can't complain. It's so beautiful here." The Beautiful Suffering At 90 kilometres, with just 12k to go, the sun came out and the countryside opened up around me. This is the strange duality of ultras - you can be utterly destroyed and still appreciate the beauty. I was wrecked, but I couldn't complain. The scenery was stunning. My watch hit 100k at 13 hours 19 minutes, but the course was actually 103k. Two and a half kilometres still to go, jogging along at nine-minute kilometres, everything hurting but knowing it was done. Under 14 hours was secured, which felt like a win given the collapse at halfway. The Finish Coming into Petersfield, people were beeping their car horns at the runners - those small acts of support that mean everything when you're that tired. The finish was at the rugby club, where the atmosphere was brilliant. England were playing Ukraine in the Euros on the screens (winning 4-0), runners were finishing to bells clanging and cheers, and there was proper food - burgers, salad, coffee, whatever you wanted. 13 hours 41 minutes 59 seconds. 103 kilometres of Surrey, Sussex and Hampshire forest trails. After a shower, I felt almost human again. Almost. The run had been really, really hard - one of those days where you go out with ambitions and end up just surviving. But that's ultrarunning. Not every race is a good race. Sometimes you grind it out, collect your medal, and learn for next time. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Phoenix Breakfast Run 2016: Monday Morning Marathon on the Thames](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/phoenix-breakfast-run-2016): Blog Running Running Phoenix Breakfast Run 2016: Monday Morning Marathon on the Thames Stephen Cousins 15 February 2016 5 min read In Brief A Monday morning marathon along the River Thames, organised by Phoenix Running. Six hours to run as many laps as you want on a flat 5km out-and-back course. Low-key, friendly, and featuring some of the most ridiculous medals in British running. 26.2mi Distance 4:27:50 Finish Time 77m Elevation 26th Position Who runs a marathon on a Monday morning? Apparently, quite a lot of us. The Phoenix Breakfast Run was my third trip to Walton-on-Thames in about two weeks, and there's a reason I kept coming back. Phoenix Running events have a vibe all their own—small, low-key, absurdly fun, and featuring medals so enormous they probably count as strength training just to wear them. The format was beautifully simple: run up and down the Thames Path for six hours. Do as many laps as you want. Stop when you've had enough. It's the kind of race that strips away all the fuss and leaves just the running and the people. The Phoenix Philosophy Before the start, I caught up with Rik Vercoe, the race director and founder of Phoenix Running. Rik's not just an organiser—he's a proper runner himself, having won the Brathay 10 Marathons in 10 Days back in 2013 and set a Guinness World Record for running 10 marathons averaging under three hours. He also finished 39th at Marathon des Sables. The man knows what runners want. "Small, low-key, lots of fun, not too serious, massive medals. That's pretty much where we focus our attention." That philosophy was evident everywhere. No chip timing pressure, no wave starts, no VIP areas. Just a table of snacks, a friendly registration, and a course so flat you could practically sleepwalk the whole thing. The medals, true to Rik's word, were absolutely ridiculous—in the best possible way. The Characters You Meet What makes events like this special isn't the course or the time—it's the people. Running laps for hours gives you plenty of opportunity to chat, and the stories I heard that morning were remarkable. There was Jackie, about to fly to Tokyo in two weeks for her 100th marathon. Her 99th was happening right here on a Monday morning by the Thames. When I asked about her favourite, she mentioned Comrades—one of the most brutal ultras in the world. A hundred marathons in six years. Some people are on a different level entirely. Then there was Paul, running his 135th marathon. His first had been London in 1999, and it hurt so much he didn't do another one until June 2012. Thirteen years between marathon one and marathon two—now that's a comeback story. I met Jude, who was running for a charity called Speak that provides therapy for people with disabilities. Her goal: twelve marathons in twelve months to raise funds. "It's a challenge to do something that you're not very good at," she said, "because doing something you're good at isn't really a challenge." Hard to argue with that logic. First-Timers and Veterans The beauty of Phoenix events is how they mix complete beginners with seasoned ultra-runners on the same course. Hayley was running her first-ever half marathon—nervous but determined. Jess and Sharla had done a few parkruns and fancied stepping up. Emma had only done one marathon before and was already planning New York for November. Meanwhile, Nuala was ticking off her 91st marathon, with Cyprus coming up in March. Her favourite? Comrades, obviously—that race came up more than once. But she had a soft spot for Brighton too. "It's my local," she said. "I've done nearly all of them." Rob told me his favourite marathon was Edinburgh, which he'd run with his wife—while nursing a broken elbow and three broken ribs. Some people's definition of "favourite" is different from mine. Eight Laps and a Hot Chocolate I finished eight laps of the 5km course—just over marathon distance—in a shade under four and a half hours. Not my fastest, but that wasn't the point. The point was running along the Thames on a February morning, chatting to strangers who'd become friends by the end, and collecting a medal that barely fit in my bag. Phoenix Running has built something special. In a world of expensive big-city marathons with corporate sponsors and wave starts and GPS tracking, there's something refreshing about a race that says: here's a path, here's some water, run until you're done. Rik and the team understand what many runners actually want—not a production, but a community. "Who runs on a Monday morning? Apparently, people who've figured out that running doesn't have to be complicated to be brilliant." I'd be back to Walton-on-Thames before long. Phoenix events have a way of drawing you in. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Manchester Marathon 2023: A Lesson in Positive Splits and Hubris](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/manchester-marathon-2023): Blog Running Running Manchester Marathon 2023: A Lesson in Positive Splits and Hubris Stephen Cousins 16 April 2023 5 min read TL;DR Returned to my hometown for the Manchester Marathon, two weeks after Paris Deliberately went out at kamikaze pace - around 2:50 marathon finish time Ran the entire race without any nutrition whatsoever Crashed spectacularly after 25km, positive split all the way home Still managed sub-3 (2:57:44) but learned a painful lesson about hubris Manchester has had a marathon since 2012, and it's now the second largest in the UK with around 30,000 runners starting and finishing near the Old Trafford football ground. The other Old Trafford - the cricket ground. I was born in Manchester some 21 years ago. Though I'm not entirely sure about that maths. I'd booked Manchester as a fallback in case my A race in Paris got cancelled. Paris had gone well - a comfortable 2:55 where I'd run conservatively in the first half. So naturally, I decided to do the exact opposite in Manchester. 42.2km Distance 2:57:44 Finish Time 902nd Position 4:13/km Avg Pace The Kamikaze Strategy Given that Paris had felt relatively comfortable and I'd run quite conservatively in the first half, I thought I would try something different. Something that any sane runner would advise against. Something that every marathon training plan explicitly warns you not to do. The plan was simple: run the first 13 miles at my half marathon pace and try to hold on as long as possible. "I'm definitely not feeling as comfortable as I did in Paris, but I am going a bit quicker." I started running at just over four minutes per kilometre. Completing the full marathon at this pace would mean a finish time of around 2 hours 50 minutes. This would be monumentally stupid even if I were fresh. I was not fresh. I had residual fatigue from Paris two weeks earlier. Adding Fuel to the Fire (Or Rather, Not) Another factor to add to my growing list of excuses for what was about to happen: partly due to lack of planning and partly down to my own stubbornness, I decided to run the entire race without any nutrition at all. Regular viewers will be aware of my hatred of gels. But that doesn't mean I don't think you need at least some carbs during a marathon to keep you afloat. In Paris I'd had half a banana and some fizzy drink around 17 miles. In Manchester, I would have nothing. Absolutely nothing. I hit halfway in 1 hour 25 minutes 30 seconds. I was tired, definitely tired. But I still believed I could hang on. The Inevitable Crash The organisers claim that Manchester is the flattest marathon in the UK. This is a complete fallacy. There are regular inclines - the bridges over the canal at Timperley, the approach to Altrincham over Timperley Brook, and the steep climb into Altrincham itself. At 25km, I was still holding together. At 30km, the wheels started to come off. At 35km, I was dying. The pain was entirely of my own making and completely predictable. "There is no worse way to run a race than a positive split where you go hard in the first half and die in the second. It's just horrible." In that last 10km, I was getting passed by so many people it was demoralising. So fatigued and tired, I just wanted to slow down and slow down and slow down. Compare that to Paris where I felt strong at the end, passing runners and getting a faster time. Manchester was the complete opposite experience. Lessons Learned Grinding out the last 5km was as tortuous as it looks on the video. And this is exactly what it looks like for every runner who goes out too hard and beyond their capability in a marathon. When you're in it, the only thing you want is for it to end. My friend Luke passed me with about a mile to go. He shouted "Come on!" and I just couldn't drag anything else out of myself. He finished in 2:51. Another runner I spoke to got 3 hours and 34 seconds - absolutely gutted to miss sub-3 by that margin. Having gone out at 2:50 pace, I finished in 2:57:44. Still my second fastest marathon at the time, but one of the least satisfying in terms of its execution. Maybe there was a happy medium between normal marathon pace and kamikaze pace, but I didn't find it that day. It was great to meet so many of you in Manchester who watch the videos and came to say hello. And particularly to those of you who tried to spur me on as you passed me in those final miles - it was truly appreciated. The Aftermath After finishing, I felt absolutely awful. Stomach cramps, feeling like being sick but not actually being sick. I'd had some water about 2km from the end because I was feeling terrible, but it made me feel even worse. Then I spent a long time sat down at the finish, trying to recover. If you've done a marathon and suffered in the last 10km, you know exactly this feeling. It's a reminder that the marathon is a distance that demands respect. Go out too hard, skip the nutrition, and it will punish you. Still, sub-3 is sub-3. And sometimes the races where we make mistakes teach us more than the ones where everything goes right. You should never, ever run a marathon like that. But at least I now have proof of exactly why.
- [Race to the Stones 2024: 100km Along Britain's Oldest Road](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/race-to-the-stones-2024): Blog Running Running Race to the Stones 2024: 100km Along Britain's Oldest Road Stephen Cousins 13 July 2024 5 min read TL;DR My first Race to the Stones—100km along Britain's oldest road. Started strong with my friend Lee, struggled in the midday heat, then ran strong in the second half as temperatures dropped. The ridiculously well-stocked aid stations and complete lack of mandatory kit made this feel more like a supported adventure than a race. Finished in 13:18:02 and immediately understood why it's a classic. 100km Distance 13:18:02 Finish Time 1,327m Elevation 269th Position It's nearly 07:00 in the morning. I've arrived in... I don't know where we are. We're in a field. We were, in fact, at Field Farm in Lewknor, Oxfordshire. The start line of Race to the Stones. I'd known about this race for years but never really thought about doing it. Then I got invited by Ed, and here I was, about to run 100km non-stop along Britain's oldest road. Britain's Oldest Road Race to the Stones takes place on the Ridgeway, said to be Britain's oldest road, with its use dating back some 5,000 years. It was used by Neolithic, Bronze, and Iron Age communities, as well as the Romans. Traders, pilgrims, and soldiers used the Ridgeway's elevated position to stay safe from ambush and wild animals in the forests below. The national trail runs 87 miles from Ivinghoe Beacon in Buckinghamshire, west to Overton Hill near the Avebury Stone Circle—and our finish line. "I'd known about Race to the Stones for years but never really thought about doing it. Then I got invited, and here I was." The Freedom of No Mandatory Kit One of the quirks of this race is the complete lack of any mandatory kit requirement. I was carrying just one water bottle in my waist belt, and with the aid stations and Victoria crewing me, I felt supported and incredibly light. It gave me such a sense of freedom and self-determination. Lee and I ran together for most of the first half, making good progress through the woods and onto the chalk trails. At this stage, the temperature was cool, and we were mostly in the shade. Just over 10km in, 1 hour 10 minutes. It's very tempting to go too fast on this route because it's relatively flat, and we feel good. We'll see if it comes back to bite us later on. The Aid Stations I have to mention the aid stations. These are insane. The sandwiches are wrapped—it's like they've been to Tesco and bought them! Sweet potato falafel wraps. Chocolate Freddos. Penguin bars, Jelly Tots, Dairy Milk chocolate. Then you've got your usual fare like bananas, watermelon, oranges, and pineapple. It's like a café. A kid's picnic. And flat Coke! How often do you actually get genuinely flat Coke at an aid station? You're really wrapped in cotton wool in this race, that's for sure. The Heat in the Middle Marathon distance done in 5 hours 20 minutes. But it was getting hot. By the time I was approaching the halfway base camp, I was getting cooked. It was humid, there was cloud cover, and everything felt very close and uncomfortable. Victoria had me a Calippo waiting at base camp, which was perfect. I couldn't stomach food at the moment—it was too hot, my mouth was too dry. Quite a few people were staying overnight here, doing 50km today and 50km tomorrow. I wouldn't have minded going to sleep in one of those tents myself. A Strong Second Half It's amazing what a difference the temperature makes to my running. Between 60 and 70km, as it started to cool down and I began to feel better, I could see the finish line beckoning. I pushed on a little. Since I wasn't carrying a head torch, I wanted to make sure I finished before dark. The entire route of Race to the Stones is completely runnable. Oddly, the further I got into the race, the more I felt like running. I was wearing my Hoka carbon-plated Skyward X road shoes—so comfortable on this easy terrain. The Mind Game at the End In the worst mind game ever, just as we got to Avebury Stone Circle, there was a cone, and we had to turn around the cone and go exactly back the way we came. I'd been able to hear the finish line from right up the top of the hill, then we had to come all the way past the finish line to the stone circle, turn around, and come back again. Torture for the last 3 or 4 kilometres. But the sun came out for us to cross the finish line—how fantastic is that? I never wanted to do Race to the Stones before, but I'm so glad I did. And I can see why it is a classic UK ultra. Looking back, my favourite thing about the race was not having to carry any mandatory kit. It gave me such a sense of freedom, and I will definitely come back and do it again one day.
- [Cape Wrath Ultra Day 4: Finding My Rhythm in the Scottish Highlands](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/cape-wrath-ultra-day-4-2024): Blog Running Running Cape Wrath Ultra Day 4: Finding My Rhythm in the Scottish Highlands Stephen Cousins 23 May 2024 5 min read By Day 4 of the Cape Wrath Ultra, the field had thinned dramatically. A combination of punishing terrain, the Scottish weather, and an unwelcome guest - the norovirus - had reduced the starting field of 172 runners to around 140. Those of us still going had survived the first two days of sunshine and heat, then the brutal Day 3 slog from Kinloch Hourn to Achnashellach. Day 4 was supposed to be shorter. It wasn't going to be easier. The Cape Wrath Ultra For those who don't know it, the Cape Wrath Ultra is Scotland's premier multi-stage ultra running event. 400 kilometres from Fort William to Cape Wrath over 8 days, winding through Knoydart, Kintail, Torridon, Assynt, and Sutherland. Five of those days are proper ultra marathons over mountainous terrain. It's described as running through "the world's most inspirational landscapes," and for once, the marketing doesn't exaggerate. The 2024 edition, however, will be remembered for something else entirely: the vomiting bug. Day 4: Finding a Rhythm After the monster that was Day 3 - 68 kilometres with over 2,300 metres of climbing - Day 4 offered something resembling relief. Shorter distance, but don't let that fool you. The terrain was rough, technical, and featured that special Scottish specialty: heather bashing. The cooler weather was a blessing after the brutal heat of the opening days. I found myself settling into something approaching a rhythm, moving steadily through terrain that would have destroyed me three days earlier but now felt almost manageable. That's the strange magic of multi-day events - your body adapts to things you thought impossible. The Invisible Enemy The norovirus had been tearing through the camp. At checkpoints, you'd hear stories of runners collapsing, of people vomiting on the trail, of DNFs not from exhaustion but from illness. The finish rate would end up at just 33% for the Ultra category - down from 51% in 2023. That wasn't because the course was harder. It was because something was very, very wrong. I was one of the lucky ones. Whether through obsessive hand hygiene or pure luck, I avoided the worst of it. The Scenery Payoff When you're struggling through a multi-day race, it's easy to forget why you entered. Day 4 reminded me. The Scottish Highlands in late May, with the sun occasionally breaking through, with lochs glittering below and mountains rolling into the distance - this is why we do it. Every aid station felt like a small victory. Every summit offered views that made the suffering worthwhile. And slowly, steadily, the finish line for Day 4 drew closer. Onwards to Cape Wrath Day 4 complete. Still in the race. Still moving north towards that lighthouse at the northwestern tip of mainland Britain. Danny Smith would eventually win the overall race in 50:28:18. Bridget Glaister took the women's title in 59:49:41 after a closely fought battle with Elsa Morgan. For the rest of us, the achievement was simpler: keep moving, stay healthy, reach Cape Wrath. Four down, four to go. Day 4 Stats Event: Cape Wrath Ultra 2024 - Day 4 Date: 23rd May 2024 Overall Winner: Danny Smith - 50:28:18 (total) Women's Winner: Bridget Glaister - 59:49:41 (total) Ultra Finishers: 57 of 172 (33%)
- [UTMB OCC 2024: Chasing My Wife's Time Through the Alps](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/utmb-occ-2024): Blog Running Running UTMB OCC 2024: Chasing My Wife's Time Through the Alps Stephen Cousins 29 August 2024 5 min read TL;DR Ran the UTMB OCC 55km race during UTMB week in Chamonix. My mission: beat Victoria's time from last year of 11 hours 25 minutes. The brutal heat made the climb to Col de Balme absolutely punishing, and despite bombing the final descent, I finished in 11:39:17. I didn't beat Victoria. She's never going to let me forget it. 55km Distance 11:39:18 Finish Time 3,287m Elevation 875th Position Last year, my wife did this race in 11 hours 25 minutes. Beating that was all I cared about. How hard could it be? OCC stands for Orsières–Champex–Chamonix. You start in this beautiful Swiss town of Orsières, make your way up to Champex-Lac, then up and over Col de Balme, down to Argentière, and finally over La Flégère and down into Chamonix. It's 55 kilometres with 3,500 metres of elevation gain—and on a hot day, it's absolutely brutal. The UTMB Experience It's the beauty and serenity of the mountains and valleys around Mont Blanc that keeps us coming back each year. That juxtaposed with the immensely exhilarating atmosphere generated in Chamonix during UTMB week. It's the highlight of the ultrarunning year for many. Somehow I managed to get to the front of wave two at the start. My friend Owen was on the mic. "Stephen, how are you feeling? Ready to rock and roll?" I told him I felt more nervous than I should be. When he asked about my goal time, I gave him the only answer that mattered: "Last year, my wife did this in 11 hours 25. Beating that is all I care about." "Last year, my wife did this in 11 hours 25. Beating that is all I care about." Switzerland to France The first kilometres were magical. Weaving through the streets of Orsières, the schoolchildren lined up to high-five us out of town. It didn't take long for the sun to start doing its thing, and because a lot of the early section was on tarmac, it was mostly runnable—so I got very warm quite early on. The beauty of Switzerland is remarkable. It's so green and lush, and the support passing through the various small villages was amazing. I loved the oversized cowbells some of the locals were ringing. After passing Champex-Lac—which I'd only ever seen in the dark on previous races—we began the long climb towards Col de Balme. The Heat Crucible This climb coincided with the hottest part of the day, and many people began to run out of water. There was an extra water station about halfway up, but there were huge queues and I didn't want to waste 20 minutes standing around, so I carried on with minimal supplies. Last year, for some reason, the OCC route was diverted and Victoria didn't have to do this section. Great for her in one sense, because I think this section is the most difficult. But it did mean she missed out on arguably the most spectacular view of all—a fantastic ledge with a sheer drop on one side and chains embedded into the cliff face to hold on to. Very exciting. In the race against Victoria, I had been ahead of her time from last year, but now I was behind—and needed to catch up. By the time I reached the aid station at Col de Balme, I was really screwed. 34 kilometres in seven hours and 16 minutes. The Final Push Cloud cover and wind significantly cooled things down for the descent. The terrain was mostly smooth and runnable, and I started to enjoy myself more as we dropped into Argentière. I was blown away when I passed some Film My Run fans from Mexico on the descent through Le Tour. How nice is that? Leaving Argentière, I had just one climb left to do. The climb up to La Flégère is quite technical, and although I was feeling relaxed and confident, I was moving very slowly by now. "All dead men walking now, I think." By the time I reached the ski lifts at La Flégère, my legs were shot. But I was determined to get down that hill as fast as I could. I remembered my CCC race from 2018 when, after 100 kilometres, I was still able to bomb down this very hill in 38 minutes. This year it took me 49 minutes—not bad for tired legs. The Finish Line Running through Chamonix with onlookers cheering, friends shouting my name, high-fives everywhere—it's amazing how many hours of pain you can put up with just for these few minutes of euphoria at the end. I've loved this feeling since my first UTMB race seven years ago, and I'm not going to be sick of it anytime soon. My official time: 11 hours, 39 minutes, 17 seconds. I didn't beat Victoria. She's never going to let me forget it.
- [Winter on the Downs 2024: Running Through Storm Darragh](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/winter-on-the-downs-2024-storm-darragh): Blog Running Running Winter on the Downs 2024: Running Through Storm Darragh Stephen Cousins 7 December 2024 5 min read TL;DR Completed the UK Ultra Winter on the Downs during Storm Darragh—the fiercest storm to hit the UK since Storm Eunice. Race almost cancelled, start location moved, and we experienced some of the worst running conditions I've ever faced. Gale force winds, driving sideways rain, and moments where we were literally blown backwards. Finished in 11:41:04 and loved every terrifying minute of it. 80km Distance 11:41:04 Finish Time 2,170m Elevation 57th Position If you could choose to avoid one specific type of weather when running, what would it be? Me—it would be the wind. If there's one thing that's guaranteed to slow you down and sap your energy on a run, it's a headwind. So imagine my joy when I realised I would be running my first UK Ultra event during Storm Darragh, the fiercest storm to hit the UK since Storm Eunice in 2022. A Changed Start The race came very close to being cancelled. Originally it was supposed to start in Eastbourne, but the marquee company refused to set up their marquees because it was too windy. So we moved to the village hall in East Dean, which meant the race was no longer 55 miles—it was about 50 miles instead. At 7:20am, with some trepidation, I made my way to the start line. It was going to be blowy, but hopefully not too wet. Famous last words. The Seven Sisters The route took us down to join the Seven Sisters cliffs just west of Beachy Head and Birling Gap. We were already being buffeted by the wind, but the moment we reached the sea and turned onto the Sisters, the storm reached another level. "It was all we could do to stay on our feet most of the time during those first few miles." Thankfully, it wasn't too long before we turned inland at the Cuckmere River and the wind didn't feel quite so strong. All I could think was: at least it wasn't raining. I was comfortable in my three layers—base layer, Montane fleece, and Montane Phase Nano jacket. The Yellow Brick Road As we climbed up towards Firle Beacon and the South Downs Way, it started to rain. I don't know about you, but rain is supposed to fall down from above. This rain seemed to be coming from the side. Very fast. Now firmly on the South Downs Way, we climbed up to what is commonly referred to as the Yellow Brick Road. And this is where Storm Darragh gave us everything it had. We were often blown backwards with the gusts. If I exposed my hands, the wind chill factor made them absolutely freezing. Progress was achingly slow, and it was an absolute relief to get to the top and make our way down to Housedean Farm and the aid station. One runner I spoke to at the checkpoint had looked at his companion at the top of the ridge and said, "I'm not sure I can do this." But he carried on, and he got it done. "Gale force winds, driving rain, freezing cold. Some of the worst running conditions I've ever been in—worse than the top of Ben Nevis." The Second Half After Housedean Farm, we left the South Downs Way and descended into Lewes—the county town of Sussex—where I met Victoria, who had hot soup and tea waiting. My back and hips were aching, so I took some paracetamol and pressed on. For the most part, we now had the wind behind us. It was still gusting really strong at times, making it fun to momentarily fly through the air. The worst of the storm was definitely behind us. One of the 100-mile runners I passed told me about his night out in the storm. "The wind could move you at its worst," he said. "Disgusting." These hardy souls had been out there in the darkness while I was tucked up in my van. The Long Man in the Dark The route brought us down off the South Downs Way to see the Long Man of Wilmington—the famous chalk figure on the hillside. Of course, by the time I got there it was dark, so I couldn't actually see it. Then we had to climb all the way back up to the ridge again. Pretty pointless, really, but very nice of UK Ultras to include it on the route. An Adventure Worth Having I finished in 11 hours 41 minutes at East Dean village hall. Race director Neil Kirby told me it had been very touch and go whether the race would even happen. So many people had got in touch saying they wanted to do it, and they were really up for it, that he decided not to let people down. The UK Ultra Winter on the Downs was everything an ultra should be. It was an exhilarating and at times potentially perilous adventure on a lovely course with lots of support throughout. All great ultra races combine a scenic route, challenging weather, and that slight element of danger. That's what raises the satisfaction and enjoyment level of these events above the others. I was having type two fun for most of it, definitely. But looking back? I loved every terrifying minute.
- [Hurtwood 50k 2025: Mud, Rain, and a Mandatory Kit Error](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/hurtwood-50k-2025): Blog Running Running Hurtwood 50k 2025: Mud, Rain, and a Mandatory Kit Error Stephen Cousins 7 December 2025 5 min read TL;DR Completed the Hurtwood 50k in 6:57:51—just scraping under my seven-hour target. Pouring rain, howling wind, treacherous mud, and a rookie mandatory kit error when I forgot my water bottles. A fellow runner called John saved my race by lending me one of his. Classic December trail running in Surrey. 50km Distance 6:57:51 Finish Time 1,458m Elevation 196th Position This is Dorking. What county is Dorking in? Surrey, I think. West Sussex? Who knows? Who really cares? I was there to do the Hurtwood 50k, organised by my friend Tom Sutton with Freedom Racing. A little over 50 kilometres on a lollipop-shaped course—out, around a loop, and back. Starting and finishing in Dorking. The Name Game I've known about the Hurtwood 50k race for a long time, and I always assumed it was called Hurtwood because the route is predominantly through the woods, and because of the terrain and elevation, it hurts. Clever—but no. Hurtwood is actually the name given to 2,000 acres of common land in Surrey. The word hurt either comes from the hurt berries, which grow wild in and around the wooded areas, or from the Old English word chert, meaning a rough common overgrown with gorse, broom and bracken. So now you know. The Rookie Error One major catastrophe from the night before. I packed everything and then slept in the van. Got up in the morning, packed my kit into my race vest. What's the one thing I forgot to put in my race vest—and I've never forgotten this before? "I've completely forgotten to put my water bottles into my vest. I have a cup, but technically I've failed mandatory kit." At the first checkpoint at 12 kilometres, I had to confess my sin. I didn't want to get disqualified—I was fine for water, it was just the official kit requirement I'd failed on. Thankfully, a fellow runner called John very kindly gave me one of his water bottles to carry with me. Racing community at its finest. Three Peaks of Surrey The course takes in three significant summits: Leith Hill (the highest point in Surrey and the highest point on the race), Holmbury Hill, and Pitch Hill. Unfortunately, there were no views from any of them—just grey skies, pouring rain, and very slippy descents. The descents were treacherous. Very, very slippy. I went over once. You don't want to grab the barbed wire fences because that's going to rip your hand open, so you have to be very careful. How the fast guys came down these trails, I don't know. Speaking of fast guys—I'd started an hour ahead of the mass start using the rolling start option, and by now the speedsters were overtaking me. The winner would complete the course in 3 hours 43 minutes, breaking the record by 58 seconds. Hugh Tibbs came second in 3:57. These guys were completing the course over three hours quicker than me. The Loop Just south of Farley Green, we ran along an amazing ancient sunken pathway that looks like an old railway line but has just been carved out of the rock over centuries of use. I hit halfway in 3 hours 21 minutes—right on pace for a sub-seven-hour finish. The loop section complete, I headed back on the return leg with just over a half marathon to go. Marmite sandwiches and Coke at the checkpoint, and then back up Pitch Hill. By now, the high-vis marshal at the trig point had obviously given up and gone for a cup of tea—and I don't blame him one bit. The wind had increased and the rain was lashing down harder than ever. The Final Push I was really hoping the Protein Rebel gel, the Coke and the food I'd had at the last stop would kick in soon because I'd definitely slowed. If things didn't pick up, I wouldn't even make my C goal of seven hours. I got back up to Leith Hill tower with the rain making filming almost impossible, and thought: well, it's now or never. And I started to run. Thankfully, the descent off Leith Hill is fairly runnable, and I started to claw back a few minutes. With less than 5k to go, I had 40 minutes—meaning I needed to do 8 minutes per kilometre to finish under seven hours. It was going to be tight. What I thought was a super-fast final 5k probably looked like a weary trudge through the mud. I was still in the woods with less than a kilometre to go, the finish seeming impossibly far away. But eventually I made it to the road. Nearly there now. 6:57:51. Just made it under seven hours. Thank goodness. Classic December ultra running: mud, rain, wind, a mandatory kit error, a kind stranger lending a bottle, and a finish time that came down to the wire. The Hurtwood might not technically be named after hurting, but by the end, it certainly felt like it should be.
- [Race to the Stones 2025: Running Happy on Britain's Oldest Road](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/race-to-the-stones-2025): Blog Running Running Race to the Stones 2025: Running Happy on Britain's Oldest Road Stephen Cousins 12 July 2025 5 min read TL;DR Returned to Race to the Stones for a second year, this time deliberately running slower to enjoy the day. Finished in 15 hours 36 minutes—about two and a half hours slower than last year—but had a brilliant time on one of Britain's most ancient trails. Sometimes running happy beats running fast. 103km Distance 15:36:08 Finish Time 1,414m Elevation 255th Position What an absolutely beautiful morning it was. Having done Race to the Stones last year, I was so impressed—I loved it so much—that I was back again for a second time. Over the years, Race to the Stones has managed to carve out a reputation as one of the ultra-distance events of the year, attracting both beginners and seasoned runners. The flat, easy terrain gives the elites a fast, runnable course and those new to ultra distances a less intimidating entry point to the sport. A Different Approach Last year I finished Race to the Stones in just over 13 hours. I knew from the start that if I was going to enjoy my day, this year would have to be slower. I deliberately adjusted my expectations to account for the conditions. If you're just starting out in ultrarunning, it's important that you think about what you want to achieve and why. "I'd rather run happy than miserable and hurting, and I'd rather finish the race in a slower time than DNF trying to push harder for a fast time." Early on, the trails were smooth, dry and busy, with runners chatting enthusiastically about the adventure that lay ahead. It was very tempting to go out hard early when it was cool and get some miles banked. Let me tell you, banking miles is possibly the worst thing you can do in a race of this length. You just have to accept that you're going to need to go nice and easy and, hopefully, have something left in the second half. Running Through History The Ridgeway is one of Britain's most ancient pathways. The stuff I was walking on, people 5,000 years ago were walking on. The Romans used it. It was used in the Iron Age. Pilgrims used it. Travellers, soldiers. It's just a fantastic ancient trail that I absolutely adore. One of my favourite sections is along Grim's Ditch—a raised earthwork dating back to the Iron Age that runs parallel to the Ridgeway. You're literally running on history. Later we passed Barbury Castle, an Iron Age hill fort from around 700 BC. Part of a chain of hill forts along the Ridgeway, these forts controlled movement, trade and territorial boundaries, and served as refuges along the route. There's evidence the fort on Barbury Hill was used later by the Romans and was even used by the American military during World War II. The Well-Oiled Machine Unlike many other ultra-distance races, Race to the Stones doesn't have a mandatory kit list—so you're not required to carry anything. Given there are regular pit stops en route, and I had Victoria crewing me as well, I felt I'd have enough support on course to manage without a backpack. I carried a soft flask of water, but that was all I needed between support points. Threshold's pit stops are some of the most well-stocked I've ever experienced. You're not going to go hungry on Race to the Stones, with sandwiches, crisps, fruit, chocolate, sweets, gels and plenty more. Victoria kept me supplied with ice bandanas, cups of tea, and all sorts of treats throughout the day. Base Camp at Halfway The halfway point at base camp is quite something. It's like a festival—with merchandise stalls, burgers, pizzas, coffee, ice creams. Some people choose to do this event over two days, finishing at the 50K mark, sleeping in tents, and continuing the next day. For those of us doing it in one go, it's very tempting to stay too long. The music's playing, people are cheering as runners come in to finish their 50Ks—it's a real hive of activity. But there was still work to be done. If I wanted to walk a bit, I just walked a bit—it was fine. If I got in after dark, it would be fine. We weren't going to worry about it. The Final Push At 66 kilometres—just over 41 miles—your legs might start feeling a little heavy. Joints ache, muscles feel tired, feet a little beaten up. This is where I felt the benefit of good cushioning and just taking it easy when needed. The sun was still not setting as we hit 86 kilometres. The scenery was incredible—total blue skies with a few wispy clouds. If I'd finished earlier, I wouldn't have got to see this. There can't be many more classic English scenes than rolling hills on a summer's day, a farmer working in his field down in the valley. Absolutely amazing. At this stage, it really is just a mental battle. You've got to force yourself to keep moving forward. Everything in your body and your mind is telling you to stop. You've just got to keep going. The Sting in the Tail Race to the Stones has a cheeky little sting in the tail. You quite literally run to the Stones in Avebury, but then you turn around and come back out again to get to the finish line. With 5 kilometres to go, if you listen carefully, you can hear the announcer at the finish line—because you're actually only about 2 kilometres away as the crow flies. Then there's a gnarly field and 600 metres of farm road before the finish. What a beautiful, difficult, gorgeous, challenging yet fantastic day it had been. We finished under 16 hours, which I was fairly pleased with—about two and a half hours slower than last year, but this time I'd actually enjoyed myself. Sometimes the best race is the one where you don't try to race at all.
- [Manchester Marathon 2025: When It's Not Your Day](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/manchester-marathon-2025): Blog Running Running Manchester Marathon 2025: When It's Not Your Day Stephen Cousins 27 April 2025 5 min read In Brief Manchester Marathon 2025 - the biggest day of marathon running in UK history with London and Manchester on the same day. I arrived not believing in myself, started sluggish, and capitulated spectacularly in the second half. Finished in 3:40:48. Sometimes it's just not your day. 26.2mi Distance 3:40:48 Finish Time 136m Elevation 4,901st Position If I'm going to have the perfect run, everything needs to have fallen into place. Training, fitness, weather. But most of all, you need to truly believe you can do it. I arrived in Manchester worrying about the heat and not really believing in myself. 27th April 2025 was the biggest day of marathon running in UK history. London Marathon and Manchester Marathon on the same day, with a combined 76,000 runners. 36,000 of us were in Manchester, 140,000 spectators lining the streets. Two Years Before Two years ago I had felt totally invincible. I started Manchester Marathon in 2023 knowing I was fitter than I'd ever been, went out at kamikaze pace, and scraped in just under three hours. When I crossed the start line this year, I was far less convinced of my ability. Manchester also hosted the 2025 English Championships, bringing 70+ elite athletes to the start line. Josh Griffiths won in 2:16:56. Tessa McCormick took the women's title in 2:34:53. I, meanwhile, was about to demonstrate exactly how not to run a marathon. "It's going to be really hot and I'm not feeling super confident. We're just going to start out really slowly and see what happens." Sluggish From the Start The crowds were out in force on a beautiful day. I had two of my children with me supporting, filming at various points around the course. Even running at 4 minutes 30 per kilometre - which should be fairly comfortable for me - I felt sluggish from the outset. 5km in 22 minutes 10 seconds. 10km in 44 minutes 30 seconds. Still not feeling confident, getting warm. By nine miles in, I think I'd already given up and was beginning to drop off the pace. The goal had been 3 hours 10 minutes or under. And if you're already feeling the pace less than an hour in, you know you're in trouble. The Wheels Come Off I went through halfway having only lost around 90 seconds off my goal pace - 1:36:28. I thought I might salvage something around 3:25. However, over the next five kilometres, I really hit a wall and things deteriorated significantly. 25 kilometres done. One hour 55 minutes. I stopped to drink some water. "I'm screwed. Just not today. Not today." "Got nothing. Got no motivation, got no desire." All those gradual inclines over the railway and canal bridges, and that stupid hill in Altrincham, were taking their toll. Despite this, my boys were there to meet me in Sale. "You got this?" my son asked. "Yeah, I'll finish, but I can't get the time." He reminded me that I'd got him to the end of his Centurion 100. If only running a marathon when you've blown up was as simple as walking a hundred miles. Dark Moments There are some lonely, dark moments when you're capitulating in the back end of a marathon. No amount of crowd support can help. All you can do is keep placing one foot in front of the other, knowing that however much you walk, the finish line will eventually appear. The final 10km wasn't even a battle between body and mind as both were in full agreement that I could walk as much as I wanted. Let's avoid a heart attack at all costs and let's not be in the least bit concerned about time anymore. Hundreds of runners, some of them having a great day, others dealing with their own internal demons, silently overtook me in those last miles. I felt the pressure to run through the pockets of crowd support, but slowed to a walk again the minute I turned back onto the quiet residential streets. Reflections 3 hours 40 minutes 48 seconds. Over 30 minutes slower than my goal. When it's not your day, it's not your day. But it's about mindset, isn't it? I started this run feeling negative about it, and that's exactly how it turned out. The heat didn't help, but the real problem was between my ears. A massive thank you to everyone who shouted out to me on course and those who came up to say hi. I really appreciate it and I hope you all had a great day. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Lakeland 100 2022: How Hard Can It Be?](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/montane-lakeland-100-2022): Blog Running Running Lakeland 100 2022: How Hard Can It Be? Stephen Cousins 29 July 2022 5 min read "It's only 100 miles - how hard can it be?" Those were my actual words at the start line in Coniston. I'd come off the back of a solid 14-week training block, feeling confident and hoping to finish in under 30 hours. Looking back at that footage now, I can only shake my head at my own naivety. The Montane Lakeland 100 was about to teach me a lesson in humility. TL;DR My first Lakeland 100 attempt 105 miles with 6,000m+ of elevation Targeted sub-30 hours, finished in 34:36:56 Rotting feet - never took my shoes off the entire race "Definitely harder than the Arc" 34:36:56 Finish Time 170th Position 6,247m Elevation 105 miles Distance One of the Iconic Must-Do Races There are very few iconic must-do 100-mile races in the UK, but the Lakeland 100 is undoubtedly one of them. Despite not reaching a single Wainwright peak, the race packs over 6,000 metres of elevation gain into its 105-mile route, running clockwise from Coniston to Buttermere, through Keswick, around Ullswater, through Ambleside, and back to Coniston. What makes the Lakeland special isn't just the brutal terrain - it's the friendly community feel. The cutoff times are generous, making it an accessible goal for a much greater proportion of the ultra running community. The First Night Climbing the first hill out of Coniston, I met Laura - just 20 years old, attempting her first 100-miler. She'd already completed the Lakeland "Legend" kids' race at 14 and the 50-miler the previous year. Now she was going for the triple crown - the first person ever to complete all three races. Two hours in, we'd covered nearly 10 miles. It was fairly easy going with a couple of steep hills and some boggy sections. The light was fading though, and I knew we'd soon be reaching for headtorches. It was incredibly humid overnight, and I found myself drinking far more water than normal. By the time we hit Wasdale Head at 32 kilometres, I'd been going for over five hours and gratefully accepted a bowl of hot soup from volunteers dressed as 101 Dalmatians. When the Wheels Came Off I've done a few hundreds now, and the one thing I've learned is you can't plan for every eventuality. All you can do is train and prepare the best you can, then hope nothing unexpected comes along to derail your race. A broken pole was annoying - one of my trekking poles simply refused to extend - but manageable. "My legs are really done in. Another 50 miles to go. Well, more than that really." At Blencathra aid station, 42 miles in, I had breakfast toast and finally put on my rain jacket after it had been raining for four hours. In retrospect, that was a bit stupid. But despite the fatigue, I still believed I was on for the sub-30 hour finish. The Mental Battle Between Howtown and Mardale Head, running beside Haweswater, I found the trail extremely difficult. I ran some of this section with my friend Jeff, but he was stronger and faster, and I had to let him go. I found myself losing the mental will to keep pushing. The rain returned. My feet screamed. I went on anyway. Kentmere checkpoint served chilli pasta and ice-cold smoothies, which was superb. I'd bumped into friends Laura, Jane and Joe, which gave me a mental boost. Through Troutbeck towards Ambleside, Jane and Joe were dragging me along. The Final Dark Hours But Jane and Joe were moving too quickly for me now, and they went on ahead after Ambleside. The dark trails, the intermittent rain, and my overall fatigue conspired to prevent me filming anything more on route. It was simply survival mode from here. "I am completely wrecked totally. My feet are absolutely shot to pieces. I haven't taken my shoes off at all for the whole race. I dread to think what they look like." At 28 hours and 13 minutes, I had about 16 miles left. I was just going to walk all the way, go really slowly, and just get it done. Little did I know that the last 10 miles would take me four and a half more hours. I ran much of it with my new friend Emily, who was finishing her fifth Lakeland 100. Third Time Lucky Finally, at 4 o'clock in the morning, I crossed the line in Coniston. The official time: 34 hours, 36 minutes and 56 seconds. Over four and a half hours slower than my target. But I'd finished, and that was what mattered. "That was definitely harder than the Arc," I said to camera afterwards. And I meant it. My feet were destroyed. I never did find out exactly what they looked like underneath those shoes because I was too scared to check. Remember Laura, the 20-year-old I'd met at the start? She finished in 37 hours and became the first ever triple crown finisher. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Brighton Marathon 2025: Just Show Up](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/brighton-marathon-2025): Blog Running Running Brighton Marathon 2025: Just Show Up Stephen Cousins 6 April 2025 5 min read TL;DR Completed my 165th marathon and second Brighton in 3:59:56—just sneaking under four hours. Started as a pacer for friends Carol and Amy, but the heat and inner demons got the better of Carol at 13km, and I ended up running the second half solo. A philosophical run about why we keep coming back to 26.2 miles, even when it hurts. 42.2km Distance 3:59:56 Finish Time 197m Elevation 3,555th Position What is it about those 26.2 miles that captivates us so much? I ran my first marathon in 2012 and here I was, 13 years later, walking to the start of my 165th. Like any relationship, it's had its ups and downs. I've felt incredible lows, but no matter how much it hurts, I keep coming back. Because when it's good, it's bloody amazing. This was to be my second Brighton Marathon in as many years, and my 27th road marathon. Don't get me wrong, I'm not obsessed. I mean, it's not like I have a colour-coded marathon spreadsheet with filters and embedded links to Strava. That would be mad. The Plan: Pacing Friends I'd volunteered to pace my friends Carol and Amy. We had no set time goal in mind, just to enjoy the day together. A last-minute trip to the loo meant I missed my baggage cart and ended up starting in relative isolation—just me, Amy, and Carol, crossing the line without even a countdown. Right at the beginning of Brighton Marathon, there's a beast of a hill. You go through the start line, round a corner, and then it's up, up, up for 500 metres. I usually try and give my best shot at a road marathon, but this time I was there to support others. Marathons as Church Here's the thing about marathons. Whilst they are in many ways a huge social bonding experience where friends, family and colleagues run together, and perfect strangers call out your name and wish you well, running a marathon is also a deeply personal, insular experience. When I was a child, I used to attend church every week. I don't believe in God anymore, but running a marathon is a lot like going to church. There's this collective sense of togetherness, of shared experience and like-mindedness, and yet at the same time you're engaged in a deeply personal relationship with God—or in this case, the marathon—which no one else sees or truly understands. "Running a marathon is a lot like going to church. There's this collective sense of togetherness, and yet at the same time you're engaged in a deeply personal relationship which no one else truly understands." When the Chimp Takes Over At around 13 kilometres, Carol hit a wall. "The chimp is overtaking me," she said, referencing Steve Peters' famous mental performance model. "He's doing my head in and I can't overcome it. I'm just so tired and hot." Treadmill training for a warm marathon is not ideal, and it was warm out there. Carol decided to hang back and let us go—the pressure was off, and she could make it to the end in her own time without worrying about us dragging her along. Running Solo By 17 kilometres, I'd left both Carol and Amy. They wanted me to go so they could relax without any pressure. It felt strange abandoning my pacing duties, but sometimes the best support you can offer is stepping back. I hit halfway in 2 hours 12 minutes. Not quick, but respectable. If I could maintain that, I'd sneak under four hours. The question was whether my legs—and more importantly, my head—would cooperate. The Last 10km There's something really special about the last 10 kilometres. Even on a good day, this is where you find out what you're made of. When your head is doing more work than your legs. This is where the demons lurk, shouting "Why? Why?" And it's in finding the answer that salvation lies. See, there must be a reason why we're all here. And the only way to find out why is to run the race, to compete, to fight for your place, knowing that at any moment you could fall short—and taking the risk anyway for that one moment of euphoria when you can say: I made it, I did it, I'm not a failure. Just Show Up I pushed hard at the end and managed to scrape in just under four hours. I really started to struggle in the last 10k—it's not so warm when you're standing around because there's a breeze, but when you're running, it's really warm. It wasn't a fast time by my standards, but it was fun. I waved at the crowd, I chatted to strangers, and I held the demons back for another day. I found peace in my footfall and the rhythm of my breathing, and a joy in that process. "You don't run 26.2 miles for a medal. You run it to remember what it feels like to be fully alive." You don't run 26.2 miles for a medal. You run it to remember what it feels like to be fully alive. To wrestle with your limits, to face your fears, to be broken but continue on. The marathon gives you nowhere to hide. It strips everything back until all that's left is the real you—raw, laid bare. Life isn't a marathon. It's hundreds of them strung together. Some calm, some stormy, some beautiful. You may never truly know why you're here. All you can do is keep showing up. For yourself, for the people who believe in you, and sometimes the ones who don't. Just show up. Even when you don't feel ready. Just show up, though your legs may not be steady. Just show up—not for medals, not for praise, but to meet yourself halfway. Carol finished in 6 hours 17 minutes. Everyone who came down with us crossed the line. It had been a really lovely day—hard work, but lovely.
- [Race to the King 2025: A Lesson in Going Off Too Fast](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/race-to-the-king-2025): Blog Running Running Race to the King 2025: A Lesson in Going Off Too Fast Stephen Cousins 21 June 2025 5 min read TL;DR Finished Race to the King 2025 in 15 hours 10 minutes, but not before learning yet another valuable lesson in race management. Went off far too fast in the first half, forgot to apply anti-chafe cream, and paid the price in the brutal heat. A timely bout of rain at halfway saved the day, but the damage was already done. Finished 6th in my age group after being passed by two runners in the final 10km. 103km Distance 15:10:28 Finish Time 1,616m Elevation 77th / 6th AG Position Your comfort zone is a desolate wasteland. Nothing will ever grow there. And you miss 100% of the shots you don't take. So sometimes you need to take those shots, even if it will probably end in failure. This is a story about taking a shot—and about the importance of pre-race preparation, risk versus reward, and the consequences of ignoring everything you know about racing. It had been a manic morning getting to West Dean Gardens near Chichester. Despite living only 40 minutes away, a massive queue of traffic had made me later than I wanted to be. In the rush to collect my race number and get to the start line, I'd neglected to apply any anti-chafe cream. Keep an eye on that nugget of information as the race progresses. The Format: Two Loops of Varying Difficulty Race to the King is a 102-kilometre ultra consisting of two 50K loops. The first loop is relatively flat, following paths through Chichester Harbour and its surrounding wetlands. The second loop takes you up onto the South Downs with considerably more climbing. The sensible approach would be to conserve energy on the flat loop and bank it for the hills. Naturally, I did the exact opposite. "10 kilometres in, in just under an hour. That's probably a bit too fast." The first 10 kilometres mostly follows the Centurion Way railway path—the old Chichester to Midhurst railway that finally closed in 1991. It's easy, runnable ground, almost entirely tarmac, and far too tempting to push the pace. I hit 10K in under an hour and immediately knew I was being an idiot. Banking Time: A Strategy That Almost Never Works Against my better judgement, I made the conscious decision to try and bank some time. I never do this. I know it almost always ends in tears. But this time I thought, let's just see what happens. You never know—you might get away with it. Reader, I did not get away with it. I reached 25 kilometres in two and a half hours. If I maintained that pace for the whole race, I'd finish in 10 hours. I can't do 10 hours. On a good day, I can do 12. My target was 14. The maths wasn't mathing. When the Heat Arrives By 30 kilometres, the heat had properly arrived. I met Victoria for the first crew stop at Nutbourne, where—better late than never—I finally applied some anti-chafe cream. A man with a hosepipe offered to spray us down. I accepted gratefully. The truth was, I was already dying. Despite having now applied the cream, things were starting to rub in unmentionable places. The combination of going off too fast and the rising temperature was taking its toll. This was classic behaviour—trying to talk myself into positivity while internally acknowledging that things were falling apart. "You can see in my face that I already know I've been an idiot and the early pace is already catching up with me." A Stroke of Fortune at Halfway I reached the halfway point at West Dean Gardens in just over 6 hours, having slowed considerably in the final 10 kilometres of the first loop. Victoria hadn't made it to meet me—the traffic was as bad for her as it had been for me earlier. I had to fend for myself, grabbing some watermelon, a banana, and filling my water bottles before heading out for the second loop. And then, in the greatest news ever, it started to rain. In the worst news ever, just as it started to rain, we came into a forest, so we weren't getting the benefit of it falling on our heads. But even the sound of it was lush. Just hearing the rain made me feel cooler. The second loop heads up onto the South Downs Way, and I hit 60 kilometres in 7 hours 34 minutes. A marathon to go. The sun had gone in, I was feeling okay, and I was able to run properly for the first time in hours. The stroke of fortune I'd needed had arrived. The Exposed Sections Anyone who's watched my South Downs Way 100 videos knows that the section from Bignor Hill down to Amberley is brutally exposed. By the time I reached this stretch, the sun had come back out from behind the clouds and didn't look like it was about to disappear anytime soon. I met Victoria at Bignor Hill and got a fresh ice bandana, but couldn't manage to eat anything. My stomach was turning and nausea was becoming an issue. The 14-hour target was slipping away. At 75 kilometres, I knew I wasn't going to make it. The heat had got me. I had no ice left. All I could do was grind it out as best I could. The Arundel Park Climb The toughest section came between Swanbourne Lake and the top of Arundel Park. A long, steep, exposed climb where I slowed to an absolute crawl. Runner after runner passed me—people who had clearly managed their races much better than I had. At least the views were stunning. I may have been completely wrecked with 22 kilometres to go, but the South Downs really is beautiful. My stomach was awful, I felt like I was going to be sick at any minute, and the heat was sapping everything I had—but at least I had a nice view. "Quite often I'll try to put a brave face on things when talking to camera. Believe it or not, I do like to be positive most of the time, but this was no longer fun." The Chafing Crisis With 16 kilometres to go, a new problem emerged. The chafing had become serious. What had started as minor discomfort was now genuinely painful. The culprits were clear: not applying anti-chafe cream at the start, and then too much iced water melting down my back and into my shorts throughout the day.
- [Weald Challenge 50k 2016 | Getting Lost in Ashdown Forest](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/weald-challenge-50k-2016): Blog Running Running Weald Challenge 50k 2016 | Getting Lost in Ashdown Forest Stephen Cousins 29 May 2016 5 min read In Brief A sunny 50k through the Ashdown Forest with Richard and Tom – three weeks after Transvulcania, and the day after Richard ran a marathon PB at Kent Roadrunner. Getting lost twice despite having a GPS watch, being corrected on the race name multiple times, and finishing just over five hours. Classic grassroots ultra running. 50km+ Distance 5:19:30 Finish Time 2 Times Lost 3 Running Together Three weeks after running Transvulcania with Richard, I found myself at the start of another ultra. Richard, ever the overachiever, had run a marathon PB at Kent Roadrunner just the day before. Tom was there too. It was practically a family day out. The race was organised by Stuart Mills, and looking around the start area, I spotted half a dozen familiar faces – Shelly, Mark, Tom, Keith, Zoe, Liam. The UK ultra scene is small enough that every event feels like a reunion. The High Weald? The Weald Challenge? Who Knows I kept getting the name wrong. "The High Weald Challenge." "The Weald Challenge." "The Wheel Challenge." Alan, the race director, had to correct me multiple times on camera. For the record: this is the Weald Challenge, held in May. The High Weald Challenge is a different race, held in September. They sound similar. They are not the same thing. It matters less than it probably should. "I've got a map on my watch and we've still got lost twice." Running Through Ashdown Forest The Ashdown Forest sits halfway between Brighton and London – the inspiration for A.A. Milne's Hundred Acre Wood. On a sunny May day, it's a beautiful place to run: rolling hills, ancient woodland, open heathland. The kind of English countryside that looks effortless but hides plenty of sting in its elevation. Amazingly, the three of us stayed together through the first 10k, reaching that point in 57 minutes. We hit 20k around 1 hour 55 minutes – still together, still moving well. At 25.5k, about two and a half hours in, we were in the heart of the forest. The sub-5-hour target was slipping away, but none of us minded. The sunshine was too good, the company too easy. Getting Lost (Twice) Richard and I managed to stay together all the way to 40k. Tom was somewhere behind, having had his own navigational adventures. Despite having a GPS map on my watch – literally a moving map showing the route – we still got lost twice. The third time, it was Tom's turn, adding about 12 minutes to his day. This is the reality of small ultras with minimal marshalling. You carry a map, you pay attention, and sometimes you still end up in the wrong field. The Volunteers At one of the checkpoints, I stopped to film the volunteers. "Please tell me you're not getting paid," I asked. They weren't. They never are. Race volunteers are the unsung heroes of grassroots running. They stand at checkpoints for hours, often in questionable weather, making sure runners are fed, watered, and pointed in roughly the right direction. They do it for love of the sport, for the community, for the joy of being part of something. If you ever pass a volunteer on a race, thank them. Loudly. They deserve it. The Finish 5 hours 19 minutes and 30 seconds. A little over 50k – we ran extra distance thanks to the navigation errors, but that's part of the package. Richard, who had run a marathon PB the day before, finished alongside me. I tried to be annoyed about it but couldn't manage it. Tom came in behind, happy with his run despite the 12-minute detour. Liam finished his half marathon in 2:11. Zoe was there. Keith was there. Everyone got lost at some point. Everyone finished. "Race volunteers never ever underestimate them. Always give them thanks. They don't get paid." Final Thoughts The Weald Challenge isn't a big race. It doesn't have chip timing or a fancy expo or thousands of runners. What it has is a well-marked course through beautiful countryside, dedicated volunteers, and the kind of friendly atmosphere that makes you want to come back. And yes, if you're watching this and you're about to do the High Weald Challenge in September – that's a different race. Go find that video instead. Watch the Video Strava Activity
