And more often than not the heat gets to me and I start to feel nauseous. But so far today, I was still upbeat. 9 hou
- [London Marathon 2024: Getting What I Deserved](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/london-marathon-2024): Blog Running Running London Marathon 2024: Getting What I Deserved Stephen Cousins 21 April 2024 6 min read Imagine having the perfect marathon training block. No injury, no illness. A perfect mix of long runs and VO2 max sessions. A clear progression in fitness, speed and endurance. And then imagine executing the perfect race and having the best marathon experience of your life. Where do you go from there? In 2023, I ran a marathon PB in Paris and told myself I was capable of more. I was full of confidence, buoyed by a dream. Twelve weeks of training that had got me to the best shape I'd ever been in. I vowed that next year I would train harder, do more miles, more strength work, faster intervals, and beat my PB again. TL;DR 6th London Marathon Training decimated by illness - couldn't call it a training block Runalyze predicted 30 minutes slower than hoped Bonked hard in the final 10k Finished in 3:23:44 - same as two years ago 3:23:44 Finish Time 8,220th Position 120m Elevation 6th London Marathon The Reality of April 2024 Fast forward to April 2024 and the start line of the London Marathon. My training block had been decimated by a series of colds and flu-like illnesses such that I couldn't even call it a training block. My confidence was dented and Runalyze was predicting a finish time some 30 minutes slower than I'd originally hoped. We'd arrived in Blackheath, walking up the hill. The big question was, do I stop at Costa for a coffee or do I just carry on? It was very early - about quarter to nine - and I didn't start until 10:00. Bag dropped in, it was freezing, really cold, but we'd cope. I wasn't sure whether I should have worn my sunglasses or not, but I'd gone without. For the first time, I was in Yellow Start. This was a new part of the route I'd never done before, having previously always been over in the other start areas. "I know what level I'm at, and pretending it's anything better or that I can wing it or pull off a miracle is effectively marathon suicide." Controlling the Pace I crossed the start line and watched my club mate Penny disappear into the distance. As I reined in the urge to throw caution to the wind and follow her, I reminded myself that I knew what level I was at. My plan had been to run a controlled 20 miles at 4:40 per kilometre and then perhaps speed up in the final 10k if I felt strong enough. 5km done in 23 minutes and 10 seconds, sticking to around 4:40 per kilometre. At 10km in 46 minutes 30 seconds, we were just coming up to the Cutty Sark. Feeling all right, not great, but still sticking to the pace. One of the iconic moments of the London Marathon is running past the Cutty Sark just after 10k. Despite my lack of fitness and the disappointment of not being able to attempt a PB, I'm always grateful for the opportunity to run the London Marathon. These are special, life enriching, memory forging moments and you have to drink them in and bank them forever. Just crossing 15km in 1 hour 10 minutes. We were making progress, still sticking to the 4:40 per kilometre pace. Relatively relaxed, although I wasn't feeling like I wanted to speed up in the second half, that's for sure. 10 miles in 1:15:30. Just a parkrun to go to halfway. Tower Bridge and Halfway I was really enjoying myself. The crowds were amazing and Rotherhithe is always a great spot. Physically, I wasn't feeling quite as comfortable as I would have liked, but I was sticking like glue to my pacing strategy. 20km in 1:33 and crossing Tower Bridge - this square guy high-fived me as I ran past. And then about to hit halfway in 1:38:50, with the lead runners just coming past on the other side. It's exciting, watching the elites fly by as you slog through your own race. 1 hour 57 minutes 30 seconds for 25k. I'd had a toilet stop under the tunnel - yes, it had gone a bit crazy, but I'd get back on track. I was annoyed that I'd had to stop because I knew my beautiful even line of kilometre splits would be messed up on Strava. And I think perhaps this is where things started to fall apart. Meeting Victoria and the Wall Then I met my wife Victoria at 18 miles. But she wasn't ready for me, so I had to stop again to wait for my banana and coke. 30km in 2 hours 21 minutes and through Canary Wharf. 20 miles done in 2 hours 31 minutes. 10k to go. "Hitting the wall at 20 miles is such a cliché. I always tell people that the wall does not exist if you've done the training and your head is in the right place." And yet here I was, bonking in the last 10k. My motivation for any specific time was out of the window. My energy levels were at rock bottom and my legs were giving up. 2 hours 45 at 35km - seven k to go. I had dropped off the pace now, barely doing five minute kilometres. Quite tired. Very tired. Tower of London at 22 and a half miles. But I'd gone now. Legs had gone. 38k in 3 hours and 30 seconds. Four k to go. I was trying to follow the blue line to make the distance to the end as short as possible. The Final Struggle I kept trying to console myself by reminding my brain that I wasn't fit. This was no longer an A race. It was fine. Don't worry about it. But it still hurt, physically and emotionally, to feel every other runner coming past and to see every kilometre slower than the last. 3 hours 11 minutes and 40 seconds at 40k. I was completely dead. Nothing left. Two k to go. As I jogged in those final 2k, I thought back to all those lost days in January and February. Days when I should have been out training hard, putting in the miles. It was unfortunate that I was unwell, but maybe if I'd looked after my diet and sleep a bit better, I might not have fallen ill in the first place. There's no good or bad luck in marathon running. There's always a reason why you haven't performed on the day. I got out exactly what I put in. I got what I deserved. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Down The Mall It was really hard going in the last 10k, as is often the case, but we were there now, just passing Buckingham
- [Brighton Marathon 2024: Paul's First Sub-4](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/brighton-marathon-2024): Blog Running Running Brighton Marathon 2024: Paul's First Sub-4 Stephen Cousins 7 April 2024 6 min read I've lived within a few miles of Brighton all my adult life and have been running marathons for twelve years. And yet I'd never so much as considered entering the Brighton Marathon. The main reason has always been that it clashes with the Paris Marathon. Paris was my first marathon back in 2012 and we've returned every year since. But I've done Paris twelve times in a row now, and Brighton has recently changed hands. It's now organised by London Marathon Events and they have altered the course somewhat to remove a particularly gruesome section, making it seem almost palatable. So this year I swallowed my pride and signed up. TL;DR My first ever Brighton Marathon after 12 years of running marathons Pacing Paul to his first sub-4 hour finish Running with Zwift friends from around the world Gorgeous weather, great crowds, Fat Boy Slim sighting Finished in 3:57:50 3:57:50 Finish Time 2,801st Position 174m Elevation 1st Brighton Marathon The Zwift Gang Assembles We invited a group of friends who run with us on Zwift, and they travelled from all over the UK and abroad to run the marathon with Victoria and me. If you have a treadmill, why not come and join us on Zwift sometime? Good training, good fun and a great community. It was something after 10:00 in the morning, an absolutely gorgeous day - might even be a little bit too hot - but we were ready. I was pacing Paul to a sub-4 hour finish, his first ever. No pressure on me, just pacing. "No pressure, no pressure, no pressure," says Paul. Let's see what happens. Paula Radcliffe was just up there at the start. We tried to high five her as we went past. And then we were off in the Brighton Marathon 2024, settling in behind Paul, James, and Theo. Half an hour later, Victoria lined up at the start with another group of Zwift runners. "So we're going for 4 hours today. No pressure on me. It's pacing 4 hours." Preston Park to the Seafront Race start was in Preston Park, just north of Brighton city centre. Our first kilometre was done in 5:52, so we'd already lost 20 seconds, but we didn't mind - that was an uphill first kilometre. Now we were downhill so we were hoping it would spread out a bit and we could make up the time. And we did - we were now bang on pace. Finding our rhythm, we ran away from the centre along London Road before turning round and heading back towards the park. I was really impressed with the crowd support right from the start and the glorious sunshine made the atmosphere even better. We passed Carol and Debbie, our cheer squad for the day. 5k in and we were bang on pace - 28 minutes. First water stop at about 6k. 5:32 for kilometre six, so again we were just a little bit ahead of pace, but not too over-paced. On the right was Brighton Dome, very famous - where 50 years ago Abba performed Waterloo and won the Eurovision Song Contest. Right next to it, Brighton Pavilion, home of the Mad King. Was it Mad King George who built that? The Coastal Section The early miles in a marathon will have a significant bearing on what happens in the final miles. Running with Paul, James and Theo, I was conscious not to get sucked into an overenthusiastic, testosterone-fuelled increase in speed beyond our goal pace. It's easy to do and not so easy to rectify. We hit 10km in 55 minutes and 20 seconds - still about 5 seconds faster per kilometre than we should really be, but that would do. Nice and comfortable. We could sense the wind was going to be strong when we hit the seafront though. At about 11.5k, I suffered a major watch malfunction. Luckily I was wearing two watches, but the main watch decided to turn itself off and on again, so I'd lost four minutes and was now on the backup watch. After reaching the seafront, the Brighton Marathon route turns east onto the coast road and heads away from the centre in the direction of Rottingdean and Peacehaven. The crowds certainly thinned out here and the wind was stronger, but the views more than made up for that. We passed the impressive and imposing Roedean Girls School, built in 1898, before turning left and inland to Ovingdean. 10 miles in just under 1:30 - cruising still, nice and easy. Halfway and Heading Home Ten and a half miles in at another U-turn. It's no wonder that a few years ago, Brighton Marathon was measured long, because there are so many twists and turns. But we were still enjoying ourselves, now heading back into town past the Marina. If the views and the weather hadn't been so nice, this section could have been rather soul-destroying. As it was, I was concentrating on my pacing duties, making sure we were running evenly and efficiently, keeping an eye out for Victoria and her team coming in the opposite direction. Just past halfway in 1 hour 57 and a half - a little ahead of schedule. Let's just hope that didn't come back to bite us later. There was Victoria with her little five hour bus. We were on the four hour bus and now on the way home. "How you feeling at halfway, Paul?" "Yes, good. Really good." The Pain Cave Halfway is a great milestone to reach, especially if things have been going well up to this point, which for us, they had. Nice crowds coming into town by Brighton's Palace Pier. At the pier, the route takes a sharp turn and heads along Madeira Drive for another out and back at sea level, past a plethora of Brighton tourist attractions. 25km bang on course, running along Madeira Drive which used to be the old finish line until London Marathon Events took it over. It was warming up now and the breeze coming off the sea was very welcome. However, eyes front along here as you pass Brighton's famous nudist beach. The Concorde II music venue is also on Madeira Drive, as is the Volks Electric Railway - the oldest working electric railway in the world. Then there's the relatively new Sea Lanes outdoor swimming pool, which Victoria and I foolishly tried out in the dead of 
- [Ben Nevis Ultra 2022: Third Time Lucky](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/ben-nevis-ultra-2022): Blog Running Running Ben Nevis Ultra 2022: Third Time Lucky Stephen Cousins 18 September 2022 6 min read Life is uncertain, and that uncertainty makes life thrilling and frightening. If everything in life was guaranteed there would be nothing to strive for, nowhere to go. If you knew every time you started a race that you would cross the finish line, where's the adventure, where's the challenge in that? Surely we have to experience failure before we can truly appreciate our successes. Having failed to complete the Ben Nevis Ultra on my two previous visits, I was back in Kinlochleven for a third attempt at one of Britain's toughest 50km races. Third time lucky, as they say. Or third time certain DNF, as I was beginning to suspect. TL;DR Third attempt after two DNFs in previous years 4,000m elevation over 53km of Scottish highlands CMD Arete - knife edge boulder field at altitude Extended cutoff saved me by 28 minutes Finally finished in 12:28:00 12:28:00 Finish Time 122nd Position 3,621m Elevation 3rd Attempt The Death Race and the Baby Race All the races at the Skyline Scotland weekend start outside the Ice Factor, the ice climbing centre and café in Kinlochleven. The Ben Nevis Ultra may be tough, but on its inception, the 52km Glen Coe Skyline was dubbed the "Death Race" by some sections of the media. Standing in the registration queue, I found myself joking with fellow runners: "Under no circumstances should anybody join the Glen Coe queue. It is certain death. So we're going for Ben Nevis which is just certain DNF. What would you rather have?" At 7:30 in the morning, we watched the Glen Coe Skyline runners set off on their journey. "So they're going on the nice scary race and we're going on the baby race," I remarked. Though calling the Ben Nevis Ultra a baby race is somewhat misleading when it encompasses around 4,000 metres of elevation gain as it traverses over loose rock, boulders, wet grass, mud, deep bogs and fire track. I arrived at kit check wearing my Zwift singlet, Salomon SensePro 10 litre race vest and my new Inov8 Mudclaws. There were only five minutes to go before the first wave start, and I was the last one into the starting pen. A fellow runner approached me: "You've got a YouTube channel haven't you? I just watched your last two videos prior to coming." Whether that inspired him or scared him off, I'll never know. "This is our third time of trying this. We are gonna finish this time. We are confident, we are happy." Into the Highlands After a kilometre through the town we were on our way up. I had no problem with the terrain - I love it. The issue, historically for me, had been covering that ground at a pace fast enough to beat the cutoffs, which for a mid-pack runner like me, are aggressive. But these early miles held no surprises. I was moving well and feeling good. Ten kilometres in, one hour 48 minutes. The conditions were almost perfect - cool but not freezing cold, cloudy but not raining. Ben Nevis lurked in the clouds to our right as we traversed the valley, picking our way through very boggy terrain where at one point I went down into the water almost to my knees. It's easy to believe you're not good enough, not fast enough, not strong enough. But more often than not, it's a learning process. Rather than admit defeat after my two DNFs, I'd convinced myself I had more to give. I was sure I could do better and I wanted to prove it to myself. The CMD Arete As I started the ascent to Carn Mor Dearg, I was reminded of my fear of heights and how I struggle sometimes on exposed sections of rock. I had to have a bit of a chat with myself. I told myself to carry on doing the small jobs all day - following the red flags, one foot in front of the other to the next flag. The ridge up to Carn Mor Dearg wasn't too bad, and usually there's a view - well, not usually, but there was a beautiful panorama behind us. Sometimes I think it's better to be in the clouds, so you have no idea how far you could fall. At the top of CMD, the infamous Arete stretched ahead, shrouded in mist. "Believe me it looks awesome!" I recorded, though in truth you couldn't see a thing. The CMD Arete is basically just a boulder field. A knife edge boulder field. You have to be careful picking your way across the rocks, helping fellow runners through the tricky sections. We made it across and then it was just a matter of climbing up to the summit of Ben Nevis - my third summit of Britain's highest peak. "I really shouldn't be messing around. I should be getting down to the bottom. We've got an hour and a half so we should be okay." The Descent and the Only Aid Station The tourist route off Ben Nevis summit is mostly runnable. It's not trouble-free by any means, but if your quads aren't destroyed you can make good time down the hill. Looking at the footage and hearing myself back, I sense a little complacency creeping in. We often balance on a tightrope between confidence and complacency, between self-doubt and self-belief. Perhaps I always feel I'm a stronger runner than I really am. Whether it was complacency, lack of fitness or a combination of the two, I was slower on the descent than I should have been and found myself with less time than expected when I eventually arrived at the only aid station on the Ben Nevis Ultra course. "Just need to get out of here quick don't we?" said a volunteer as I grabbed sausage rolls, apple, crisps and a Soreen bar. Three miles of flat along the river to the next checkpoint, passing a waterfall where I remembered somebody diving off the previous year. That was the last cutoff before the end, which meant I could now run to the finish - theoretically. Uncharted Territory The route between the car park and Steall Falls had been slightly altered to take out a gnarly climb, and given the removal of the river crossing checkpoint, I felt I could relax a little. When I arrived at the river, it was a full 20 minutes after the cutoff time would have been the previous year. I 
- [Marathon Madness Day 5 | Five in Five (or One for the Lazy)](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/marathon-madness-day-5-2018): Blog Running Running Marathon Madness Day 5 | Five in Five (or One for the Lazy) Stephen Cousins 29 June 2018 4 min read In Brief Marathon Madness: five marathons in five days for the brave, one marathon for the lazy (me). Eight laps up and down the beach at Lancing, finishing in darkness. Some runners had already done four marathons this week. Tim had 255 marathons before Monday. I had ice lollies in a cool box. We all have our strategies. 26.2 Miles 4:31:34 Finish Time 8 Laps 5 in 5 Days (for some) Welcome to Film My Run. Today we're running the Marathon Madness 5-in-5. Here we are on the beach—eight times up and down, all the way to Lancing and all the way back again. Eight times. Some people have run five marathons this week, starting on Monday and finishing today. Some people have done three. I'm just doing one, because I'm lazy. The Runners At events like this, you meet runners who put your achievements into perspective. "Mark, how many marathons had you done before Monday?" "Quite a few—hopefully if I finish tonight, I'll have done my 260th." "Tim, what about you?" "255 before I started this week." "So just a relative beginner then?" "Yes, relative beginner." These are the people who show up to run five marathons in five days on a beach in the summer heat. Casual. The Heat It's been a beautiful day, but so hot. By the halfway point—two hours and two minutes in—I knew it was going to be around a 4:15 to 4:30 finish. And probably the last lap in the dark. One of the best ideas my wife ever had: put a load of ice lollies in a cool box. Cold coffee. I can't remember the last time I had a lolly during a marathon. This may be the only time. But on a day like this, it was genius. Janet had done eight marathons this week, three of them part of this event. Rest days in between, but still—eight marathons in one week. "Some people have run five marathons this week. I'm just doing one, because I'm lazy." Charity Miles I met Laura, running with her husband who was a little way behind. They'd just done the London to Brighton bike ride with a team of six, and now this—splitting the charity money between two foundations. Marathon 24 for her. That's the thing about these events. Everyone has their reason. For some it's the challenge, for some it's charity, for some it's just to see how far they can push themselves. Five marathons in five days sounds insane until you meet the people doing it. Into the Dark At the end of lap six, I had two laps to go. Very tired now. Getting lapped by Paul, who only had one lap left. Richard won. I still had two laps to go. Five kilometres to go, coming to the end of the seventh lap, and it was getting very dark. Too dark to film, really. Just passing the café, half a lap to go. And then it was done. Marathon Madness, complete. Some people did five marathons in five days. Kudos to them, because this one marathon killed me today. Watch the Film The Route
- [South Downs Way 100 2023: The Hottest Day](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/south-downs-way-100-2023): Blog Running Running South Downs Way 100 2023: The Hottest Day Stephen Cousins 10 June 2023 8 min read Why am I here? Why were any of us here? Why would any of us choose to travel 100 miles nonstop on foot? And if you've done it once, why would you choose to do it again? These were the questions rattling around my head as Victoria and I lined up in a field in Hampshire at 5:15 in the morning. Just six weeks earlier, I had completed the Thames Path 100 from London to Oxford. That should have been enough for one summer. But here I was, back for more punishment on what would turn out to be the hottest South Downs Way 100 in living memory. TL;DR Victoria's 2nd 100-miler, my 4th SDW100 Hottest conditions ever - up to 27°C Both throwing up from mile 50 onwards Finished 42 minutes inside the cutoff Victoria's verdict: "Never again" 29:18:49 Finish Time 182nd Position 27°C Peak Temperature 3,593m Elevation Gain The Calm Before the Storm This was Victoria's second hundred-miler. The Thames Path had been her first, and somehow I'd convinced her that the South Downs Way would be easier. In the past, it had been. I'd run this route three times before, and it had always felt more runnable than the Thames Path's endless river mud. But today was different. Today, the forecast was showing temperatures up to 27 degrees Celsius. Race day begins "It's going to be very warm today. We just have to drink sensibly, run sensibly and look after ourselves, because we're going to burn up otherwise." These words from my pre-race video would prove prophetic in ways I couldn't have imagined. Starting at the Back Our strategy was simple: go slowly and conserve energy for later. So slowly, in fact, that we found ourselves effectively at the back of the field within the first few miles. At 10 miles, we arrived at the first aid station to find slim pickings, having been beaten there by almost the entire field. Taking in the views At Old Winchester Hill, around the 23-mile mark, we stumbled upon Alan's Cafe. Victoria had been craving full-fat milk, and Alan obliged by giving us two cups completely free of charge. The heat was already building, and we'd been going for nearly five hours. When the Wheels Came Off From Washington at 54 miles, where we collected our drop bags, things deteriorated rapidly. I threw up massively in the toilets. Victoria had already been sick multiple times. This wasn't the race I'd promised her - I'd said it would be easier than Thames Path. The journey continues "How many times is that now that you've been sick?" "I think it's four." The night section was a blur of headtorches and nausea. Victoria developed a strategy: leave the aid station before me and get moving. She was paranoid about the cutoffs, and honestly, so was I. Sunrise and Survival At Alfriston, with just eight miles remaining, I made the mistake of taking a swig of Coke. My stomach had other ideas and I threw up everywhere. Victoria left without me again - she was determined to beat those cutoffs. Pushing through The final stretch through Eastbourne to the finish at the Western Lawns felt interminable. We crossed the line in 29 hours and 18 minutes - just 42 minutes inside the cutoff. Only ten runners finished behind us. "It's not easier than Thames Path. Never again." The hottest South Downs Way 100 on record had broken us, but not completely. Victoria's assessment was right though: never again. At least not until we forgot how bad it was. - [Paris Marathon 2023: Finally Breaking Three Hours](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/paris-marathon-2023-breaking-three-hours): Blog Running Running Paris Marathon 2023: Finally Breaking Three Hours Stephen Cousins 2 April 2023 6 min read In Brief After years of chasing it, I finally broke three hours at the Paris Marathon. My 11th Paris, my 85th marathon, and the day everything clicked: 2:55:44. A new PB by over three minutes, a London qualifier, and proof that those cold winter training runs were worth it. 2:55:44 Finish Time 42.2km Distance 1,466th Position 85th Marathon Do you ever have one of those perfect days when everything seems easy? Paris Marathon 2023 was one of those. It was my 11th time lining up on the Champs-Élysées, but this year felt different. I'd trained hard through the winter with one goal: break three hours. Standing in the sub-3 pen with Marcus from Richmond, Virginia—who was attempting his first Paris Marathon—we were both nervous but determined. A Chaotic Start The start was almost comically French. We nearly went off before we were supposed to, leaving everyone worried we'd accidentally activated our chip timers. Then two emergency medical bikes came screaming through the start area. But finally, with the three-hour pacer bouncing on his toes ahead of us, we heard the countdown: Trois, deux, un... I settled in behind the pacer and made my way down the Champs-Élysées. Over 50,000 runners had lined up that morning—one of the biggest marathon fields in the world. Victoria was starting ninety minutes behind me in a later wave, her focus simply on finishing without injury ahead of Boston and London. "I'd trained hard for three months to break my PB, and speeding up down the final hill felt like a victory lap." Running to Feel Five kilometres in just under 21 minutes. I was ahead of the three-hour pacer now, running to feel rather than obsessing over the numbers. The cool weather was perfect for marathon running—if a little cold for the spectators. By 10k (42 minutes), I was still feeling comfortable. The bands and drummers along the route into Bois de Vincennes helped distract from the knowledge that there was still such a long way to go. I decided not to look at my watch for a while, just letting the miles flow. I didn't need anything from the aid stations in the first half, which meant I could avoid the congestion, trip hazards, and potentially race-ending crashes that happen when hundreds of runners dive for water at once. The Maths in My Head Just past halfway in 1:28. Not doing too badly. But I'd realised I was running slightly slower than planned, so I made a conscious decision to speed up. At 25k (1:45), I was constantly doing calculations in my head. I had one hour and fifteen minutes to cover the remaining 17 kilometres. This is where things can go wrong in Paris. The tunnels—each with a short but significant climb out of them—can sap your legs and your spirit if you're not prepared. The first tunnel is the longest, and it was uncomfortably warm. There's even a DJ playing in one of them, which either helps or makes you want to scream, depending on how your race is going. Stronger in the Second Half But something strange happened after 30k. I'd eaten half a banana—my only fuel of the race—and instead of fading, I felt stronger. More determined. The Eiffel Tower came into view through the tunnel exits, and I knew I was getting close. 35 kilometres done. "Just a parkrun to go," I told myself. The new route this year meant less time trudging through Bois de Boulogne and more time on the city streets where the crowd support was electric. "When you're this close to the end, the sense of pride, relief, achievement and exhaustion combine to create a unique feeling—an emotional high that has to be experienced to be understood." The Finish With 3k to go, I was tired but running on pure adrenaline. The crowds were incredible. Rounding the final bend onto the Avenue Foch, I sprinted as hard as I could. 2:55:44. My secret goal had been 2:55:00. I'd missed it by 44 seconds. But I'd smashed my PB. I'd gone under three hours. And I'd qualified for London next year. Victoria and Sarah finished about ninety minutes later, having enjoyed the sights, the gingerbread cake at the aid stations, and the experience of running through one of the world's most beautiful cities. Victoria filmed far more than I did—I was too focused on the task at hand to pull out the camera much. What It Meant The course was better than it had been in previous years. There was a little wind occasionally, but nothing significant. The cool conditions were ideal. Everything had aligned. Eleven Paris Marathons. Eighty-five marathons total. And finally, the sub-3 I'd been chasing. Those cold winter training runs, the 4am alarm clocks, the months of structured work—it all paid off on one perfect April morning in Paris. I learned a long time ago that the key is to couch it as a family holiday. We've been coming to the Canary Islands for ten years now, and we genuinely do love Gran Canaria. The running is just a... bonus. Trans Gran Canaria has always been a stellar event, but since joining the World Trail Majors series, it's been elevated even further. The expo is bigger, there are more runners, and it feels properly prestigious. This year there were plenty of Brits on the island, many of whom keep coming back just like us. At registration I met Steve, who was there for his fifth time. His best finish was 21 hours 20 minutes back in 2017 - the kind of time I could only dream about. I was simply hoping to finish inside 24 hours, something I'd never managed in my two previous attempts. At the expo finish line we spotted James Elson from Centurion Running, who was doing the marathon distance. Because we were near the back, it took us a while to actually cross the timing mat - but eventually, away we went. The first 400 metres is a procession along the beach, then up onto the promenade for the next four kilometres. I was very happy to be wearing my HOKA Skyward X road shoes for this section. The climb started early and it was steep - with over 6,000 metres of elevation gain, you spend most of Trans Gran Canaria going uphill. Through the Night By 11 kilometres I arrived at the first aid station, Tenoya. Having done this race twice before, I knew what was coming - and sometimes that knowledge is more daunting than helpful. You can plan and manage your race, but you're also fully aware of the magnitude of what lies ahead. The trails were dry and dusty, a stark contrast to my 2022 experience when a storm had turned this section into a treacherous river of mud. This year it was much better - still steep, but doable. I pushed on through the night, making good time through the various checkpoints. By the time the sun rose, I'd covered a marathon distance during the cool hours of darkness. As the sky brightened, all I could think was: please don't get too hot. The National Parks This is where Trans Gran Canaria comes into its own. The national parks around the centre of the island are stunning - spectacular views at every turn. With the rising sun came new energy and positivity, and I absolutely loved this section. Before the heat set in and before I'd accumulated too much fatigue. The descent into El Hornillo was technically demanding, requiring full concentration despite the inspiring scenery around me. From there I crossed the Los Peroz Dam and made my way up another long climb through beautiful green forests against a deep blue backdrop without a cloud in sight. On a clear day you can see Tenerife and Mount Teide, the highest mountain in Spain, from these ridges. The Trouble Begins I arrived at Artenara around halfway, thoroughly exhausted. While I was trudging to this checkpoint, American runner Caleb Olsen was crossing the finish line in 12 hours 17 minutes to win the 2025 Trans Gran Canaria Classic. Jonathan Albon came second, and his wife Henriette won the women's race in 15 hours 2 minutes. Our friend Mark Darbyshire, ably crewed by his mother Helen, finished in 13th place in 15 hours 27 minutes. I, meanwhile, was sitting in the shade wondering if I could move my legs ever again. The climb out of Artenara was relentless, and the sun was absolutely roasting. My stomach felt dodgy after mixing milk with orange juice - probably not my smartest nutritional decision. By the time I reached Tejeda, my foot was really hurting and I was cutting it fine on the cutoffs. "According to the race predictor app, I'm not going to make it to the cutoff at the next checkpoint." To his credit, he refused to make that decision for me - but he did offer to pick me up from Garanon if I didn't make it. Chasing Cutoffs And so began my battle against the clock. As darkness fell, I was fighting to reach every checkpoint, so focused on moving forward that I barely touched my camera for the rest of the race. I made it to Garanon with about 
- [Southend Pier Marathon 2018: The Longest Pier in the World](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/southend-pier-marathon-2018): Blog Running Running Southend Pier Marathon 2018: The Longest Pier in the World Stephen Cousins 11 March 2018 5 min read In Brief A marathon on the longest pleasure pier in the world. Southend Pier stretches 1.34 miles into the Thames Estuary, and to run a marathon on it you have to run back and forth approximately ten times. It sounds tedious. It was brilliant. Sub 3:30 on a freezing March day, collecting wristbands with every lap. 26.2mi Distance 3:29:01 Finish Time ~10 Laps 1.34mi Pier Length What made you want to run up and down a pier? It's a fair question. The Southend Pier Marathon is exactly what it sounds like - a marathon distance run on the longest pleasure pier in the world. Out to the end, round the cone, back to the start. Collect a wristband. Repeat until you've done enough laps to cover 26.2 miles. Standing at the end of the pier before the start, looking back towards Southend, I wondered what I'd signed up for. The pier stretches 1.34 miles into the Thames Estuary. It's a proper Victorian structure, built in 1830 and extended multiple times. Running it ten times seemed either brilliantly simple or simply mad. The Field This wasn't a mass participation event. The field was small and friendly, which is exactly what you want for a race this unusual. Among the runners was Simon Lewis, who was on his 158th marathon. One hundred and fifty-eight. And here I was, still counting mine on fingers and toes. The format was simple: run to the end of the pier, round the cone, back to the start. Collect a wristband. When you've got ten wristbands, you're on your last lap - come back and collect your medal instead. Race director Jay gave the briefing, and we were off. The Rhythm of Repetition Running the same stretch of pier repeatedly sounds monotonous. In practice, it was oddly meditative. The Thames Estuary to your left, then to your right. The pier stretching ahead, then behind. Other runners passing in the opposite direction, a nod of acknowledgement each time. By lap three I'd settled into a rhythm. By lap six we were over halfway, and the cheesecake at the aid station was calling. One of the unique pleasures of a small, friendly race - proper food at the turnaround. "Running the same stretch of pier repeatedly sounds monotonous. In practice, it was oddly meditative." The Business End End of lap seven, I finally took on some nutrition - a bit of Coke because I'd barely had anything the whole race. Still on target for 3:30, which was the goal. The pier stretched out ahead for the eighth time, and I was starting to feel it. The wind off the estuary was bitter. March in Essex, exposed on a pier with nothing between you and the North Sea - it wasn't warm. But the running kept the cold at bay, mostly. Two laps to go and it was really starting to hurt. That's the thing about these point-to-point-to-point races - you can't hide from the pace. Every lap is the same distance, same terrain, same mental challenge. You know exactly how far you've come and exactly how far you have to go. One lap to go. Twenty minutes to stay under 3:30. The Final Lap The last out-and-back felt longer than all the others combined, as final laps always do. But the pier had become familiar by now - I knew every section of decking, every slight change in surface. Round the cone one last time, and then the final push back to the finish. 3:29:01. Sub 3:30 on the longest pier in the world. Not many people can say that. "We've just run up and down Southend Pier about ten times. And now I'm getting really cold." Final Thoughts The post-race chill hit hard. Standing around in sweaty kit on an exposed pier in March - not ideal for recovery. But the sense of achievement was real. This wasn't a tough course in the traditional sense - no hills, no technical terrain - but it had its own challenges. The mental game of repetition, the relentless wind, the knowledge that there's nowhere to hide. Thanks to Sussex Trail Events and Danny and the team for putting on something genuinely different. Not every marathon needs mountains. Sometimes a pier is enough. Watch the Video Strava Activity
- [Swiss Alps 100 2025: Two Attempts, Two DNFs](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/swiss-alps-100-2025): Blog Running Running Swiss Alps 100 2025: Two Attempts, Two DNFs Stephen Cousins 12 July 2025 8 min read In Brief Second attempt at the Swiss Alps 100 in Fiesch, Switzerland. After DNF'ing last year, I was determined to finish this time. Made it further than before - all the way to the top of Breithorn at 2,500m - but my stomach gave out completely. Spent the final climb throwing up, arrived 10 minutes over cutoff. Two attempts, two DNFs. The mountains won again. ~75km Distance (DNF) ~5,000m Elevation DNF Result 2nd Attempt The good thing about DNF'ing a race in Switzerland is that you get to come back and do it all over again. I was in the beautiful Swiss town of Fiesch, about two hours' drive from Geneva, ready for my second attempt at the Swiss Alps 100. It was 6:30 in the morning, we were going to spend the day climbing the Swiss Alps, running alongside the biggest glacier in the Alps, crossing the Aspi-Titter suspension bridge. What could possibly go wrong? Confidence is born out of experience - the knowledge that you've been here before, you've crushed tougher challenges in the past, and you've learned from your mistakes. Arriving for my second attempt, I was absolutely determined to succeed. And without being overconfident, I totally believed I would make it to the finish line. The Start: Fiesch At the start I met Chris from Brighton. We were both hoping to finish before the 28-hour cutoff - if we got in at 26 hours 59 minutes, nobody would care. The first kilometre was all tarmac uphill, then into the climb up towards the Aletsch Glacier. About 1,500 metres of climbing to start with - the longest climb and highest elevation of the entire race. Five and a half kilometres in, we were above the tree line and into the sunshine. At the first checkpoint I saw my family, which was lovely after that initial shock to the system. "If there's one reason alone to come and run the Swiss Alps 100, it's to experience running alongside the largest glacier in the Alps." The Aletsch Glacier Without question, this is the highlight of the course - climbing up to the pass at Bettmerhorn and then running 5km alongside the largest glacier in the Alps. The depth of the deepest part is about 900 metres. From the ice down to the base of the valley - that much ice. It's around 22 kilometres long and absolutely breathtaking. Unfortunately, there had been a landslide, so the course was diverted. What used to be a lovely smooth path alongside the glacier was now a 150-metre climb through a boulder field. It all adds to the fun, doesn't it? At 15km the path turned away from the glacier towards Gletscherstube checkpoint. A mountain rescue helicopter had to come out to pick up a runner who'd injured their leg badly in a fall - a reminder that these races can be dangerous. The Aspi-Titter Bridge Leaving the shade of the mountain and the cool glacier air, we descended into a stunningly beautiful but baking hot valley. The descent was punishing - very technical, very steep. One wrong step and you'd mash your face on the rocks. I watched Frank go right over in front of me. He was okay, but it was a stark reminder to concentrate. The Aspi-Titter suspension bridge is about a metre wide with a 100-metre drop to the gorge below. It scares the bejesus out of me, but you've got to get it done. Last year I ran across it, which completely shattered me. This time I walked it sensibly - heart rate still going with adrenaline from the crossing. Feeling Good... Too Good? Last year, by Bellwald at 25km, the heat was already too much and my stomach had turned. This time the heat wasn't quite so intense and I was able to take advantage of the easy trails. I was half an hour faster on this section, making good progress. The Swiss countryside was gorgeous. Beautiful cafes (which I wisely didn't stop at), spectacular colours on the hillsides, and those fantastically positioned water troughs - not for cattle, but fresh, cold water for human consumption. I couldn't believe how good I was feeling. At Blitzingen, 45km in, I felt so much better than the previous year. "I don't know what I was going on about last year," I told the camera. Famous last words. "This is where I decided I was DNF'ing last year, this exact spot. But it's not happening today. I am making it today." The Wheels Come Off Climbing the road up to Chäserstatt, I couldn't help but think back to how I felt 12 months before. It was on this road that I knew my race was done last year. Things couldn't have been more different this time - I was happy, full of confidence and belief. But whilst I had rested at Chäserstatt, I hadn't eaten very much. As the heat dissipated and I made my way onto new trails in the evening light, things were about to change. At 57km, there was some very steep terrain to negotiate before the summit of Eggerhorn at 2,500 metres. Head torch on as the sun went down, I began the 6km descent to Binn, needing to arrive by midnight. It was on this descent that I started feeling more and more nauseous. As it usually does on hot days, my stomach had finally turned. Binn and the Final Climb Inside the Binn checkpoint, I knew I had to eat, but looking at the food, there was nothing I could stomach. I took a couple of bites of watermelon and immediately knew I was going to be sick. The ladies at the checkpoint wanted me to stop. But I wasn't stopping - I'd just thrown up massively downstairs, which is part of the course, isn't it? That's what we do. One massive climb left - 1,200 metres up to Breithorn. And even after that, another 20km with 500m of climbing to the finish. I set off across a lovely bridge, eating chocolate, trying to stay positive. The Summit of Breithorn Since leaving Binn, I'd been throwing up all the way up. So much so that I was now dry heaving, which is horrendous. But I was pretty much at the top of the climb, and it was incredible up there. I felt very sick. I had weak legs and no energy because I couldn't keep any food down. It was ver
- [Trans Gran Canaria 2022 | When Paradise Turned to Ice](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/trans-gran-canaria-2022-when-paradise-turned-to-ice): Blog Running Running Trans Gran Canaria 2022 | When Paradise Turned to Ice Stephen Cousins 4 March 2022 10 min read TL;DR My second Trans Gran Canaria - 125km from Las Palmas in the north to Maspalomas in the south, with 6000m of climbing. The weather was brutal: freezing rain, howling winds, and treacherous mud that turned this into one of the hardest races I've ever done. Finished in 26:46:10, grateful just to have made it. 125 Kilometres 26:46:10 Finish Time 6,000m Elevation 2nd Attempt I would never have believed it could be that cold in Gran Canaria. That's what I kept telling myself as the wind howled and the rain lashed down, somewhere in the mountains at 2am with 80 kilometres still to go. This was supposed to be a sunny island ultra. Instead, it turned into a survival exercise. Back to the Canaries This was my second Trans Gran Canaria. I knew the course, or at least I thought I did. The race starts at 11pm in Las Palmas on the north coast and traverses the entire island to finish in Maspalomas on the south coast. 125 kilometres with 6000 metres of climbing - it's a monster of a race, and one of the most prestigious ultras in Europe. The format was slightly different this year, finishing in a new location, making it marginally shorter. But as I would discover, shorter doesn't mean easier when the mountain decides to throw everything it has at you. Into the Storm The first aid station came at 19 kilometres, with 107 still to go. By aid station two at 31 kilometres, we were nearly five hours in and I was moving efficiently - quick stops, just enough to refuel, back on the trail within three minutes. I was hoping for a 24-hour finish. Then the weather turned. By 7am, as we climbed into the mountains, it was wet, cold, and windy in a way that felt utterly wrong for the Canary Islands. The Spanish runners were struggling badly - they weren't used to this kind of weather. As a Brit, I'd seen worse conditions, but that didn't make it pleasant. "This is beyond a joke now. It is so cold I would never have believed it could be that cold in Gran Canaria." Artanara: The Breaking Point At Artanara aid station, about 67 kilometres in, the race began falling apart for many runners. The wind was absolutely howling. It was freezing. The rain had been non-stop since we started climbing back up. Plenty of people were sitting there, defeated, having decided they'd had enough. I was contemplating it too. I wasn't afraid to pull out if conditions got ridiculous. But then a kind stranger named John offered me his gloves. It's the small acts of kindness in ultra running that get you through. I put them on and decided to push a little further. The Turning Point Something remarkable happened as I climbed over the spine of the island. On the north side - still horrendously windy, rainy, cloudy. But on the south side, occasionally the sun would touch your legs. Just a hint that better weather was on the way. At Tejeda, I finally got some sunshine, though drizzle still hung in the air. My legs were wrecked. The 24-hour goal had slipped away somewhere in the mud. But I was still well ahead of cut-off, and the weather was improving. By Garañón, with 43 kilometres to go, I could see clear skies ahead. A marathon left to run, but suddenly it felt achievable again. The Views We Came For With a full marathon still ahead, I crossed a dam and caught my first proper view of the day. This - this was what Trans Gran Canaria was supposed to be. Valleys cascading down to the sea, mountains stretching into the distance, and there on the horizon, Tenerife and Mount Teide, the highest mountain in Spain at 3500 metres. That's what we should have had all day. Instead, we got wind and rain and mud. But seeing it now, even just for the final section, made the suffering worthwhile. The Final Push From the final aid station, 14 kilometres remained. The route snaked down the mountain - absolutely stunning but technical, demanding constant attention to footing. It felt like running through the jungle at times, the vegetation so lush and dense. And then, somehow, I was at the finish. The family had come out to see me, waiting far longer than any of us had expected. "I have no idea how I finished this," I said to the camera. And I meant it. That had been the hardest race I could remember. Watch the Film I captured the full brutality and beauty of Trans Gran Canaria on film. Here's the race video: The Route Lessons in Resilience Trans Gran Canaria 2022 taught me something important about ultra running: you can't control the conditions, only your response to them. When I stood at Artanara watching people drop out, I understood their decision. The weather was genuinely dangerous - hypothermia was a real risk. But something made me stay. Maybe it was John's gloves. Maybe it was the knowledge that conditions would improve on the other side of the mountain. Maybe it was just stubbornness. Whatever it was, I'm glad I pushed through. The finish time - 26 hours 46 minutes - wasn't what I'd hoped for. But on a day like that, finishing at all felt like victory. Sometimes the race isn't about time or position. It's about discovering what you're capable of when everything goes wrong. Trans Gran Canaria remains one of the great ultras. I'll be back. Hopefully next time the island will show me the sunshine it's famous for.
- [UTMB CCC 2018 | My First Taste of Mont Blanc](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/utmb-ccc-2018-first-taste-of-mont-blanc): Blog Running Running UTMB CCC 2018 | My First Taste of Mont Blanc Stephen Cousins 5 September 2018 12 min read TL;DR My first UTMB event - 101km around Mont Blanc with 6,000m of climbing. A brutal lesson in humility. The mountain broke me early, a rerouted course added technical misery, and I scraped under 24 hours by three minutes. I didn't respect Mont Blanc. It made sure I knew it. Date: 31st August 2018 | Distance: 101km (63 miles) | Time: 23:57:30 | Elevation: 6,100m There is a place, a mystical, magical place known only to ultra runners. A Mecca, if you will. For one week in August, the greatest ultra runners in the world convene in Chamonix to run races from 15km up to 300km, circumnavigating the highest mountain in Western Europe. This was my first pilgrimage, and Mont Blanc was about to teach me a lesson I wouldn't forget. A Family Affair As an ultra runner with a young family, every holiday has a race attached to it. And, ergo, every race becomes a family holiday. We spent the early part of the week in Chamonix - riding the cable car, hiking up the side of Mont Blanc, and watching the kids run 5km from a glacier down to town. The same children who regularly resist our attempts to get them up for parkrun on a Saturday morning. My kids were fortunate enough to meet and interview Jim Walmsley at the Running Expo. "How far do you run in your races?" they asked. We watched an amazing finish to the TDS race. The atmosphere was electric. This was everything I'd hoped it would be. The Terrifying Kit Check Unless you've done it, you have absolutely no idea how terrifying pre-race mandatory kit check and number collection can be. Honestly, have I remembered everything? Two head torches, taped seams on my coat, ID, that extra layer, waterproof gloves. Will I be disqualified before I even get to the start line? It's nerve-wracking. Part of what makes UTMB so unique is its entry system. You can't just rock up on the day, pay your money and run. You have to qualify through a series of races over multiple years, earning points. And even with enough points, you enter a ballot - it could take three years before your name is drawn. Getting that race number felt like an achievement in itself. The First Climb Broke Me The CCC starts in Courmayeur, Italy, at 9am. It's the opposite version of Chamonix on the Italian side of Mont Blanc. The atmosphere at the start was incredible - they really ramp it up. We started as though we were running a 10K race, full of adrenaline. Then, literally ten minutes in, we started climbing. And kept climbing. Before I started, I thought 20 hours was a realistic target. Two and a quarter hours in, I was already questioning whether I'd complete the course at all. At the top of the first climb - 10.6km in 2 hours 17 minutes, 1,434 metres climbed - I was destroyed. Twenty kilometres in and I was suffering a crisis of confidence. I hadn't accounted for how steep and long that first climb was. Single-track trails meant pressure from runners behind, pushing me faster than I should have gone. By 20km I was genuinely shattered with 80km still to go. "That first climb got me," I admitted to anyone who'd listen at the aid station. "I didn't realise how steep it was and I took it too fast." Finding a Rhythm One thing kept my spirits up: the scenery. I've run in some great places, but this was something else entirely. Crossing from Italy into Switzerland, climbing to 2,537 metres at Col Ferret, the views when the clouds lifted were breathtaking. The ultra running community is remarkably small. I bumped into Dave Ross from Thames Meander Marathon, running on a torn meniscus. "We're going to carry on, we're going to soldier on, we're going to do this bad boy," he said. That's the spirit of these events. By the marathon mark - 42km in 8 hours 23 minutes - I was starting to feel like I was getting into the race. The descent from Grand Col Ferret reminded me of England back home. The weather, the terrain underfoot, all very similar to the South Coast where I train. At halfway, my watch showed 9 hours 51 minutes. If I could maintain that pace, I'd come in under 20 hours. But with three big climbs still ahead, I knew the likelihood was slim. The Rerouted Nightmare What I didn't fully appreciate was that the course had been rerouted. Earlier in the week, a hiker had died in a rockfall. The organisers had added a different section to make up the elevation - a series of intense technical climbs followed by rocky, rooty descents. With nine and a half kilometres to go, the terrain became almost unrunnable. Just rocks and roots, horrific on completely trashed legs. My watch hit 100km but there were still at least seven more kilometres. Everything was longer than marked. I was so tired. My legs were hurting, my brain was aching. I just wanted it to finish. But we kept going up when I thought we should be going down. I'd put my poles away ages ago because I thought we were descending. I was wrong. Racing the Clock If you've suffered in an ultra, you'll know that feeling of longing for the last aid station to appear. We were waiting for La Flégère at 1,900 metres. Would it ever come? The 20-hour goal had gone long ago. Now even the 24-hour target was slipping away. When I finally passed the last aid station, I didn't stop. I just wanted to get home. And then I ran. Downhill, steep, six or seven kilometres to go. My watch showing 101km. As a final reminder of who's really in charge, the mountain had kept me climbing longer than expected, and now time was running out. I had to run hard. 23:57:30 We made it under 24 hours. Not the original goal, but it would do. Crossing the finish line felt strange. I didn't really take it in because I'd been trying so hard to beat the clock. Just a few hours later, I was back in the crowd to welcome home Xavier Thévenard, the UTMB winner, claiming his third victory. Damien Hall finally broke the top ten at UTMB, finishing fifth. Tom Evans won my race, the CCC. I 
- [Royal Wedding and running](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/royal-wedding-and-running): Blog Running Running Royal Wedding and running Stephen Cousins 16 May 2011 2 min read The wedding of William and Kate took place a couple of weeks ago which was considered to be one of the best event insurance wedding ever in this year. I had to work but there was a street party on our road. Victoria decided not to attend once she eyed up the other party goers. She thought we wouldn't fit in and I agreed once I arrived home. Bit too chavvy for us. So that happened and then Osama Bin Laden got shot by the Americans in Pakistan. I suppose it's better that he's been found but it really annoyed me the way the American public celebrated like they'd won a football match. They really don't help their cause. On the home front, Victoria is nearing due date and we have been given a cot by Wriggly. I have started running again on a regular basis. Once a week I do something called Parkrun in Hove Park. It's a 5km run round the park and you get timed and given a stats breakdown on the website later the same day. It's fun and I took Hal and Jev along a week last Saturday. They both did really well but Jevan has the makings of a real runner. He had loads of energy left at the end and did it in a time of 28.31. I have been at court this last week for a final session about access. I get the boys for a week at Easter, a week at Christmas and two weeks in the summer, plus they stay over here every other weekend. Not bad really. There's more I could shout about but I can wait to see if Debbie will acquiesce over the coming years. Running
- [Ridgeway Challenge 2025: 140km on Britain's Oldest Road](https://filmmyrun.com/blog/ridgeway-challenge-2025): Blog Running Running Ridgeway Challenge 2025: 140km on Britain's Oldest Road Stephen Cousins 31 May 2025 5 min read TL;DR Completed the full 140km Ridgeway Trail from Ivinghoe Beacon to Avebury Stone Circle in 24 hours 23 minutes. Struggled badly in the heat during the first half, survived on ice bandanas and power naps, then found my legs in the final 10km to secure 3rd place in the V55 age group for the British Trail Running Championships. 140km Distance 24:23:36 Finish Time 2,166m Elevation 51st / 3rd V55 Position I'd wanted to run the full Ridgeway for years. One of Britain's oldest roads, it follows in the footsteps of herdsmen, traders, travellers and soldiers from Neolithic and Celtic tribes, right through the Roman and medieval periods. When Runaway Racing took over the event for 2025 and it was selected as the ultra distance race for the British Trail Running Championships, I knew I had to be there. We walked the 600 metres up to Ivinghoe Beacon for what has to be one of the most spectacular start lines in UK ultra running. The whole field gathered on this hilltop in Buckinghamshire, about to embark on 140 kilometres of ancient trail all the way to Avebury Stone Circle in Wiltshire. "What a start line at this place this year." The Chilterns: A Tale of Heat and Matching Shoes The first section through the Chiltern escarpment was a mix of shaded woodland and exposed countryside. I reached 10 miles in just under two hours, which felt about right. I even encountered two runners running together who, completely by accident they assured me, were wearing the same top and the same running shoes. We passed through Wendover, where a brand new bridge over the HS2 construction site marked perhaps the most modern addition to this ancient route. I couldn't help but think the ancient Britons probably didn't walk this particular detour. The climb up to Coombe Hill and its monument—erected in 1904 to commemorate those who died in the Second Boer War—was relentless. The steepest hill of the race so far, and in that heat, it was properly cruel. When Heat Becomes the Enemy Here's the thing about me and heat: we don't get along. For anyone watching, it was probably 20, maybe 22 degrees—nothing really. But for me, it felt like I was boiling in an oven. Victoria, my wife and crew chief extraordinaire, met me at various points along the route with ice bandanas, freeze pops, and endless patience. "It's so hot for me. For you—wherever you're watching—it's probably nothing. But for me, it feels like I'm boiling in an oven." By 34 kilometres, I was in survival mode. The pattern became familiar: 100 metres running, 200 metres walking. The ice in my bandana helped, but I was managing expectations rather than chasing times. Any hopes of that age group podium were fading fast. It took me 6 hours and 7 minutes to reach marathon distance. On any normal day, that would be disappointing. But this wasn't a normal day, and I knew that if I could just survive until the temperature dropped, I might find something resembling running legs again. Grim's Ditch and the Art of Crewing The section along Grim's Ditch was some of the most peaceful running of the entire route. This linear prehistoric earthwork dating back to the Bronze Age wound through enchanting woodland, and I could feel the weight of time on my shoulders as I shuffled along these ancient trails. Just like running on the South Downs Way, there's something profound about following paths that humans have used for thousands of years. Victoria's crewing was masterful. At each meeting point, she'd have a selection of options ready—because what you think you want at the next checkpoint isn't necessarily what you actually want when you get there. Cream cheese, Marmite and cucumber bagels. Marmite crisps. Earl Grey tea. Cold lattes. Paracetamol for my aching back and legs. Crossing the Thames at Goring At 71 kilometres, I crossed the River Thames at Goring—just over halfway. I was feeling the accumulated fatigue of the day, my back was aching, my legs were killing me, and the mental challenge of knowing I was only halfway through was significant. But I'd been here before. I'd had this pain before, these mental challenges. And I knew I'd get it done. Night Terrors and Power Naps As darkness fell, the character of the race changed completely. At one point, I felt like I was in an episode of An American Werewolf in London. Over in the forest, there was this horrendously frightening noise—some creature making sounds that would have sent me running if I'd had any running left in my legs. It went on for about 10 minutes as I approached, and I was genuinely relieved when I finally passed it. I started having five-minute power naps in the van every time I met Victoria. The cold had arrived with a vengeance, and I'd borrowed her fleece because mine was soaking wet. Each time I stopped, it was harder to start again—but the alternative was weaving all over the path with my eyes closed. "Don't feel good. Wish it was over. But we've done this before. We've been here before." The Final Push I reached 100 kilometres in 16 hours and 47 minutes. The sunrise perked me up, and as the temperature rose to something more pleasant (for normal humans, anyway), I started to consider whether that podium position might still be possible. The truth was, I hadn't trained properly for this race. I'd basically used it as the start of my training block for the Swiss Alps 100 later in the summer. And it showed—I was wrecked for the majority of the run. To make matters worse, I'd forgotten to bring my reliable socks and had to buy some at the last minute. They were fine for a marathon, but after 100 kilometres, my feet were in bits. Around the 120-kilometre mark, at the final checkpoint, I'd laid down for a rest. What knocked me out of my slumbers was hearing one of the volunteers say, "Oh, there can't be that many left to come in now." That got me up. Victoria told me there were quite a few runners

# Recent news stories on the site
- [Olsen and Lawrence win 100km world titles in Spain as Britain's Milne takes bronze](https://filmmyrun.com/news/olsen-and-lawrence-win-100km-world-titles-in-spain-as-britain-s-milne): News Olsen and Lawrence win 100km world titles in Spain as Britain's Milne takes bronze Olsen and Lawrence win 100km world titles in Spain as Britain's Milne takes bronze 26 September 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Courtney Olsen and Charlie Lawrence won the IAU 100k World Championships in Ames, Spain, on Sunday 20 September, giving the United States both titles. Britain's Alex Milne , the reigning IAU 50k world champion, took bronze in the men's race in 6:17:50. He had been 10th and more than four minutes down in the early laps. He reached fourth on lap 16 and moved onto the podium on lap 18. The course had a 4.8km opening loop followed by 19 laps of 5km, mixing road and bike path through town and tree-lined sections. Conditions were clear but hot. The temperature rose from 16C at the 8:30am start to 32C by the finish. There were 147 men and 102 women on the start line from 44 countries. Lawrence, the 50-mile world record holder, went past early leader Masato Tanaka of Japan on the 10th lap. He reached halfway in 3:00:34 and for a while looked capable of threatening the 6:05:35 world record. His laps drifted beyond 19 minutes from lap 15 and that chance went. He still held off Lithuania's Aleksandr Sorokin to win in 6:09:25. Sorokin, the world record holder, was second in 6:12:41 and also won the World Masters Athletics 100k title held within the race. The women's race turned late. Miho Nakata of Japan led for roughly the first 75km, but Olsen came through from sixth and took the lead on lap 17. Olsen, 39, won in 7:10:31. Nakata was second in 7:11:57. Gemma Arenas of Spain was third in 7:17:50. Olsen also took the World Masters Athletics women's title. Britain's Sarah Webster, the 24-hour world record holder, had climbed to third and was the fastest runner on the 13th lap. She dropped out on the final lap while in a podium position. Naomi Robinson, the other British runner named in reports, ran sixth in the opening laps. Noora Honkala of Finland was fourth in 7:21:37 and Croatia's Nikolina Šustić-Stanković fifth in 7:21:57. Croatia won the women's team title ahead of Italy and Spain. Originally reported in Athletics Weekly ,
- [UTMB cuts age-based direct qualification places for Chamonix Final from 210 to 60](https://filmmyrun.com/news/utmb-cuts-age-based-direct-qualification-places-for-chamonix-final-fro): News UTMB cuts age-based direct qualification places for Chamonix Final from 210 to 60 UTMB cuts age-based direct qualification places for Chamonix Final from 210 to 60 26 September 2026 Photo: Leon Butler/Ultra Trail Whistler by UTMB / Canadian Running UTMB has cut the number of age-based direct qualification places for its World Series Final in Chamonix. There were 210 such slots. There will now be 60, split across the UTMB, CCC and OCC races. The change removes 150 places and has drawn a wave of confused and critical reaction from runners. Under the revised system, direct qualification from the World Series major races goes only to the top 10 men and top 10 women at each distance. Those distances are 50K, 100K and 176K. There are four majors on the circuit. Running Stones are unchanged, and runners who take part in a major still have their stones doubled. That improves their odds in the lottery for a place in one of the Final races. UTMB says the aim is to widen access to Chamonix. Its argument is that runners can build lottery chances at races nearer home rather than travelling to majors in search of an age-group slot. The organisation has confirmed that a new age-group rule will cover the entire circuit. It has not yet said what that rule will be. On Instagram it described the rules as being finalised and due to be announced "very shortly". Many runners responded on the announcement post with the concern that older athletes would lose out. One commenter said the change "puts older age groups at a disadvantage" because a top-10 finish is far harder for them. Others worried about runners who commit to attending the majors each season. UTMB replied that the intention was not to take that achievement away. It said it wanted a qualification route across the whole circuit rather than one tied to a handful of events. The changes apply to every race in 2027. The exception is HOKA Ultra-Trail Australia by UTMB, held in May, where they take effect in 2028. The announcement comes as UTMB faces pressure from the mayor of Chamonix, François-Xavier Laffin. He has been calling for a smaller footprint for the event, with fewer racers and smaller crowds. UTMB has not said whether it will make changes in response. It plans to meet local officials and race organisations by the end of October. Originally reported in Canadian Running Back to News
- [Hartmuth and Zhao lower both course records at Tor des Géants](https://filmmyrun.com/news/hartmuth-and-zhao-take-course-records-at-tor-des-geants-as-german-runn): News Hartmuth and Zhao lower both course records at Tor des Géants Hartmuth and Zhao lower both course records at Tor des Géants 26 September 2026 Photo: Canadian Running Both course records fell at the Tor des Géants 330K in Italy's Aosta Valley. China's Jiaju Zhao won in 65:55:22. Germany's Katharina Hartmuth defended her women's title in 67:10:09 and placed third overall, 75 minutes behind him. Earlier in 2026 she also set the fastest women's time recorded on the Bob Graham Round in England. Hartmuth's previous record stood at 79:10:40 from her 2024 win, when she became the first woman to go under 80 hours. She has now cut 12 hours and 31 seconds from that. She is the first woman to break 70 hours and the first to reach the overall podium. Reports say she slept for roughly 15 minutes in the whole race. Zhao, 31, led from early on and held the front for most of the distance. His time was 13 minutes inside the 66:08:22 set by Victor Richard in 2025. He is the first runner from China to win the event. Switzerland's Jonathan Schindler was second in 66:55:06. The race is a single stage that starts and ends in Courmayeur. This year's course came out at about 336 km with around 24,000 metres of ascent on high Alpine trails. The cut-off is 150 hours, so competitors must decide for themselves when to rest and sleep. Zhao did not enjoy it. Afterwards he described nosebleeds, heavy fatigue and severe pain in the soles of his feet. He said he had slapped his own face to stay awake. He called the experience "a living hell" and said he would not race beyond 168 km again. Hartmuth's season had already brought a win at Madeira Island Ultra-Trail. - [Agnes Ngetich wins world half marathon title in Copenhagen with women-only world record](https://filmmyrun.com/news/agnes-ngetich-takes-world-title-and-women-only-half-marathon-record-in): News Agnes Ngetich wins world half marathon title in Copenhagen with women-only world record Agnes Ngetich wins world half marathon title in Copenhagen with women-only world record 26 September 2026 Photo: Jasmine Fehr / Canadian Running Agnes Ngetich of Kenya won the women's half marathon in Copenhagen on Sunday 20 September in 1:05:15. The time is a new world record for a race run by women alone. It improves by one second on the mark Peres Jepchirchir set when she took the world half marathon title in 2020. The 25-year-old won the gold medal at the World Athletics Road Running Championships by 50 seconds. Her Kenyan teammate Veronica Loleo took silver in 1:06:05. Florence Niyonkuru of Rwanda was three seconds further back for bronze in 1:06:08. The overall women's world record still belongs to Ethiopia's Letesenbet Gidey at 1:02:52. Ngetich credited her coach, who she said had told her she could win gold. She said she was very happy and grateful to add the half marathon record to her collection. She already has form at 10km. In 2024 she won a mixed road race in Valencia in 28:46, the first woman to go under 29 minutes. In April 2025 she ran 29:27 to become the first woman under 30 minutes in a women-only race. Her plans now point towards the track. Ngetich said she would talk to her coach about what comes next but intends to race on the track in 2027, the year of the World Athletics Championships. A track gold is, in her words, "the only one I am missing". It was a deep women's field. Canada's Jadyn Keeler, 23, finished 16th in 1:08:03 to break the national record. Andrea Seccafien's 1:09:38 from 2020 fell by one minute and 35 seconds. Keeler had made her half marathon debut only five weeks earlier in Edmonton. She called the Copenhagen atmosphere incredible. The men's title went to Sweden's Andreas Almgren . He crossed the line in 58:06, taking 35 seconds off his own European record. Originally reported in Canadian Running , LetsRun ,
- [Becky Atkinson leads all-female top three at Rasselbock Backyard Ultra in Derbyshire](https://filmmyrun.com/news/becky-atkinson-leads-all-female-top-three-at-rasselbock-backyard-ultra): News Becky Atkinson leads all-female top three at Rasselbock Backyard Ultra in Derbyshire Becky Atkinson leads all-female top three at Rasselbock Backyard Ultra in Derbyshire 26 September 2026 Photo: BBC Sport Women took all three podium places at the Rasselbock Backyard Ultra at the Hardwick Estate in Derbyshire. Organisers say it is the first all-female podium recorded at a backyard ultra in the UK. Becky Atkinson, from west Wales, won on her debut in the Rasselbock series. She lasted 40 hours and covered 166.4 miles. Hayley Wilson, from Worksop in Nottinghamshire, finished second. Hollie Jones, from Easby in Yorkshire, was third. The race began on a Saturday with 141 starters. Women made up 21% of the field and men 79%. The format asks runners to complete a 4.16-mile loop every hour, on the hour. The last runner still going wins. Event organiser Eric Keeler said the team had checked thousands of results worldwide. He found only one previous all-female winning line-up, in Iceland. He described Atkinson's 40-hour debut as "an exciting result" for the event. Keeler said Hardwick is a hard venue. Matt Dillon, from Hardwick Hall, said it felt "fitting" that women had made their mark there. More than 700 Rasselbock Backyard Ultra events are held worldwide each year. - [World Athletics cuts Olympic marathon fields to 70 for LA 2028](https://filmmyrun.com/news/world-athletics-cuts-olympic-marathon-fields-to-70-for-la-2028): News World Athletics cuts Olympic marathon fields to 70 for LA 2028 World Athletics cuts Olympic marathon fields to 70 for LA 2028 22 October 2026 Photo: Kevin Morris / Canadian Running World Athletics has made the Olympic marathon harder to reach. Under the qualification system for LA 2028, announced on Wednesday, the men's and women's fields each drop from 80 places to 70. That removes 20 places in all. A top-five finish at the London Marathon, or at another Platinum Label race, will count towards a place. The qualification window opens on 1 November and runs until 30 April 2028. The qualifying times will not be published until December. They are expected to mirror the standards for the 2027 World Championships, which are 2:06:00 for men and 2:23:20 for women. Estimates for the Olympic marks sit nearer 2:07 and 2:25. They could still end up tougher, given how quickly the sport is getting faster. Entry standards will be set so that 40 per cent of each field qualifies on time. The other 60 per cent will come through the World Athletics World Rankings. If more athletes hit the standard than there are places, the best performances take priority. A qualifying time is therefore no guarantee. World Athletics figures show 89 men under 2:06 and 82 women under 2:23 so far in 2026. Each nation may send no more than three men and three women. Top-five finishers at the Platinum Label marathons will be treated as having met the standard. Those races are London, Berlin, Boston, Chicago, New York City and Tokyo. Progress can be followed on the Road to LA online tracker. On 19 March 2028 the top 55 in each list become safe and cannot be displaced. The last 15 places will be filled on ranking criteria, including times and finishing position. National Olympic Committees will also have more freedom to hand quota places to athletes who have not otherwise qualified. To be eligible, a runner must have run 2:11 for men or 2:29 for women during the window. Any such swaps must be completed by 30 April 2028. That rule could matter most in the United States. The US Olympic Trials are set for 25 March 2028, six days after the rankings cut-off. Three American athletes have already gone under 2:06 since the start of 2026. If American places are secured by 19 March, the national committee could use reallocation to give them to the top three at the trials, even to runners without the standard. The same approach could apply to the women's team. Originally reported in Canadian Running
- [BYU women move to No. 1 after beating NC State at Pre-Nationals](https://filmmyrun.com/news/byu-women-move-to-no-1-after-beating-nc-state-at-pre-nationals): News BYU women move to No. 1 after beating NC State at Pre-Nationals BYU women move to No. 1 after beating NC State at Pre-Nationals 22 October 2026 Photo: BYU Athletics - Official Athletics Website - BYU Cougars BYU's women have taken over at the top of the US college cross-country rankings. Taylor Rohatinsky finished ninth in her first race of the season. Jenna Hutchins and Karrie Baloga were also among the Cougars' best placed runners, as were Lexi Goff-Thompson and Taylor Lovell. Zariel Macchia and Nelah Roberts also came home inside the top 30, giving BYU seven runners there. The team raced without Jane Hedengren, an NCAA All-American, and are still unbeaten this season.
