- [Kipchoge wins Melbourne Marathon in course record at 41](https://filmmyrun.com/news/kipchoge-wins-melbourne-marathon-in-course-record-at-41): News Kipchoge wins Melbourne Marathon in course record at 41 Kipchoge wins Melbourne Marathon in course record at 41 11 October 2026 Eliud Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon on Sunday 11 October in a course record 2:09:10. The 41-year-old Kenyan broke clear inside the final 10 kilometres of the 42.2km race and finished inside the Melbourne Cricket Ground, two seconds inside the previous course best. It was his first marathon victory since Berlin in 2023 and the third leg of his world tour, in which he plans to run a marathon on every continent, including Antarctica. He beat Australian Thomas Do Canto into second place (2:10:35), with fellow Australian Reece Edwards third in 2:15:57. In the women's race, New Zealand's Camille French won in 2:28:25, 23 seconds ahead of Australia's Sinead Diver. Kipchoge said afterwards that his body was still peaking. "I believe that my body is still peaking — still able to compete with the next generation," he said. "The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the gen Zs." He spent more than half an hour after the finish celebrating with fans along the MCG boundary fence, and noted the stadium had hosted the start and finish of the marathon at the 1956 Olympics, 70 years ago. The win answers questions that have followed Kipchoge since ninth place at the 2025 Sydney Marathon, his only previous race in Australia. He had said in the days before Melbourne that the visit was about more than one race, and used the occasion to celebrate the city's sporting history. Originally reported in The Guardian , ABC News , Olympics.com Back to News
- [London on 17 July as 2027 Diamond League calendar is confirmed](https://filmmyrun.com/news/london-on-17-july-as-2027-diamond-league-calendar-is-confirmed): News London on 17 July as 2027 Diamond League calendar is confirmed London on 17 July as 2027 Diamond League calendar is confirmed 14 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly The Diamond League has confirmed its calendar for 2027. The series, now in its 18th season, will visit 15 cities on four continents between May and August. London is the only British stop, on 17 July. The season opens in Doha on 7 May and closes with a two-day final in Zurich on 25 and 26 August. Doha returns as the opening meeting for the first time since 2023, after three straight seasons began in China. China still follows soon after. Shanghai/Keqiao hosts on 15 May, with a second Chinese meeting a week later on 22 May. Rome is on 27 May, then Rabat in Morocco three days later. Oslo on 3 June and Stockholm on 6 June come next. A gap of almost three weeks follows before Paris on 25 June. Eugene stages the only American meeting on 3 July. Monaco on 9 July and Lausanne on 13 July lead into London four days later. A break of about a month follows, mostly given over to national championships. Silesia on 15 August and Brussels on 20 August are the last chances to collect points. There is one more meeting than in 2026, on a tighter calendar. Athletes in 32 disciplines chase points across 14 series meetings, and the most successful go through to Zurich, where the winners take the Diamond League title in their event. The 2026 final was held in Brussels. The timing matters next year. The World Championships in Beijing run from 10 to 19 September, which leaves a little over two weeks between the final and the first day of the championships. The series says it is broadcast in more than 170 territories and has 6.8 million followers on social media. Originally reported in Athletics Weekly , Wanda Diamond League , FloTrack ,
- [Amos Kipruto runs 2:01:09 and Hawi Feysa defends her title at Chicago Marathon](https://filmmyrun.com/news/amos-kipruto-runs-2-01-09-and-hawi-feysa-defends-her-title-at-chicago): News Amos Kipruto runs 2:01:09 and Hawi Feysa defends her title at Chicago Marathon Amos Kipruto runs 2:01:09 and Hawi Feysa defends her title at Chicago Marathon 12 October 2026 Photo: Metered Exposure / Canadian Running Amos Kipruto won the Chicago Marathon on Sunday 11 October in 2:01:09, the second fastest time ever run on the course. Only Kelvin Kiptum's 2:00:35 from 2023 has been quicker there. Ethiopia's Hawi Feysa defended her women's title in 2:13:33, a big personal best. Britain's David Weir took third in the men's wheelchair race, and Charles Hicks, who recently switched allegiance from Great Britain to the United States, was eighth in 2:05:35. The men's race went out at two-hour pace, with halfway reached in 60:21. Once the pacemakers stepped off, defending champion Jacob Kiplimo of Uganda pushed on. By 30km, reached in 1:25:28, only he and Kipruto were still running at two-hour speed. Near 20 miles the 34-year-old Kenyan broke clear and opened a 12-second gap. Kiplimo, racing for the first time since third in London in April, faded to fourth in 2:04:18. Ethiopia's Tadese Takele was second in 2:02:56 and Milkesa Mengesha third in 2:03:46. Kipruto, who had been third in 2024 and second in 2025, staggered over the line and lay on the ground. He said it had been "win or die" this year. Feysa's race came down to a long duel with Sharon Lokedi of Kenya, the two-time Boston champion, who was making her Chicago debut. The pair were together at 30km in 1:34:16 and still swapping the lead at 25 miles. Feysa finally broke away in the last mile. Lokedi was second in 2:14:07 and Brigid Kosgei third in 2:14:55. Feysa's winning time was quicker than the 2:14:04 Kosgei ran on this course in 2019, which was then the world record. Feysa said she was sure of victory after 35km. Further back, Clayton Young was the first American in seventh in 2:05:23, a personal best run on a torn hamstring. Conner Mantz's American record of 2:04:43 survived. Vinny Mauri was on record pace at 30km but stopped with cramp and finished 10th in 2:06:45. Galen Rupp, now 40, ran 2:06:55 for 11th, a US masters record by more than three minutes. In the women's race Emma Grace Hurley set a US debut record of 2:20:48 in seventh, just behind Australia's Issy Batt-Doyle, whose 2:20:38 was an Australian record. In the wheelchair races, Weir was beaten in a photo finish by Lito Anker of the Netherlands, both timed at 1:30:11. Switzerland's Marcel Hug won his seventh Chicago title in a course record of 1:21:34. His compatriot Catherine Debrunner broke her own world record with 1:33:16, a minute inside the 1:34:16 she set in Berlin in 2023.
- [Engelhard and Beaudoin Rousseau win World Cup uphill race at Mont-Sainte-Anne](https://filmmyrun.com/news/engelhard-and-beaudoin-rousseau-win-world-cup-uphill-race-at-mont-sain): News Engelhard and Beaudoin Rousseau win World Cup uphill race at Mont-Sainte-Anne Engelhard and Beaudoin Rousseau win World Cup uphill race at Mont-Sainte-Anne 12 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly The uphill race at Quebec's Défi des Couleurs went to Nina Engelhard of Germany and the American Meikal Beaudoin Rousseau on Saturday 10 October. It opened the final weekend of the 2026 WMRA World Cup. Scotland's Kirsty Skye Dickson was second in the women's race and finished the season second in the uphill standings. Britain's Edward Hobbs, 21, placed sixth among the men. Canada was hosting the World Cup for the first time. Runners started beside the Jean Larose Falls and ran a quick flat stretch to the resort. Then came a climb of just over 3km up the ski slopes to the finish on the 800m summit of Mont-Sainte-Anne. The sun shone but a cold wind blew across the top. Visa problems stopped several Kenyans from travelling. Richard Atuya, Michael Saoli and Patrick Kipngeno all missed out. Between them they held the three places behind the leader in the men's standings. That left Kenya's Philemon Kiriago , who arrived leading on 304 points, as the man to beat. A pack of about 10 stayed together over the first 2km. Canada's Remi Leroux led once the climb began, with Kiriago close behind. Beaudoin Rousseau made the break that counted and won in 28:55. Leroux was second in 29:04 and Cameron Smith of the USA third in 29:12. Kiriago was fourth and Italy's Andrea Elia fifth. Engelhard is the reigning uphill world champion and took both titles at the 2025 World Championships. After a season disrupted by injury she led from the start and was clear by 2km. Skye Dickson headed the chase on the climb but could not close the gap. Engelhard won by 1min 49sec. Erin Moyer of the USA was third, 12 seconds behind Skye Dickson. France's Nelie Clement came through for fourth and Switzerland's Celine Aebi was fifth. World Cup leader Ruth Gitonga and Miriam Chepkirui were also absent because of visas. Joyce Muthoni Njeru of Kenya finished eighth, which was enough to take the women's uphill title on 134 points. Skye Dickson had 126 and Gitonga 110. In the men's uphill standings Atuya's 142 points were enough for the title. Kiriago finished on 110 and Kipngeno was third with 100. Skye Dickson, who races for Carnethy, was third at the 2025 World Cup final in Slovenia. The final race of the World Cup was set for Sunday 11 October. It was the Classic up-and-down format, 11km long with 800m of climbing.
- [Moab 240 called off after flooding strands 70 at Bridger Jack aid station](https://filmmyrun.com/news/moab-240-called-off-after-flooding-strands-70-at-bridger-jack-aid-stat): News Moab 240 called off after flooding strands 70 at Bridger Jack aid station Moab 240 called off after flooding strands 70 at Bridger Jack aid station 12 October 2026 Photo: Canadian Running The 2026 Moab 240 was halted on Sunday 11 October once storms, floodwater and strong winds left sections of the route too dangerous to run. No runner had officially finished. Aaron Kubala of California led the men with roughly 35 miles left. Ashley Paulson led the women's race. Both were chasing the Triple Crown of 200s this season, having already raced the Tahoe 200 and Bigfoot 200. Kubala won both of those, setting a course record at Tahoe in June. The trouble began on Saturday night. The Bridger Jack aid station sits at about 96 miles (154.4km). A few miles further on, Cottonwood Creek swelled until it could no longer be crossed safely. Runners approaching the crossing turned back, and others were held at the aid station. When the access road became impassable, about 70 runners and volunteers spent the night there. Organisers had sent extra shelters, heaters, propane and food ahead of the storm. Those stranded had heated tents, hot food and drinking water. A helicopter surveyed the area early on Sunday to find a safe way out. The San Juan County Sheriff's Office worked with race staff, and buses began collecting runners at around 11am. By 12:45pm everyone stranded on the route had been brought out. Later that day Destination Trail, which runs the event, ended the whole race. It cited aid station structures blowing away, falling trees, rain and freezing temperatures, with conditions expected to worsen overnight. Anyone still out on the route was asked to halt at whichever aid station came next and stay put until a crew or shuttle arrived. A wind advisory covered southeastern Utah, including Moab and Canyonlands National Park. It warned of south winds of 20 to 30mph and gusts up to 50mph. The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel were bringing flooding to several western states. One pacer, Andrea Christensen, described freezing rain and lightning on the climb of Shea Mountain. The slope there was left exposed by a burn scar from the Babylon Fire, and she called the mud "so slick" on the way up and down. She left the race at mile 115 while her runner carried on. The Moab 240 is a single loop of about 240 miles that starts and finishes in Moab. It crosses desert, canyons and two mountain ranges, with nearly 9,500m of climbing. This year's race began on Friday morning. Runners had 113 hours, with the cut-off at 11pm on Tuesday. The event dates from 2017. Courtney Dauwalter won the first edition outright in 57:55:13. Michael McKnight's 55:49:58 from 2021 is still the overall course record. Organisers apologised to entrants and said the safety of runners, crews and volunteers had to come first.
- [Julie-Anne Staehli takes fourth straight Canadian 5K title in Montreal](https://filmmyrun.com/news/julie-anne-staehli-takes-fourth-straight-canadian-5k-title-in-montreal): News Julie-Anne Staehli takes fourth straight Canadian 5K title in Montreal Julie-Anne Staehli takes fourth straight Canadian 5K title in Montreal 12 October 2026 Photo: Marathon Beneva de Montreal / Canadian Running Julie-Anne Staehli has won the Canadian 5K Championships for a fourth year running. She crossed the line in 15:49 on Saturday in Montreal, where the national road titles were part of the opening days of the Marathon Beneva de Montréal. It was not a comfortable margin. Makenna Fitzgerald, from Cochrane, Alberta, finished just two seconds back in 15:51. Siona Chisholm took third in 15:59. Staehli, who comes from Lucknow, Ontario, represented Canada over 5,000 metres at the Tokyo Olympics. In the men's race the gap was smaller again. Matthew Beaudet and Jean-Simon Desgagnés, both from Quebec, were each given an official time of 14:18. Beaudet was awarded the title. Desgagnés took the runner-up spot, and Liam Donnelly came home two seconds later in 14:20. Beaudet arrived in good form. In May he won the La Clinique du Coureur 5K in Lac-Beauport, Quebec, in 13:49, and later that month ran a 5,000m personal best of 13:32.24 on the track in Brussels. Desgagnés is a steeplechaser who competed for Canada at the Paris 2024 Olympics. He placed eighth at the 2023 World Athletics Championships and won the event at the 2023 Pan American Games. The championships were run alongside the sold-out Sports Experts 5K. That race also hosted the national masters age-group titles over the distance, open to anyone 35 or older. Around 35,000 people took part across the weekend's events. One of 21 cheering stations on the marathon route, at 19.76km, marked the 50th anniversary of the Montreal Olympic Games. Originally reported in Canadian Running , CityNews Montreal Back to News
- [Poskin and Abma win Kodiak 100 Mile as Campbell and Gibson take 50K titles](https://filmmyrun.com/news/poskin-and-abma-win-kodiak-100-mile-as-campbell-and-gibson-take-50k-ti): News Poskin and Abma win Kodiak 100 Mile as Campbell and Gibson take 50K titles Poskin and Abma win Kodiak 100 Mile as Campbell and Gibson take 50K titles 12 October 2026 Photo: UTMB Kodiak 2024 / Hold W Club Cody Poskin won the 100-mile race at Kodiak Ultra Marathons by UTMB in 16:46:21. The race set off from the Rim Nordic Ski Area on Friday afternoon, with the start at 1 p.m., and he reached the finish in the Village at Big Bear Lake, California, at 5:46 a.m. on Saturday. Max Jolliffe made it an all-American men's podium in 18:15:45. Canada's Nichole Abma won the women's 100 miles in 20:43:40 and was 11th overall. Her compatriot Madeline Wighardt was second in 22:05:50. Charlotte Saunders took third in 22:39:31. Across the 50K, 100K and 100-mile races, the men's 100K was settled by the narrowest margin. Spain's José Ángel Fernández Jiménez won in 8:33:09, only 2 minutes and 31 seconds ahead of Gavin Prior. Stephen Kersh was third in 8:59:04. Lotti Brinks of Germany won the women's 100K in 10:15:44. Becca Bramley followed in 10:25:04 and Lindsay Allison in 10:28:08. Cole Campbell took the men's 50K in 3:20:42. - [Engelhard wins both races in Quebec as Kiriago keeps his World Cup title](https://filmmyrun.com/news/engelhard-wins-both-races-in-quebec-as-kiriago-keeps-his-world-cup-tit): News Engelhard wins both races in Quebec as Kiriago keeps his World Cup title Engelhard wins both races in Quebec as Kiriago keeps his World Cup title 13 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Germany's Nina Engelhard won both races at the Défi des Couleurs at Mont-Sainte-Anne in Quebec. Kenya's Philemon Kiriago took Sunday's classic race on 11 October to secure a second successive men's WMRA World Cup title. The weekend was the 2026 World Cup final, and the first final held outside Europe. Scotland's Kirsty Skye Dickson finished third in the women's overall standings with 264 points, after placing second to Engelhard in Saturday's uphill race. The classic course covered about 16km with 1,200m of ascent over three climbs and descents. A galloping horse led both fields up the first climb. The route included L'Escarpée, a hard singletrack climb through the woods. A second, more direct ascent of Mont-Sainte-Anne went straight up a ski slope from 480m to 800m. The women set off five minutes before the men. Engelhard, the 2025 world champion in both uphill and up and down, pulled clear on the first wide climb. She was more than a minute ahead at the first summit and won in 1:20:34. The other places were settled on the fast 4km descent to the finish. France's Nelie Clement had passed Kenya's Joyce Muthoni Njeru on the second climb, but Njeru got back past her with about 3km left. Njeru was second in 1:23:45 and Clement third in 1:23:51. Italy's Arianna Dentis was fourth in 1:27:09, two seconds ahead of America's Erin Moyer. On Saturday Engelhard had won the uphill race in 31:43, finishing 1:49 clear of Dickson, who ran 33:32. Moyer was third in 33:44. Kiriago, fourth in the uphill race, led the men's classic from the start. He was 22 seconds ahead of America's Mason Coppi at the first summit, with Canada's Remi Leroux and Italy's Tiziano Moia next. Coppi chased him all the way down the final descent but finished 19 seconds back in 1:11:43. Kiriago won in 1:11:24. Leroux, the home favourite, was third in 1:13:21. Mexico's Brayan Rodriguez was fourth in 1:15:02 and America's Adam Sjolund fifth in 1:15:06. Britain's Edward Hobbs, 21, was sixth in Saturday's uphill race and among those moving through the field on Sunday. The uphill was won by America's Meikal Beaudoin Rousseau in 28:55, from Leroux in 29:04 and Cameron Smith in 29:12. Kiriago finished the series on 396 points, ahead of Richard Atuya on 290 and Michael Saoli on 223. Ruth Gitonga, the women's leader, could not travel to Canada because of visa problems. Njeru's second place drew her level with Gitonga on 384 points, but Gitonga took the title because she had won more races during the season. Gitonga also topped the women's classic standings, finishing on 150 points. Njeru was next on 92, and Dentis took third place on 84. Saoli won the men's classic standings with 100 points, with Ephantus Njeri and Atuya tied on 92. Atuya won the men's uphill title with 142 points, ahead of Kiriago on 110 and Patrick Kipngeno on 100. Njeru was the women's uphill winner, ending the series on 134 points. Dickson was eight points back in second, and Gitonga's 110 put her third.
- [Julian Moynihan, 19, wins Great Eastern Run with big personal best](https://filmmyrun.com/news/julian-moynihan-19-wins-great-eastern-run-with-big-personal-best): News Julian Moynihan, 19, wins Great Eastern Run with big personal best Julian Moynihan, 19, wins Great Eastern Run with big personal best 13 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Julian Moynihan, a 19-year-old from Ely, won the AEPG Great Eastern Run half-marathon in Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, on Sunday 11 October. He crossed the line in 65:23. That took more than a minute off his previous best. It was a close finish at the front. Josh Holman was second in 65:29, just six seconds back, and he too ran faster than ever before. A Ben Israel took third in 65:36. That put the first three within 13 seconds of each other. - [Boden leads Wallasey AC one-two as Wirral 10K returns to The Dips](https://filmmyrun.com/news/boden-leads-wallasey-ac-one-two-as-wirral-10k-returns-to-the-dips): News Boden leads Wallasey AC one-two as Wirral 10K returns to The Dips Boden leads Wallasey AC one-two as Wirral 10K returns to The Dips 14 October 2026 Photo: RunABC North Wallasey AC clubmates Joseph Boden and Oliver Chadwick took the top two places at the BTR Wirral 10K in New Brighton on Sunday 11 October. Only three seconds separated them. Boden won in 31:59 and Chadwick finished in 32:02. In all, 1,191 runners completed the 13th edition of the Wirral race. The start and finish were back on King's Parade beside The Dips, a spot the race last used in 2021. The revised course was fast, fairly flat and out-and-back along the waterfront. The route went by Fort Perch Rock and the boating lake, then ran along the promenade, heading for Seacombe Ferry and turning back at halfway for New Brighton. Entries had passed 1,000 a month before race day. Every finisher received a medal, a T-shirt and a goody bag. Elliot Clayton of Warrington AC was third man in 33:09. Boden and Chadwick have now shared a run of BTR podiums this year. They were also first and second at the Mersey Tunnel 10K in April. Both were winners again at Port Sunlight in June, Boden over 5K and Chadwick over 10K. The organisers now move on to the Liverpool Santa Dash, a festive 5K, on Sunday 6 December. Originally reported in RunABC North , Wirral Globe , Wirral Today
- [Sifan Hassan pulls out of New York City Marathon after illness](https://filmmyrun.com/news/sifan-hassan-pulls-out-of-new-york-city-marathon-after-illness): News Sifan Hassan pulls out of New York City Marathon after illness Sifan Hassan pulls out of New York City Marathon after illness 15 October 2026 Photo: Kevin Morris / Canadian Running Sifan Hassan will not start the TCS New York City Marathon on 1 November. New York Road Runners confirmed on Wednesday 14 October that the Dutch athlete had scratched after a setback in training. Hassan, 34, said an illness had slowed her preparation and left her short of where she wanted to be. She added that things sometimes simply fail to go to plan. It is the second major marathon in a row she has missed. An Achilles injury ruled her out of London in April. Her last race of any kind was New York a year ago, when she finished sixth in 2:24:43. That was her third marathon of 2025. She had been third in London in 2:19:00 and had won in Sydney in 2:18:22 two months before New York. Hassan won the Olympic marathon in Paris in 2024 and took 5,000m and 10,000m gold at the Tokyo Games. She also holds the women's one-hour world record of 18.93km. Because illness rather than injury stopped her this time, a race later in the year has not been ruled out. Without New York, though, she is unlikely to race in 2026. Fiona O'Keeffe of the United States has also withdrawn. The 28-year-old had surgery on her left hamstring at the Steadman Clinic in Vail last week. A scan at the end of September showed that a partial tear she picked up before Boston had become a full tendon tear. She missed Boston in April too. O'Keeffe was fourth in New York last year in 2:22:49, the fastest time an American woman has run on the five-borough course. The women's race is still led by Kenya's Hellen Obiri, the defending champion. She set the course record of 2:19:51 last year and ran a personal best of 2:15:53 for second in London this spring. Sheila Chepkirui , who won in 2024 in 2:24:35 and was third last year, returns. So does Uruguay's Julia Paternain, the world championship bronze medallist in Tokyo. Weini Kelati, the US half marathon record holder, makes her marathon debut. Benson Kipruto starts on Staten Island as the men's defending champion. He won last year by a fraction of a second from Alexander Mutiso. Former winners Abdi Nageeye and Geoffrey Kamworor are also entered, along with Conner Mantz. Sweden's Andreas Almgren makes his marathon debut. He won the world half marathon title in Copenhagen in September in a European record of 58:06. Originally reported in ,
- [Thomas Nobbs runs 2:08:35 to lead Canadian finishers at Chicago Marathon](https://filmmyrun.com/news/thomas-nobbs-runs-2-08-35-to-lead-canadian-finishers-at-chicago-marath): News Thomas Nobbs runs 2:08:35 to lead Canadian finishers at Chicago Marathon Thomas Nobbs runs 2:08:35 to lead Canadian finishers at Chicago Marathon 16 October 2026 Photo: Christopher Kelsall/Athletics Illustrated / Athletics Illustrated Magazine Thomas Nobbs was the fastest Canadian at the Bank of America Chicago Marathon on Sunday 11 October. The Vancouver runner finished 17th overall in 2:08:35. That moves him up to third on the Canadian all-time marathon list. His previous best was 2:09:25, set in New York's Rockland State Park at the McKirdy MicroTQ. Before the race only Cameron Levins, Ben Preisner and Rory Linkletter had gone faster among Canadian men. Levins holds the national record at 2:05:36. Nobbs had built up to the race on unusually heavy mileage. Sixteen of his last 18 weeks reportedly fell between 208 and 235km. Every marathon he has run so far has been quicker than the one before. He debuted in Toronto in 2:15:22 and then ran 2:12:27 at the Marathon Project in Chandler, Arizona. Ben Flanagan of Kitchener, Ontario was the second Canadian man, 28th overall in 2:12:36. It was only his second marathon and took 3:03 off his debut of 2:15:39. Thomas Fafard , the Olympian from Quebec, was 38th in 2:16:23. That was slower than the 2:10:29 Quebec record he set on his debut in Chandler. Vincent Chénier of Timmins, Ontario ran 2:19:29 and was ninth in the M20-24 category. Craig McMillan of North Vancouver ran 2:22:42 and finished second in the M45-49 age group. The time is a Canadian record for the category. It beats the 2:25:31 Jim Finlayson set in 2018. Rory Linkletter had not been on the elite start list but did turn up in Chicago. He paced the American Dakotah Popehn to a personal best of 2:24:00 and was timed at 2:23:59 himself. Claire Sumner of Calgary led the Canadian women. She was 18th in the women's race in 2:32:21. Katarina Mayer of Toronto followed in 2:39:14, 11th in the W25-29 group. Alyse Gilliver of Brockville, Ontario ran 2:43:31 for seventh in W35-39. Rachel Bowick of Toronto was 18th in W30-34 in 2:47:00. More than 55,000 runners took part in the 48th edition of the race. Kenya's Amos Kipruto won the men's race in 2:01:09, a personal best. Ethiopia's Hawi Feysa defended her women's title in 2:13:33. She broke clear of Kenya's Sharon Lokedi only in the final mile and won by 34 seconds. Originally reported in ,
- [Olympic 800m champion Athing Mu-Nikolayev expecting first child](https://filmmyrun.com/news/olympic-800m-champion-athing-mu-nikolayev-expecting-first-child): News Olympic 800m champion Athing Mu-Nikolayev expecting first child Olympic 800m champion Athing Mu-Nikolayev expecting first child 16 October 2026 Photo: NBC Sports Athing Mu-Nikolayev is expecting her first baby. The American, who won 800m gold at the Tokyo Olympics, shared the news on Instagram on Thursday 15 October. She posted photos of herself in a long white dress in a grassy field, alongside her husband Yegor Nikolayev, a former athlete. The pair held up a sonogram image. Her caption read "Baby on board" and said she could not wait to meet "our little Sunshine". Fans and fellow athletes responded with a flood of congratulations. The couple announced their engagement in September 2024 and married in March 2025. Mu-Nikolayev, now 24, took the Tokyo 800m title in 2021 in 1:55.21. She was 19. She also won gold in the 4x400m relay at those Games. She added the world 800m title in Oregon in 2022. No woman had ever held Olympic and world gold in the same individual athletics discipline at a younger age. She began working with coach Bobby Kersee in 2023. That August she took bronze over 800m at the World Championships in Budapest. Weeks later she won at the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene. She then largely stepped away from racing and later spoke about the mental strain that had come with her success. Her Olympic defence ended at the 2024 US trials in Eugene. She had torn a hamstring about six weeks beforehand. In the final, her legs appeared to touch those of Raevyn Rogers around 200m in. Mu-Nikolayev fell, got back up and finished ninth, in last place. She missed the Paris Games, where the title went to Keely Hodgkinson . Her last race came at the US outdoor championships in Eugene in August 2025. She ran 1:59.79 to finish fourth in her semi-final and did not reach the final. She has since moved to Dallas. Kersee confirmed in December 2025 that the two had parted ways. She appeared in a Nike marketing campaign in April but has not competed this season. Originally reported in LetsRun , NBC Sports ,
- [British-born George Scholey runs 5:09.25 Rubik's Cube mile in Toronto](https://filmmyrun.com/news/british-born-george-scholey-runs-5-09-25-rubik-s-cube-mile-in-toronto): News British-born George Scholey runs 5:09.25 Rubik's Cube mile in Toronto British-born George Scholey runs 5:09.25 Rubik's Cube mile in Toronto 16 October 2026 Photo: Daniel Pham / Canadian Running George Scholey , a 24-year-old originally from the United Kingdom, has set a new Rubik's Cube mile world record. He ran 5:09.25 at Central Tech Stadium in Toronto on Monday 12 October. The previous best was 5:22.75, set in June by Jake Hanson of the United States. The mark still awaits approval from Guinness World Records. The format adds puzzles to a standard track mile. Scholey solved a cube before setting off, then stopped for another after each of the first three laps, making four solves in all. The distance is four laps plus a further 9 metres to reach a full mile. Each cube was handed over fresh, so he had no chance to study it before starting the solve. He averaged nine seconds per solve, with the quickest at about 8.5 seconds. His laps averaged 67 seconds, and he covered the closing 409m in the same time. Scholey said he knew the record was on after 800 metres and his second solve. A practice run six days earlier had shown him how hard it was to solve straight after a fast lap. He described the attempt as "objectively the most difficult" of his records. A certified cube shuffler, witnesses, timers and camera crews were present to record the run for Guinness. Pacers and a crowd of supporters were there too. If ratified, it will be his fourth Guinness title. His earlier records include 6,931 cubes solved in 24 hours in 2022, 500 solved while skateboarding and 520 solved during the 2024 London Marathon. Scholey has been solving cubes for 11 years but has run for only three. He has a marathon best of 2:34. He moved to Toronto in 2025 to work as an associate brand manager for Rubik's Cube. After the Boston Marathon in April he switched to speed work for the mile. His next target is The Marathon Project in Chandler, Arizona, in December, where he hopes to break 2:30. Originally reported in Canadian Running , BBN: Bonkers Broadcasting Network
- [BYU women beat NC State by four points and Syracuse men win Pre-Nationals](https://filmmyrun.com/news/byu-women-beat-nc-state-by-four-points-and-syracuse-men-win-pre-nation): News BYU women beat NC State by four points and Syracuse men win Pre-Nationals BYU women beat NC State by four points and Syracuse men win Pre-Nationals 17 October 2026 Photo: Maddi Sponsel and Kieran IntemannAlthough NCAA All-American / BYU Athletics - Official Athletics Website - BYU Cougars BYU's women beat top-ranked NC State by four points at the Pre-National Invitational in Terre Haute, Indiana, on Friday 16 October. The Cougars scored 84 to the Wolfpack's 88 on a cold morning at the LaVern Gibson Championship Cross Country Course. It was NC State's first cross country defeat in almost two years. Syracuse won the men's title from a field of 44 teams. BYU were without Jane Hedengren, ruled out through illness less than a day before the start. Senior Taylor Rohatinsky, racing for the first time this season, led them home in ninth in 19:33.1 for 6km. Taylor Lovell was 14th in 19:42.7, Lexi Goff-Thompson 18th in 19:50.6 and Karrie Baloga 20th in 19:53.7. Jenna Hutchins completed the scoring in 23rd in 19:57.3. BYU were second at both 2km and 4km before overtaking NC State, and their top seven finished within 27 seconds of each other. Rohatinsky spoke of the chance to "race for each other". The individual race belonged to NC State senior Hannah Gapes . She ran alone at the front and finished in 18:57.6, the fastest women's 6km recorded on the course. The previous mark of 19:14.0 had been set less than a month earlier by Eastern Kentucky's Brighter Jepchumba. Auburn's Faith Chelangat was second in 19:15.5, 18 seconds behind, and Kentucky's Anna Lemirisho third in 19:16.8. NC State were missing Grace Hartman and Sadie Engelhardt, neither of whom has raced in 2026. Notre Dame were third team on 213 points. In the men's race Syracuse scored 115 to beat Villanova on 127 and Notre Dame on 148. Both rivals had their first runner ahead of Syracuse's, but the Orange packed tightly. Connor Ackley was 15th in 23:30.5, followed by Benne Anderson in 16th in 23:32.3, Ben Gabelman in 18th in 23:34.3 and Louis Small in 22nd in 23:39.9. That put nine seconds between their first four. Connell Alford closed their scoring in 44th in 23:57.1. Villanova's Bailey Habler was sixth in 23:23.4 and Notre Dame's Daelen Ackley fourth in 23:20.5. Tulane's Silas Kiptanui took the individual win in 23:17.4, his second victory of the season. Wichita State's Elkana Kipruto was second in 23:18.8 and Nicholas Kipchirchir third in 23:19.8, and their team placed fourth. BYU's women race next at the Big 12 Championships in Stillwater, Oklahoma, in two weeks. The NCAA Championships follow on 21 November. Originally reported in LetsRun ,
- [Puppi and Młynarczyk win Grand Trail des Templiers as women's course record falls](https://filmmyrun.com/news/puppi-and-m-ynarczyk-win-grand-trail-des-templiers-as-women-s-course-r): News Puppi and Młynarczyk win Grand Trail des Templiers as women's course record falls Puppi and Młynarczyk win Grand Trail des Templiers as women's course record falls 19 October 2026 Photo: mytrails.com Francesco Puppi of Italy won the Grand Trail des Templiers in Millau on Sunday 18 October in 6:32:20. That left him one second short of the course record set in 2021 by the British runner Albon. Martyna Młynarczyk of Poland took the women's race in 7:41:18, a new course record. New Zealand's Caitlin Fielder had held the old record of 7:42:24 since her win in 2024. The 32nd edition started from Millau at 5:10am behind two Knights Templar on horseback. The 80.4km loop climbs about 3,430 metres across the limestone plateaus of the Grands Causses. The last 11km hold the steep climbs to Le Cade and La Pouncho, where the race is often settled. Mild autumn weather made for fast running. The winners each took 10,000 euros. Puppi was second here in 2023 and came back for the win. He sat behind the leaders for most of the day as France's Dimitri Morel-Jean went clear, at one point by more than three minutes. Puppi said he lifted the pace at 55km. He was within 30 seconds of Morel-Jean by Massebiau at 69km, then went past and was 5:15 ahead by the top of Le Cade. Morel-Jean, who called it the best race of his life, was second in 6:39:27. Benjamin Roubiol held off Pierre Galbourdin on the last climbs to finish third in 6:44:09, with Galbourdin fourth in 6:45:00. Tracen Knopp of the United States was fifth in 6:46:27. Puppi was runner-up at the Western States 100 in June. Fielder had won the previous two editions but withdrew at the last minute. Młynarczyk led from the opening kilometres and was four minutes clear soon after halfway. She said her plan was to concentrate on her own race. She tired after Massebiau but kept enough in hand. Her win followed a DNF at the Western States 100 after an injury early in the season. She also won the 50K at Trail Alsace by UTMB this year. Alexandra Cassan-Ferrier of France, 37, a former national-team triathlete, was second in 7:46:22 on her first attempt at the course. She closed steadily over the final climbs. Audrey Tanguy was third in 7:51:05 despite severe stomach pain. Anna-Stiina Erkkilä of Finland was fourth in 7:55:29 and Charlotte Mouchet fifth in 8:04:14. Originally reported in iRunFar ,
- [Buze Diriba takes 40 seconds off Amsterdam Marathon course record](https://filmmyrun.com/news/buze-diriba-takes-40-seconds-off-amsterdam-marathon-course-record): News Buze Diriba takes 40 seconds off Amsterdam Marathon course record Buze Diriba takes 40 seconds off Amsterdam Marathon course record 19 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Buze Diriba of Ethiopia broke the women's course record at the Amsterdam Marathon on Sunday 18 October. She ran 2:16:12, which is 40 seconds inside the 2:16:52 set by Yalemzerf Yehualaw in 2024. One report gave her time as 2:16:10. The run was also a Dutch all-comers' record and lifts the 32-year-old to 16th on the world all-time list. Chelsea Stokes was the first British woman home, 16th in 2:31:51. Marc Scott led the British men in 27th in 2:10:14. It was wet and cold at the World Athletics Platinum Label race. Diriba and the defending champion, Aynalem Desta, were at the front from the start. Mestawut Fikir and Meseret Belete ran with them, and the four reached halfway in 1:08:34. Fikir was in trouble by 30km, passed in 1:37:23, and dropped 17 seconds over the following kilometre. Desta and Diriba then left Belete behind. Diriba was 30 seconds clear by 40km and crossed the line almost a minute ahead, with the second half quicker than the first. Desta finished second in a personal best of 2:17:06. Belete was third, also in a personal best, with 2:18:06. Diriba's previous best was 2:19:34, so she has improved by more than three minutes. It was her third marathon under 2:20 in the past 12 months. Lemi Berhanu made it an Ethiopian double in the men's race. He won in 2:03:33, three seconds outside the 2:03:30 course record set last year by Geofry Toroitich Kipchumba. Kipchumba, the defending champion, dropped out not long after halfway, which the lead group reached in 1:02:24. Justus Kangogo of Kenya took up the pace at 30km, passed in 1:28:48, once the pacemakers had stepped aside. Close to the Vondelpark, Nicholas Kipkorir pushed on and Berhanu went with him. They were level at 40km in 1:57:25 before Berhanu broke away. He covered the second half in 1:01:09 and took about a minute off the personal best he ran in January. Kipkorir was second in 2:03:39, a personal best in only his second marathon. Patrick Mosin was third in a personal best of 2:03:58. The first eight men all finished under 2:05, only the third time that has happened in one race. Mikky Keetels was the leading Dutch woman, 14th in 2:30:36. Noah Schutte was the first Dutch man, 25th in 2:09:35, seven seconds outside his best. Originally reported in Athletics Weekly ,
- [Kadar Omar and Hannah Irwin win UK 10-mile titles at the Great South Run](https://filmmyrun.com/news/kadar-omar-and-hannah-irwin-win-uk-10-mile-titles-at-the-great-south-r): News Kadar Omar and Hannah Irwin win UK 10-mile titles at the Great South Run Kadar Omar and Hannah Irwin win UK 10-mile titles at the Great South Run 19 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Kadar Omar and Hannah Irwin are the new UK 10-mile champions. Portsmouth's AJ Bell Great South Run doubled as the national 10-mile championships once more on Sunday 18 October, and the pair took the two elite titles. Omar, of Birchfield Harriers, won the men's race in 47:26. Irwin, of Cambridge & Coleridge AC, took the women's title in 53:34, three seconds clear of the defending champion, Verity Ockenden. It was Omar's first Great South Run win, and the margin was a comfortable one. He finished 24 seconds ahead of Andy Butchart of Central AC, who clocked 47:50 on his first appearance in the race. Butchart has run the 5000m at two Olympic Games and won 5000m silver at this year's UK Championships after coming back from injury. Alex Durant of City of Sheffield & Dearne AC completed the podium in 48:00. Omar was 13 when he fled Ethiopia, travelling with an uncle and his brother. For a time the family lived in a Kenyan refugee camp. In 2017 he lined up in the 5000m at the World Championships in London as part of the Refugee Team. He has since become a British citizen and trains with Birchfield in Birmingham. Last month he became UK half-marathon champion at London's Big Half, running 1:01:51 to beat Jack Rowe, a three-time winner. He credits the sport with having "saved me". The women's race stayed tight for most of the distance before Irwin pulled clear. Ockenden, of Swansea Harriers, crossed the line in 53:37. That was three minutes quicker than her winning time of 56:37 last year, when the weather was wet and windy. Daisy Glover of Framlingham Flyers was third in 54:53. Irwin was born in Cambridge but competes for Northern Ireland, and holds its 10km and half-marathon records. She brought the 10km mark down to 31:32 in Valencia in January. Conditions were fresh but sunny. The mainly flat course began on the seafront near the Avenue de Caen and looped past the Spinnaker Tower, Portsmouth Harbour and the naval base before finishing near Southsea Castle. Olympian Iwan Thomas started the race and then ran it himself. Dale Muffett was the first wheelchair finisher in 51:12. Every finisher went home with a blue and gold medal whose design drew on the Mary Rose, marking Portsmouth's centenary as a city. Organisers said 26,000 runners took part across the weekend, which also included a 5K on Saturday. Neither course record was troubled. Eilish McColgan 's 50:43 from 2021 remains the women's best and a European 10-mile best. The men's record still belongs to Kenya's Joseph Ebuya, who ran 45:15 in 2010.
- [Gabriela DeBues-Stafford breaks 37-year-old Canadian 10K record in Jarrow](https://filmmyrun.com/news/gabriela-debues-stafford-breaks-37-year-old-canadian-10k-record-in-jar): News Gabriela DeBues-Stafford breaks 37-year-old Canadian 10K record in Jarrow Gabriela DeBues-Stafford breaks 37-year-old Canadian 10K record in Jarrow 19 October 2026 Photo: Canadian Running Gabriela DeBues-Stafford has broken a Canadian road 10km record that had lasted 37 years. She did it in England, winning the Jarrow 10K in South Tyneside on Sunday 18 October in 31:37.8. The 31-year-old from Toronto took more than six seconds off the 31:44 run by Lynn Williams in Orlando, Florida, on 11 March 1989. The race is a road event, but it starts and finishes on the track at Monkton Stadium in Hebburn. In between, runners cover two flat laps of the streets of Jarrow. The stadium is the home track of Steve Cram , the British middle-distance runner nicknamed "The Jarrow Arrow" after his home town. DeBues-Stafford also cut more than two minutes from the course record. The previous mark of 34:08 was set by Britain's Sophie Hicks in 2025. Only seven men finished ahead of her. Rose Harvey was second woman in 34:10, placing 29th overall, with Rachel Brown third woman in 34:16 and 30th overall. The men's race went to Omar Ahmed in 29:40. Joseph Niven was second in 29:45 and Anthony Sayers third in 31:00. Williams, who now races as Lynn Kanuka, took bronze over 3,000m at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. Angela Chalmers ran faster at the 1996 Vancouver Sun Run, clocking 31:05. That time never counted as a national record because the course drops overall. The new mark is worth 1159 points on the World Athletics scoring tables. It is the first national record for DeBues-Stafford in more than four years. She now holds eight current Canadian records across eight events, including 3:56.12 for 1500m from the 2019 world championships in Doha. In June she won her third national 5,000m title in a row, her seventh Canadian title in all. She went on to place 14th over 5,000m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Last month she finished ninth in the road mile at the World Athletics Road Running Championships in Copenhagen, with a personal best of 4:30.59. The two-time Olympian was fifth in the 1500m at the Tokyo Games. After spells disrupted by injury in Portland, Glasgow and Victoria, she has settled in Scotland. She is coached by her husband, Rowan. Originally reported in Canadian Running ,
- [Hugo Deck wins longest Diagonale des Fous in 22:54:19 as Ruth Croft takes women's race](https://filmmyrun.com/news/hugo-deck-wins-longest-diagonale-des-fous-in-22-54-19-as-ruth-croft-ta): News Hugo Deck wins longest Diagonale des Fous in 22:54:19 as Ruth Croft takes women's race Hugo Deck wins longest Diagonale des Fous in 22:54:19 as Ruth Croft takes women's race 19 October 2026 Photo: Réunion La 1ère Hugo Deck won the 34th Diagonale des Fous on Réunion on Friday 16 October. He reached La Redoute stadium in Saint-Denis shortly before 9pm in 22:54:19. It was his first attempt at the race. The 26-year-old from the Var ran the longest course in the event's history, 180km with 10,200m of climb from the start in Saint-Pierre. Cilaos was removed from the route this year and more of the hard ground was concentrated in Mafate. His time was four minutes faster than the previous best, set by François D'Haene in 2013 on a route of about 167km. Britain's Tom Evans finished seventh in 26:21:23. He spent a long spell near the front, and Deck described much of the race as a contest with Evans and the Swiss runner Jean-Philippe Tschumi . Robin Juillaguet , also a debutant, was second in 23:51:54 after sitting 13th at Hell-Bourg. The Belgian Jérôme Vanderschaeghe took third in 24:10:35 on his third Diagonale, having been fifth last year. Judicaël Sautron was fourth in 24:38:40. Vincent Esmiol led through the night and into the morning. Deck never dropped out of the top four. He was third at Notre-Dame de la Paix, fourth at Nez-de-Boeuf and second at Hell-Bourg after pulling clear of Tschumi. He finally passed Esmiol on the climb out of Mafate towards Maïdo Tête Dure, more than 1,000m of ascent in the midday heat. He led for the final 57km. He admitted the last descent to La Redoute frightened him because he feared a fall. He called it "a perfect day" after ten years of work, and he is probably the third youngest winner of the race. Ruth Croft won the women's race in 27:13:23 and placed 11th overall. The 37-year-old New Zealander crossed the line at 1:13am on Saturday 17 October, on her first visit to Réunion. She already had UTMB and Western States wins to her name. She worked through the field steadily, from 25th overall at Grand-Place to 21st at the Maïdo and 16th at Chemin Ratinaud. She said the first 65km had been very hard and described it as the toughest race of her life. Alyssa Clark was second in 28:26:53 and Agathe Bes third in 29:05:19. - [WADA chief urges Kenya to take a zero-tolerance line on doping before Nairobi 2029](https://filmmyrun.com/news/wada-chief-urges-kenya-to-take-a-zero-tolerance-line-on-doping-before): News WADA chief urges Kenya to take a zero-tolerance line on doping before Nairobi 2029 WADA chief urges Kenya to take a zero-tolerance line on doping before Nairobi 2029 22 October 2026 Photo: Africanews The head of the World Anti-Doping Agency has told Kenya to aim for zero tolerance of drugs in sport as it prepares to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships. Witold Bańka spoke at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi earlier this month. He said a country that calls itself the Home of Champions must also be clean if it is to stay "respected and credible". He asked for a more determined approach to preventing doping. He also wants Kenya to go after the people who make, smuggle and traffic steroids to athletes. Nairobi will be the first African city to stage the championships. That puts the country's anti-doping system under close international watch. The figures explain the pressure. The Athletics Integrity Unit was set up in 2017, and since then it has sanctioned more than 140 Kenyan athletes, most of them long-distance runners. Only India has more positive cases in total. Kenya remains one of the countries rated at highest risk. Ruth Chepng'etich, the marathon world record holder, was provisionally suspended in 2025 after testing positive for hydrochlorothiazide, a banned diuretic often used to mask other drugs. In 2024 Rhonex Kipruto received a six-year ban and lost his 10K road world record. Lawrence Cherono, who won the Boston and Chicago marathons in 2019, was banned for seven years in the same year. The Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya now tests far more often than it did. It carried out about 1,000 tests a year a few years ago. That rose to 4,300 in 2024-25, and the target is 5,000 by the end of 2026. Testing now covers Kenyan athletes training abroad as well as those at home. It takes place both at competitions and out of competition. This followed a difficult period. In 2024 the government announced a cut of roughly 90 per cent in the agency's funding, and WADA raised concerns. World Athletics is led by Britain's Sebastian Coe , the 1980 and 1984 Olympic 1500m champion. He said he had persuaded the Kenyan government to put more money into the fight against doping. The government has reported a commitment to strengthen the programme over several years. On a visit to Kenya, Coe met President William Ruto. The president restated his commitment to meet the championships' requirements, including those on anti-doping. Kenya's compliance record has also been under review. In 2024 WADA listed 35 fixes it wanted from the national programme. They dealt with the law, the way the agency was run, how much testing it could manage and whether it was free to act on its own. A year later, in September 2025, WADA accused the national agency of breaching the World Anti-Doping Code. That put restrictions at risk, including on Kenya's right to host events. Kenya answered with a corrective action plan. In March 2026 WADA closed the procedure and took the agency off its non-compliance watchlist. Meeting those rules shows that specific failings have been fixed. It does not mean doping has stopped. Kenya has three years to show that cases are investigated properly and that violations are dealt with consistently.
- [USA win Backyard Ultra team worlds as Great Britain set a national record](https://filmmyrun.com/news/united-states-lead-backyard-ultra-team-worlds-as-dave-phillips-wins-uk): News USA win Backyard Ultra team worlds as Great Britain set a national record USA win Backyard Ultra team worlds as Great Britain set a national record 22 October 2026 Photo: Rasselbock Running The United States are the Backyard Ultra world team champions. Belgium, the defending champions and holders of the team record of 1,147 from 2024, were the last nation still running. Racing at Sherwood Pines Forest in Nottinghamshire, hosted by Rasselbock Running, the team set a new national record of 939 yards, fifth in the world. Dave Phillips won the UK race with 90 yards, about 603 km in 90 hours, and is now the UK male distance record holder. His qualifying mark for the team was 65, from the Suffolk Backyard Ultra in June. The hosts described Phillips as "the cool cucumber from day one", steady and consistent throughout. Matthew Blackburn stayed with him until the end and could not finish yard 90, taking the assist on 89. When Phillips completed his victory lap, his first thought was for Blackburn. "Matt was there for me when I was in a dark place and got me out of it," he said, "so I wanted to be there for him and lift him out of it but I couldn't." Matthew Blackburn on the Sherwood Pines loop. He took the assist with 89 yards. Photo: Rasselbock Running Sixty-seven nations started together on 17 October at 12:00 UTC. Each yard measures 6.706 km and starts on the hour. All 15 runners in a team score, one point per completed yard. Spain's race was halted at yard 25 by severe weather and will be run again, so the final classification is still to be confirmed. The top 50 national champions earn places at Big's in Bell Buckle, Tennessee, which starts on 16 October 2027. In Japan, Kengo Takahashi dropped out partway through yard 105, leaving Kazuhiro Kawahata the winner on 105. Christophe Baud won in France with 101 after Julien Pierlot stopped at 100. Nicholas Steel went 94 yards for the United States before stopping. At Kembla Grange in the Illawarra, Dan Camac was the last Australian standing with 87 yards. Jonathan Ash, one of only two Australians to have reached 100, went out over the time limit on his 41st lap with knee bursitis and called it "one of the most painful experiences" of his life. Phil Gore, whose 119 yards was the world record until the Belgians passed it, was injured and helped the team from the sidelines. Poland's last runner was Michał Sitarek on 83 yards. Canada's was Michael Serani on 82, while Ivan Zaborsky finished alone on 81 for the AIN team. Sam Harvey took New Zealand's with 77 and Martin Stiller Germany's with 69. National records fell all over the world, with 18 countries' winners going further than their nation's listed best. Reyna Raymundo added ten yards to Guatemala's record with 43. In Iceland, Gunnar Karlsson pushed the mark up by seven to 69, and Anders Johnsen did the same for Norway with 73.

- [Jane Maus runs 37:07 for women's First Flatiron FKT in Boulder](https://filmmyrun.com/news/jane-maus-runs-37-07-for-women-s-first-flatiron-fkt-in-boulder): News Jane Maus runs 37:07 for women's First Flatiron FKT in Boulder Jane Maus runs 37:07 for women's First Flatiron FKT in Boulder 10 November 2026 American trail runner Jane Maus now holds the women's FKT for the First Flatiron in Boulder, Colorado. On 5 November she completed the route in 37:07. That is 3:59 quicker than the 41:06 recorded by Bailee Mulholland in November 2022. The Flatirons are steep, tilted slabs of sandstone on the eastern flank of Green Mountain. The five main ones are numbered First to Fifth from north to south. Maus climbed the Direct East Face, graded 5.6, as part of a 3.9km (2.4-mile) round trip from Chautauqua Park with about 457m of ascent. She went solo and unsupported, using no ropes or climbing protection. For a long time the First Flatiron was a climb she steered clear of, despite seeing it from town every day. She first went up it in March 2025 with Boulder climber James Lucas and returned a few more times before deciding the risk was not worth it. This year her partner Victor Medeiros and his friends coaxed her back. An injury kept her from running for much of the summer, so she spent far more time on the rock. A time trial three weeks earlier produced 41:53, an effort she said felt like "full gas". On the day her aim was simply to beat Mulholland's mark, with sub-40 minutes as a stretch target. She credited the gap to treating Thursday as a proper record attempt rather than a test. Kyle Richardson, who holds the men's FKT on the route, was there to take photographs, along with Medeiros and other friends. Maus thinks the record can come down by another couple of minutes, mainly through a cleaner line and quicker down-climbing. She also believes a handful of other women have the mix of running speed and climbing skill to go faster. Originally from Salt Lake City, she took up technical scrambling around 2016 and moved to Boulder two and a half years ago. She was seventh in the short trail race at the 2025 Trail World Championships in Spain and set the women's Grand Teton FKT of 3:45:34 that year. In 2026 she won the Black Canyon Ultras 50K in 3:47:04. Originally reported in iRunFar , guide.theultraminute.com
- [World Athletics ratifies Josh Kerr's 3:42.66 mile world record](https://filmmyrun.com/news/world-athletics-ratifies-josh-kerr-s-3-42-66-mile-world-record): News World Athletics ratifies Josh Kerr's 3:42.66 mile world record World Athletics ratifies Josh Kerr's 3:42.66 mile world record 10 November 2026 Photo: World Athletics / Canadian Running Josh Kerr 's mile world record is now official. On Monday 9 November, World Athletics confirmed it had ratified the 3:42.66 the British runner set at the Novuna London Athletics Meet on 18 July. The meeting was a Diamond League fixture. The time took 0.47 seconds off the 3:43.13 run by Morocco's Hicham El Guerrouj in Rome on 7 July 1999. That mark had lasted 27 years and was one of the oldest records on the track. Around 60,000 spectators were in the stadium in London to see it fall. Kerr had pacemakers for the early laps. He went through 400m in 55.3 and 800m in 1:51.1, then reached 1,200m in 2:46.39. He passed 1,500m in 3:27.62. That split was quicker than his own British record for the distance, so the run also produced a new national mark. World Athletics ratified three other world records in the same announcement, all set in Buenos Aires and Zurich in August. Kerr's was the first of the four to be run. - [Merijn Geerts and Ivo Steyaert run 124 yards together for new backyard ultra world best](https://filmmyrun.com/news/merijn-geerts-and-ivo-steyaert-run-124-yards-together-for-new-backyard): News Merijn Geerts and Ivo Steyaert run 124 yards together for new backyard ultra world best Merijn Geerts and Ivo Steyaert run 124 yards together for new backyard ultra world best 22 October 2026 Photo: Jacob Zocherman / iRunFar Merijn Geerts and Ivo Steyaert have pushed the backyard ultra world best out to 124 yards. The Belgian pair ran every lap together at the Backyard Ultra World Team Championships in Retie and stopped together after 831.5km. That is five laps and 33.5km beyond the old mark. Phil Gore ran his 119 in rural Queensland in 2025, at Dead Cow Gully. Racing began at 14:00 local time on Saturday 17 October. Each yard is a 6.706km loop that must be finished inside the hour, with the next one starting on the hour. Geerts, 52, and Steyaert, 56, passed Gore's mark when they completed their 120th lap at 14:00 on Thursday. They carried on for four more hours and finished the 124th at 17:57. The course had its own wobble. Just before lap 117 the inflatable arch at the finish deflated and spectators held it up so the race could go on. Neither man was declared the winner. Under the rules the last runner must complete a full lap after the assist, the second-to-last runner, has dropped. If the final two both retire on the same lap, nobody wins. The pair chose not to start lap 125, as they had planned to finish side by side. It is a familiar finish for them. In 2022 they stopped together after 101 yards, the first runners to pass 100 laps. In 2024 they shared a 110-yard world best with their teammate Frank Gielen . In October 2025 Steyaert was runner-up at the individual world championship with 113 yards. The United States won the team title. Their 15 runners totalled 1,120 yards between them, and the last of them out was Mark Dowdle , who stopped after 107 yards with Jon Noll as his assist. Australia were second on 1,069, with Dan Camac their final runner at 87 yards. Gore was missing from their team after an injury. Belgium, the defending champions, took third on 1,058, and the 248 yards from Geerts and Steyaert lifted them above Japan, fourth on 1,038. Canada were ninth with 830, a national best, led by Michael Serani on 82 yards. Originally reported in iRunFar ,
- [Former Tokyo Marathon winner Ruti Aga banned for six years after forged prescription](https://filmmyrun.com/news/former-tokyo-marathon-winner-ruti-aga-banned-for-six-years-after-forge): News Former Tokyo Marathon winner Ruti Aga banned for six years after forged prescription Former Tokyo Marathon winner Ruti Aga banned for six years after forged prescription 23 October 2026 Photo: Kevin Morris / Canadian Running The Athletics Integrity Unit has banned Ruti Aga for six years. The Ethiopian, 32, won the Tokyo Marathon in 2019. The AIU announced the sanction on 22 October. It covers a positive test for methylprednisolone and a separate charge of tampering. The ban runs from 15 March 2026. The sample was taken at the Meishan Renshou Half Marathon on 15 March. Aga had taken victory at the Chinese race in 1:08:04. Methylprednisolone is a glucocorticoid. The WADA Prohibited List bans it in competition when it is given by injection, orally or rectally. The positive test carried a two-year sanction. Tampering added four more years. Aga said the drug had been used to treat a knee injury. The prescription she supplied named a clinic that does not exist. The "doctor" who wrote it was a relative with no medical registration. Questioned by the AIU, the relative said they had used an old prescription pad from a previous employer. That clinic said the relative had never worked there and that the prescription did not come from it. The AIU's investigation, with help from the Ethiopian Anti-Doping Authority, found the document had been forged. The tampering charge relates to false information Aga gave AIU investigators in an interview on 21 April, and to a "forged/manipulated document" she produced on 4 May. She was provisionally suspended on 17 September. When the AIU put the forgery evidence to her she did not reply, and the charges were decided without a hearing. AIU chief executive Brett Clothier said the case showed that "attempts to cheat will be exposed". Her Tokyo win in 2019 came in 2:20:40. Before that she was third in Berlin in 2016, then second in Berlin in 2017 and 2018 and second in Tokyo in 2018. She was also third at the 2019 New York City Marathon. She won the past two editions of the Xiamen Marathon, a World Athletics Platinum Label race. The second of those wins came on 11 January this year in 2:22:45. - [Kat Clewley runs 100 km backwards in 15:29:01 on a Hamilton track](https://filmmyrun.com/news/kat-clewley-runs-100-km-backwards-in-15-29-01-on-a-hamilton-track): News Kat Clewley runs 100 km backwards in 15:29:01 on a Hamilton track Kat Clewley runs 100 km backwards in 15:29:01 on a Hamilton track 23 October 2026 Photo: courtesy Kat Clewley / Canadian Running Kat Clewley has run 100 km backwards in 15:29:01. She did it on Saturday 17 October at Hamilton's Ray Lewis Track and Field Centre in Ontario. The time is now awaiting verification by Guinness World Records. The distance took 250 laps of the track. Clewley used lanes one and two rather than sticking to the inside lane, so that she would cover the full 100 km. Her Garmin logged more than 104 km by the end of the day, once trips to the toilet and stops to greet supporters were added. She puts the number of toilet stops at about 50. She took six pairs of ASICS Superblast to the track, changed shoes seven times and finished in the pair she started in. She fuelled on peanut butter and jam sandwiches, pizza, chips and pastries. Clewley took up retro running in the summer of 2015. She had turned round on a run to keep an eye on her dog, Vanilla, a giant schnauzer, and found she enjoyed going backwards. Later that year she ran the Road2Hope Marathon in Hamilton in reverse in 4:48:42. In 2016 she won four gold medals at the Retro Running World Championships in Essen, Germany. She went back to Road2Hope in 2017 and lowered her time to 4:26:06, which still stands as the women's retro marathon record. Neither marathon was recognised by Guinness. On both occasions the camera filming her ran out of battery before the run could be properly documented. The 100 km attempt was partly a second go at the record books. Clewley, a former professional footballer, has also finished 14 100-mile races and two Ironmans. She stopped racing backwards when a fall in a reverse half marathon on the road left her with a broken wrist. Covid, and then losing both her mother and her grandmother, kept her out of the sport for longer. Her training fitted around work as a group fitness instructor for the YMCA and the City of Hamilton. She teaches around 20 classes a week and added two 30-minute backward sessions, with her longest runs on Sunday mornings from 6am. "I just like to move," she said. Local runners were invited to join her on the track during the day. Family and friends ran the last 10 laps with her. The attempt raised money for the Good Shepherd's Steps to Health programme, which runs free exercise, nutrition and cooking sessions for adults in the city who have a mental health diagnosis. The fundraiser passed its CA$6,200 target and is open to donations until 31 October. Originally reported in Canadian Running ,
- [Baystate Marathon winners lose Olympic Trials qualifiers over missing USATF sanction](https://filmmyrun.com/news/baystate-marathon-winners-lose-olympic-trials-qualifiers-over-missing): News Baystate Marathon winners lose Olympic Trials qualifiers over missing USATF sanction Baystate Marathon winners lose Olympic Trials qualifiers over missing USATF sanction 23 October 2026 Photo: Runner's World Spencer Friske and Caitlin McGinley both won the Baystate Marathon in Lowell, Massachusetts, on 18 October inside the qualifying standards for the 2028 US Olympic Marathon Trials. A day later they were told the times would not count. The course was certified by USA Track & Field, but the race itself held no USATF sanction. Friske, 32, from Boston, won the men's race in 2:15:04 (one report gives 2:15:05), more than five minutes clear and nearly three minutes inside his previous best. The men's standard is 2:16. McGinley, 29, from Coatesville, Pennsylvania, took the women's race in a personal best of 2:36:08 against a standard of 2:37. She had also won Baystate a year earlier, in 2:37:12, missing the mark by 12 seconds. Both had been heading for St. Louis in 2028 and will probably now need another qualifier. The distinction is a fine one. Certification means the course has been measured accurately, with a drop of no more than 3.3 metres per kilometre. Sanctioning confirms that the event follows competition rules, safety requirements and proper event management. USATF's Trials rules require both. Its database shows Baystate holding a sanction from 2017 to 2020 but not since. For a field the size of this year's 2,385 finishers across the marathon and half marathon, a sanction would have cost about $2,000. USATF spokesperson Jay Holder said the federation had tried to make the rule clear to race directors and Trials hopefuls but would now step up those efforts. He said it did not want hard work to "end in disappointment". He could not explain how Annie Heffernan had been eligible after qualifying for the 2024 Trials at Baystate in 2023. Race director Glenn Stewart, 76, said he could not yet comment on the 2026 race. He added that making the event eligible for qualifying times was his responsibility alone. There is a recent precedent. Tessa Barrett ran 2:34:08 at the unsanctioned Marine Corps Marathon in 2025, saw the time rejected, and later qualified at the California International Marathon. Marine Corps has since secured a sanction for its race on 25 October. Friske and McGinley declined interviews beyond thanking the organisers. Baystate remains popular with Boston Marathon hopefuls, since Boston qualifying requires only a certified course. Athletics Canada is bringing in a framework from 1 January 2027 that will require races to hold provincial sanction before results count towards rankings, records and qualifying standards. - [Geoff Wightman recruits four young women for new training group through Instagram](https://filmmyrun.com/news/geoff-wightman-recruits-four-young-women-for-new-training-group-throug): News Geoff Wightman recruits four young women for new training group through Instagram Geoff Wightman recruits four young women for new training group through Instagram 23 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Geoff Wightman has a new training group. - [Steyaert and Geerts share 124-yard backyard world record as USA take team title](https://filmmyrun.com/news/steyaert-and-geerts-share-124-yard-backyard-world-record-as-usa-take-t): News Steyaert and Geerts share 124-yard backyard world record as USA take team title Steyaert and Geerts share 124-yard backyard world record as USA take team title 23 October 2026 Photo: Canadian Running Magazine Belgian pair Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts ran 124 yards each at the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, a new world record they will share. They covered about 831km in 124 hours in Retie, Belgium. Neither started yard 125, so the race ended at around 6pm on Thursday. The record still needs official confirmation from Big's Backyard Ultra. The format is unforgiving. Runners set off on a 6.706km loop at the start of every hour and must be back on the line when the next hour begins. In the team event, each nation races on its own course at the same time, and the yards of all 15 runners are added together. This year 990 runners from 67 nations took part. The two Belgians ran every yard side by side. Geerts is 52 and Steyaert 56. They equalled the previous best of 119 at about 1pm on Thursday, went past it an hour later and kept going for four more. The old mark belonged to Australia's Phil Gore. He set it last year on home soil in Queensland, at the Dead Cow Gully Backyard Ultra. Their final loop took 57:12, slower than the 56:20 they ran on yard 120. Because neither finished a loop alone, Belgium has no national winner. The pair had stopped together before, after 101 yards in 2022 and after 110 in 2024. The record did not bring the title. The USA won with 1,120 yards, racing at Bell Buckle in Tennessee. Mark Dowdle was their last runner, completing yard 107 alone, roughly 717km. Jon Noll stopped one yard earlier on 106. It is the second American team title after 2022, and the second-highest team total in the championship's history. Belgium's record of 1,147 from 2024 still stands. Australia were second on 1,069 yards at Kembla Grange in the Illawarra. Their team was out after yard 87, when Dan Camac finished as the last Australian. Gore missed the event through injury. Belgium took bronze on 1,058, overtaking Japan, who finished fourth on 1,038. To win, Steyaert and Geerts would have needed to reach yard 156. Further down the table, Canada were ninth with 830 yards, a national best, led by Michael Serani on 82. Germany finished 15th on 620, their highest total, with Martin Stiller managing 69. At 124 yards, this was the longest edition of the team championship so far. Originally reported in ,
- [Peres Jepchirchir provisionally suspended after EPO finding in sample taken before Sydney win](https://filmmyrun.com/news/peres-jepchirchir-provisionally-suspended-after-epo-finding-in-sample): News Peres Jepchirchir provisionally suspended after EPO finding in sample taken before Sydney win Peres Jepchirchir provisionally suspended after EPO finding in sample taken before Sydney win 24 October 2026 Photo: Sydney Marathon / Canadian Running Peres Jepchirchir , the Olympic and world marathon champion and a former London Marathon winner, is under a provisional suspension imposed by the Athletics Integrity Unit. The AIU announced on 23 October that an out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya had returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO. The sample was taken before the 33-year-old won the Sydney Marathon on 30 August. Sydney was her first race of 2026. She had pulled out of the London Marathon earlier in the year with an injury. She won in 2:18:31, more than three minutes clear of fellow Kenyan Irene Chepet Cheptai in 2:22:11. Shure Demise was third in 2:22:33. Sydney became the seventh of the world marathon majors in 2025. The suspension is not a finding of guilt. Jepchirchir can ask for her B sample to be analysed. The case will then either lead to a charge or be closed. She cannot race while it is unresolved. If she is sanctioned she could have to give up her Sydney prize of AUD$30,000. An admission could take a year off any ban. EPO is a hormone made in the kidneys that raises the number of red blood cells, and synthetic forms are banned. Her Olympic title came at the delayed Tokyo Games, where she ran 2:27:20. Brigid Kosgei took silver in 2:27:36 and Molly Seidel bronze in 2:27:46. She won New York later that year in 2:22:39 and Boston in 2022 in 2:21:02. In London in 2024 she ran 2:16:16, a women-only world record since lowered to 2:15:41 by Tigist Assefa. She returned to Tokyo to win the world title in September 2025. Three months later she ran 2:14:43 for second in Valencia, which puts her ninth on the all-time list. Over the half marathon she set world records four times, once in 2017 and three times in 2020. Gianni Demadonna, listed by World Athletics as her athlete representative, said he felt "terrible about what happened". He added that athletes who use performance-enhancing drugs should be disqualified. The case adds to a long list of Kenyan doping cases. More than 140 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned since 2017. The 2016 Olympic marathon champion, Jemima Sumgong, is serving an eight-year ban for EPO. Nairobi is due to stage the World Athletics Championships in 2029. Originally reported in Canadian Running ,
- [UK Athletics names 62 athletes for lottery funding as Jade O’Dowda moves up and Marc Scott drops off](https://filmmyrun.com/news/uk-athletics-names-62-athletes-for-lottery-funding-as-jade-o-dowda-mov): News UK Athletics names 62 athletes for lottery funding as Jade O’Dowda moves up and Marc Scott drops off UK Athletics names 62 athletes for lottery funding as Jade O’Dowda moves up and Marc Scott drops off 24 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly UK Athletics has nominated 62 British athletes for its Olympic World Class Programme for 2026-27. The money comes from the National Lottery via UK Sport, and the target is the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 and beyond. Keely Hodgkinson and Josh Kerr lead the list. Heptathlete Jade O’Dowda moves up to the top tier, and 10 athletes join for the first time. The podium level again has 21 names, including Dina Asher-Smith, Matthew Hudson-Smith, Laura Muir and Jake Wightman . Emile Cairess, coached by Renato Canova, is also there. Marcia Sey, Jake Minshall and Stephen Mackenzie are among the 10 newcomers at confirmation level. The other seven are Kimani Jack, Owen Heard, Sam Bennett, Arlo Ludewick, Abbie Donnelly, Charlotte Henrich and Joel Clarke-Khan. Calli Hauger-Thackery and Patrick Dever are also at that level. Revee Walcott-Nolan, Jess Warner-Judd and Alastair Chalmers have come off the confirmation list. Hannah Kelly and Bianca Williams have gone from the relay group, while Lee Thompson stays at relay confirmation. Ben Jefferies is new on a Relay Support Package, which carries no Athlete Performance Award. Those on the programme get competition opportunities, training camps and help from the governing body's performance, sports science and medical staff. Many can also receive an Athlete Performance Award towards living and sporting costs. Every nomination still has to be ratified by UK Sport, and each athlete must sign an agreement with UK Athletics. Paula Dunn, the performance director, said the group showed the "strength and depth" of British athletics, with established medallists alongside a younger generation. She thanked UK Sport and the National Lottery for their investment. To those left out, she acknowledged the work they had put in and said development "looks different for everyone".
- [Helsinki to stage 2030 European Athletics Championships for a record fourth time](https://filmmyrun.com/news/helsinki-to-stage-2030-european-athletics-championships-for-a-record-f): News Helsinki to stage 2030 European Athletics Championships for a record fourth time Helsinki to stage 2030 European Athletics Championships for a record fourth time 24 October 2026 Photo: Athletics Weekly Helsinki will host the 2030 European Athletics Championships. The Finnish capital was chosen ahead of Brussels at a meeting of the European Athletics executive board in Lausanne on Thursday 22 October. Both cities presented to the board in the final stage of bidding. Zurich had also been expected to bid but withdrew before the decision. It will be the fourth time Helsinki has staged the championships, after 1971, 1994 and 2012. No other city has hosted them four times since the first edition in 1934. The city also held the World Championships in 1983 and 2005. The 2030 event will again use the Olympic Stadium, which reopened in 2020 after an extensive renovation. The championships will run for a week in August 2030, with seven evening sessions and five morning sessions. Exact dates are due to be fixed over the winter with European Athletics and broadcasters. Public events linked to the championships will run over two weeks. Tickets go on sale in Finland in 2027, with home fans and the country's 500 athletics clubs given priority. International sales could open in June 2028, after the European Championships in Poland. Harri Aalto, general secretary of the Finnish Athletics Federation (SUL), said the bid rested on the modernised stadium and a compact city-centre plan that kept shuttle bus use to a minimum. He added that no major new investment would be needed. Federation president Riikka Pakarinen said the decision rewarded a three-year bid. Deputy Mayor Paavo Arhinmäki argued that the northern climate suits top performances, calling Helsinki "a cool city". European Athletics president Dobromir Karamarinov said Helsinki holds "an outstanding place" in the history of the sport. Chief executive Christian Milz pointed to strong Finnish television audiences for the 2026 championships. Viewing peaked at 1.3 million for Alisa Vainio's win in the women's marathon on the final day. Originally reported in Athletics Weekly , City of Helsinki ,
- [Belgians Steyaert and Geerts share 124-yard backyard world record as USA take team title](https://filmmyrun.com/news/belgians-steyaert-and-geerts-share-124-yard-backyard-world-record-as-u): News Belgians Steyaert and Geerts share 124-yard backyard world record as USA take team title Belgians Steyaert and Geerts share 124-yard backyard world record as USA take team title 24 October 2026 Photo: Canadian Running Magazine Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts of Belgium have set a new backyard ultra world record. Runners can use any spare minutes to eat, change or sleep, but must be on the line when the next hour begins. National teams race at the same time on their own home courses, and the yards of all 15 runners in each team are added together. The team championship comes round every other year. In the odd years the solo world title is decided instead, at Big's Backyard in Tennessee. The United States won with 1,120 yards. Their last runner, Mark Dowdle , stopped after 107. Australia were second on 1,069 yards, racing at Kembla Grange in the Illawarra region of New South Wales. Dan Camac was their last man standing with 87 laps. Gore was missing from the team after injuring himself during his Project 168 attempt and spent the race helping the other runners. Belgium took bronze with 1,058 yards, only 20 ahead of Japan on 1,038. The 248 yards the two record-breakers ran between them made the difference.
